prior_work.title: SelfCheckGPT: Zero-Resource Black-Box Hallucination Detection for Generative Large Language Models
prior_work.abstract: Generative Large Language Models (LLMs) such as GPT-3 are capable of generating highly fluent responses to a wide variety of user prompts. However, LLMs are known to hallucinate facts and make non-factual statements which can undermine trust in their output. Existing fact-checking approaches either require access to the output probability distribution (which may not be available for systems such as ChatGPT) or external databases that are interfaced via separate, often complex, modules. In this work, we propose "SelfCheckGPT", a simple sampling-based approach that can be used to fact-check the responses of black-box models in a zero-resource fashion, i.e. without an external database. SelfCheckGPT leverages the simple idea that if an LLM has knowledge of a given concept, sampled responses are likely to be similar and contain consistent facts. However, for hallucinated facts, stochastically sampled responses are likely to diverge and contradict one another. We investigate this approach by using GPT-3 to generate passages about individuals from the WikiBio dataset, and manually annotate the factuality of the generated passages. We demonstrate that SelfCheckGPT can: i) detect non-factual and factual sentences; and ii) rank passages in terms of factuality. We compare our approach to several baselines and show that our approach has considerably higher AUC-PR scores in sentence-level hallucination detection and higher correlation scores in passage-level factuality assessment compared to grey-box methods.

prior_work.title: On Faithfulness and Factuality in Abstractive Summarization
prior_work.abstract: It is well known that the standard likelihood training and approximate decoding objectives in neural text generation models lead to less human-like responses for open-ended tasks such as language modeling and story generation. In this paper we have analyzed limitations of these models for abstractive document summarization and found that these models are highly prone to hallucinate content that is unfaithful to the input document. We conducted a large scale human evaluation of several neural abstractive summarization systems to better understand the types of hallucinations they produce. Our human annotators found substantial amounts of hallucinated content in all model generated summaries. However, our analysis does show that pretrained models are better summarizers not only in terms of raw metrics, i.e., ROUGE, but also in generating faithful and factual summaries as evaluated by humans. Furthermore, we show that textual entailment measures better correlate with faithfulness than standard metrics, potentially leading the way to automatic evaluation metrics as well as training and decoding criteria.

prior_work.title: Measuring Massive Multitask Language Understanding
prior_work.abstract: We propose a new test to measure a text model's multitask accuracy. The test covers 57 tasks including elementary mathematics, US history, computer science, law, and more. To attain high accuracy on this test, models must possess extensive world knowledge and problem solving ability. We find that while most recent models have near random-chance accuracy, the very largest GPT-3 model improves over random chance by almost 20 percentage points on average. However, on every one of the 57 tasks, the best models still need substantial improvements before they can reach expert-level accuracy. Models also have lopsided performance and frequently do not know when they are wrong. Worse, they still have near-random accuracy on some socially important subjects such as morality and law. By comprehensively evaluating the breadth and depth of a model's academic and professional understanding, our test can be used to analyze models across many tasks and to identify important shortcomings.

prior_work.title: On Calibration of Modern Neural Networks
prior_work.abstract: Confidence calibration -- the problem of predicting probability estimates representative of the true correctness likelihood -- is important for classification models in many applications. We discover that modern neural networks, unlike those from a decade ago, are poorly calibrated. Through extensive experiments, we observe that depth, width, weight decay, and Batch Normalization are important factors influencing calibration. We evaluate the performance of various post-processing calibration methods on state-of-the-art architectures with image and document classification datasets. Our analysis and experiments not only offer insights into neural network learning, but also provide a simple and straightforward recipe for practical settings: on most datasets, temperature scaling -- a single-parameter variant of Platt Scaling -- is surprisingly effective at calibrating predictions.

prior_work.title: LLaMA: Open and Efficient Foundation Language Models
prior_work.abstract: We introduce LLaMA, a collection of foundation language models ranging from 7B to 65B parameters. We train our models on trillions of tokens, and show that it is possible to train state-of-the-art models using publicly available datasets exclusively, without resorting to proprietary and inaccessible datasets. In particular, LLaMA-13B outperforms GPT-3 (175B) on most benchmarks, and LLaMA-65B is competitive with the best models, Chinchilla-70B and PaLM-540B. We release all our models to the research community.

S0264af612cef.title: DRG-LLaMA: Tuning LLaMA Model to Predict Diagnosis-related Group for Hospitalized Patients
attribution_passages: Abstract In the U.S. inpatient payment system, the Diagnosis-Related Group (DRG) is pivotal, but its assignment process is inefficient. The study introduces DRG-LLaMA, an advanced large language model (LLM) fine-tuned on clinical notes to enhance DRGs assignment. Utilizing LLaMA as the foundational model and optimizing it through Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) on 236,192 MIMIC-IV discharge summaries, our DRG-LLaMA-7B model exhibited a noteworthy macro-averaged F1 score of 0.327, a top-1 prediction accuracy of 52.0%, and a macro-averaged Area Under the Curve (AUC) of 0.986, with a maximum input token length of 512. This model surpassed the performance of prior leading models in DRG prediction, showing a relative improvement of 40.3% and 35.7% in macro-averaged F1 score compared to ClinicalBERT and CAML, respectively. Applied to base DRG and complication or comorbidity (CC)/major complication or comorbidity (MCC) prediction, DRG-LLaMA achieved a top-1 prediction accuracy of 67.8% and 67.5%, respectively. Additionally, our findings indicate that DRG-LLaMA's performance correlates with increased model parameters and input context lengths.

Sc2df5fa36a07.title: On-site calibration procedure and uncertainty contributions on air temperature sensors
attribution_passages: Abstract Due to the increasing demand of climate change studies, traceability of measurements according to the International System of Units (SI) becomes fundamental to establish data quality and comparability in time. With the aim of guaranteeing the traceability, in October 2022, an on-site calibration of three thermometers operated by the Osservatorio meteorologico di Moncalieri was assessed. The calibration by comparison against traceable travelling standards was performed in a transportable thermal chamber manufactured by the Istituto Nazionale di Ricerca Metrologica (INRIM). Results showed that the main uncertainty contributions to the expanded uncertainty were the interpolation method, the chamber inhomogeneity and the repeatability of the sensors under calibration. This current calibration was compared with previous calibration in 2012 (on-site calibration) and in 2016 (laboratory calibration). The comparison analysis evidenced the drift effect on the thermometers and the importance of having an active calibration program to reduce this effect. Regarding the expanded uncertainty, both on-site calibrations presented the same order of magnitude and smaller than the correction values. This paper points out the advantage of performing an on-site calibration: since the calibration involves the same dataloggers and cables in thesame environmental conditions, the calculated calibration curve represents more convincingly the real measurement conditions.

Sf0815f678905.title: Symmetry in stationary and uniformly-rotating solutions of active scalar equations
attribution_passages: In this paper, we study the radial symmetry properties of stationary and uniformly-rotating solutions of the 2D Euler and gSQG equations, both in the smooth setting and the patch setting. For the 2D Euler equation, we show that any smooth stationary solution with compactly supported and nonnegative vorticity must be radial, without any assumptions on the connectedness of the support or the level sets. In the patch setting, for the 2D Euler equation we show that every uniformly-rotating patch $D$ with angular velocity $Ω\leq 0$ or $Ω\geq \frac{1}{2}$ must be radial, where both bounds are sharp. For the gSQG equation we obtain a similar symmetry result for $Ω\leq 0$ or $Ω\geq Ω_α$ (with the bounds being sharp), under the additional assumption that the patch is simply-connected. These results settle several open questions in [T. Hmidi, J. Evol. Equ., 15(4): 801-816, 2015] and [F. de la Hoz, Z. Hassainia, T. Hmidi, and J. Mateu, Anal. PDE, 9(7):1609-1670, 2016] on uniformly-rotating patches. Along the way, we close a question on overdetermined problems for the fractional Laplacian [R. Choksi, R. Neumayer, and I. Topaloglu, Arxiv preprint arXiv:1810.08304, 2018, Remark 1.4], which may be of independent interest. The main new ideas come from a calculus of variations point of view.

S91b7ac5da2a7.title: PowerPulse: Power Energy Chat Model with LLaMA Model Fine-tuned on Chinese and Power Sector Domain Knowledge
attribution_passages: Recently, Large-scale Language Models (LLMs) such as Chat Generative Pre-trained Transformer (ChatGPT) and Generative Pre-trained Transformer 4 (GPT-4) have demonstrated remarkable performance in the general domain. However, Inadaptability in a particular domain have led to hallucination for these LLMs when responding in specific domain contexts. The issue has attracted widespread attention, existing domain-centered fine-tuning efforts have predominantly focused on sectors like medical, financial, and legal, leaving critical areas such as power energy relatively unexplored. To bridge this gap, this paper introduces a novel power energy chat model called PowerPulse. Built upon the open and efficient foundation language models (LLaMA) architecture, PowerPulse is fine-tuned specifically on Chinese Power Sector Domain Knowledge. This work marks the inaugural application of the LLaMA model in the field of power energy. By leveraging pertinent pre-training data and instruction fine-tuning datasets tailored for the power energy domain, the PowerPulse model showcases exceptional performance in tasks such as text generation, summary extraction, and topic classification. Experimental results validate the efficacy of the PowerPulse model, making significant contributions to the advancement of specialized language models in specific domains.

S51c6888a2a72.title: Extending Nirenberg-Spencer's question on holomorphic embeddings to families of holomorphic embeddings
attribution_passages: Nirenberg and Spencer posed the question whether the germ of a compact complex submanifold in a complex manifold is determined by its infinitesimal neighborhood of finite order when the normal bundle is sufficiently positive. To study the problem for a larger class of submanifolds, including free rational curves, we reformulate the question in the setting of families of submanifolds and their infinitesimal neighborhoods. When the submanifolds have no nonzero vector fields, we prove that it is sufficient to consider only first-order neighborhoods to have an affirmative answer to the reformulated question. When the submanifolds do have nonzero vector fields, we obtain an affirmative answer to the question under the additional assumption that submanifolds have certain nice deformation properties, which is applicable to free rational curves. As an application, we obtain a stronger version of the Cartan-Fubini type extension theorem for Fano manifolds of Picard number 1. We also propose a potential application on hyperplane sections of projective K3 surfaces.

Sb4f4e2906c1b.title: Pre/Post-Merger Consistency Test for Gravitational Signals from Binary Neutron Star Mergers
attribution_passages: Gravitational waves from binary neutron star (BNS) mergers can constrain nuclear models, predicting their equation of state (EOS). Matter effects on the inspiral-merger signal are encoded in the multipolar tidal polarizability parameters, whose leading order combination is sufficient to capture, with high accuracy, the key features of the merger waveform. Similar EOS-insensitive relations exist for the post-merger signal and can be used to model the emissions from the remnant. Several works suggested that the appearance of new degrees of freedom in high-density post-merger matter can be inferred by observing a violation of these EOS-insensitive relations. Here, we demonstrate a Bayesian method to test such an EOS-insensitive relation between the tidal polarizability parameters (or any other equivalent parameter) and the dominant post-merger frequency using information from the pre-and-post-merger signal. Technically, the method is similar to the inspiral-merger-ringdown consistency tests of General Relativity with binary black holes. However, differently from the latter, BNS pre/post-merger consistency tests are conceptually less informative and they only address the consistency of the assumed EOS-insensitive relation. Specifically, we discuss how such tests cannot conclusively discriminate between an EOS without respecting such a relation and the appearance of new degrees of freedom (or phase transitions) in high-density matter.

S2547cf5c9dc2.title: SelfCheckGPT: Zero-Resource Black-Box Hallucination Detection for Generative Large Language Models
S2547cf5c9dc2.fulltext_snippet: Generative Large Language Models (LLMs) such as GPT-3 are capable of generating highly fluent responses to a wide variety of user prompts. However, LLMs are known to hallucinate facts and make non-factual statements which can undermine trust in their output. Existing fact-checking approaches either require access to the output probability distribution (which may not be available for systems such as ChatGPT) or external databases that are interfaced via separate, often complex, modules. In this work, we propose "SelfCheckGPT", a simple sampling-based approach that can be used to fact-check the responses of black-box models in a zero-resource fashion, i.e. without an external database. SelfCheckGPT leverages the simple idea that if an LLM has knowledge of a given concept, sampled responses are likely to be similar and contain consistent facts. However, for hallucinated facts, stochastically sampled responses are likely to diverge and contradict one another. We investigate this approach by using GPT-3 to generate passages about individuals from the WikiBio dataset, and manually annotate the factuality of the generated passages. We demonstrate that SelfCheckGPT can: i) detect non-factual and factual sentences; and ii) rank passages in terms of factuality. We compare our approach to several baselines and show that our approach has considerably higher AUC-PR scores in sentence-level hallucination detection and higher correlation scores in passage-level factuality assessment compared to grey-box methods.

Sccacb4399b42.title: On Faithfulness and Factuality in Abstractive Summarization
Sccacb4399b42.fulltext_snippet: It is well known that the standard likelihood training and approximate decoding objectives in neural text generation models lead to less human-like responses for open-ended tasks such as language modeling and story generation. In this paper we have analyzed limitations of these models for abstractive document summarization and found that these models are highly prone to hallucinate content that is unfaithful to the input document. We conducted a large scale human evaluation of several neural abstractive summarization systems to better understand the types of hallucinations they produce. Our human annotators found substantial amounts of hallucinated content in all model generated summaries. However, our analysis does show that pretrained models are better summarizers not only in terms of raw metrics, i.e., ROUGE, but also in generating faithful and factual summaries as evaluated by humans. Furthermore, we show that textual entailment measures better correlate with faithfulness than standard metrics, potentially leading the way to automatic evaluation metrics as well as training and decoding criteria.

S1e54c9085186.title: Measuring Massive Multitask Language Understanding
S1e54c9085186.fulltext_snippet: We propose a new test to measure a text model's multitask accuracy. The test covers 57 tasks including elementary mathematics, US history, computer science, law, and more. To attain high accuracy on this test, models must possess extensive world knowledge and problem solving ability. We find that while most recent models have near random-chance accuracy, the very largest GPT-3 model improves over random chance by almost 20 percentage points on average. However, on every one of the 57 tasks, the best models still need substantial improvements before they can reach expert-level accuracy. Models also have lopsided performance and frequently do not know when they are wrong. Worse, they still have near-random accuracy on some socially important subjects such as morality and law. By comprehensively evaluating the breadth and depth of a model's academic and professional understanding, our test can be used to analyze models across many tasks and to identify important shortcomings.

S2cdc1e54f79b.title: On Calibration of Modern Neural Networks
S2cdc1e54f79b.fulltext_snippet: Confidence calibration -- the problem of predicting probability estimates representative of the true correctness likelihood -- is important for classification models in many applications. We discover that modern neural networks, unlike those from a decade ago, are poorly calibrated. Through extensive experiments, we observe that depth, width, weight decay, and Batch Normalization are important factors influencing calibration. We evaluate the performance of various post-processing calibration methods on state-of-the-art architectures with image and document classification datasets. Our analysis and experiments not only offer insights into neural network learning, but also provide a simple and straightforward recipe for practical settings: on most datasets, temperature scaling -- a single-parameter variant of Platt Scaling -- is surprisingly effective at calibrating predictions.

S3ad17f3a68f7.title: LLaMA: Open and Efficient Foundation Language Models
S3ad17f3a68f7.fulltext_snippet: We introduce LLaMA, a collection of foundation language models ranging from 7B to 65B parameters. We train our models on trillions of tokens, and show that it is possible to train state-of-the-art models using publicly available datasets exclusively, without resorting to proprietary and inaccessible datasets. In particular, LLaMA-13B outperforms GPT-3 (175B) on most benchmarks, and LLaMA-65B is competitive with the best models, Chinchilla-70B and PaLM-540B. We release all our models to the research community.

S0264af612cef.title: DRG-LLaMA: Tuning LLaMA Model to Predict Diagnosis-related Group for Hospitalized Patients
S0264af612cef.fulltext_snippet: Abstract In the U.S. inpatient payment system, the Diagnosis-Related Group (DRG) is pivotal, but its assignment process is inefficient. The study introduces DRG-LLaMA, an advanced large language model (LLM) fine-tuned on clinical notes to enhance DRGs assignment. Utilizing LLaMA as the foundational model and optimizing it through Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) on 236,192 MIMIC-IV discharge summaries, our DRG-LLaMA-7B model exhibited a noteworthy macro-averaged F1 score of 0.327, a top-1 prediction accuracy of 52.0%, and a macro-averaged Area Under the Curve (AUC) of 0.986, with a maximum input token length of 512. This model surpassed the performance of prior leading models in DRG prediction, showing a relative improvement of 40.3% and 35.7% in macro-averaged F1 score compared to ClinicalBERT and CAML, respectively. Applied to base DRG and complication or comorbidity (CC)/major complication or comorbidity (MCC) prediction, DRG-LLaMA achieved a top-1 prediction accuracy of 67.8% and 67.5%, respectively. Additionally, our findings indicate that DRG-LLaMA's performance correlates with increased model parameters and input context lengths.

Sc2df5fa36a07.title: On-site calibration procedure and uncertainty contributions on air temperature sensors
Sc2df5fa36a07.fulltext_snippet: Abstract Due to the increasing demand of climate change studies, traceability of measurements according to the International System of Units (SI) becomes fundamental to establish data quality and comparability in time. With the aim of guaranteeing the traceability, in October 2022, an on-site calibration of three thermometers operated by the Osservatorio meteorologico di Moncalieri was assessed. The calibration by comparison against traceable travelling standards was performed in a transportable thermal chamber manufactured by the Istituto Nazionale di Ricerca Metrologica (INRIM). Results showed that the main uncertainty contributions to the expanded uncertainty were the interpolation method, the chamber inhomogeneity and the repeatability of the sensors under calibration. This current calibration was compared with previous calibration in 2012 (on-site calibration) and in 2016 (laboratory calibration). The comparison analysis evidenced the drift effect on the thermometers and the importance of having an active calibration program to reduce this effect. Regarding the expanded uncertainty, both on-site calibrations presented the same order of magnitude and smaller than the correction values. This paper points out the advantage of performing an on-site calibration: since the calibration involves the same dataloggers and cables in thesame environmental conditions, the calculated calibration curve represents more convincingly the real measurement conditions.

Sd1e95951f808.title: Electricity and Climate Policy Measures: The Unknown Known
Sd1e95951f808.fulltext_snippet: The Thesis focuses on researching the areas of Latvia's electricity policy that are underdeveloped or forgotten within the current electricity policy framework in order to define possible policy improvements from the perspective of achieving climate goals, providing proposals for the review of the National Energy and Climate Plan in 2023. The Thesis provides a comprehensive and systematic analysis of specific electricity policy measures using different methodological approaches, which is finalized by applying theory-based approach to integrate all parts of the research on electricity policy measures into a common result.

Sf0815f678905.title: Symmetry in stationary and uniformly-rotating solutions of active scalar equations
Sf0815f678905.fulltext_snippet: In this paper, we study the radial symmetry properties of stationary and uniformly-rotating solutions of the 2D Euler and gSQG equations, both in the smooth setting and the patch setting. For the 2D Euler equation, we show that any smooth stationary solution with compactly supported and nonnegative vorticity must be radial, without any assumptions on the connectedness of the support or the level sets. In the patch setting, for the 2D Euler equation we show that every uniformly-rotating patch $D$ with angular velocity $Ω\leq 0$ or $Ω\geq \frac{1}{2}$ must be radial, where both bounds are sharp. For the gSQG equation we obtain a similar symmetry result for $Ω\leq 0$ or $Ω\geq Ω_α$ (with the bounds being sharp), under the additional assumption that the patch is simply-connected. These results settle several open questions in [T. Hmidi, J. Evol. Equ., 15(4): 801-816, 2015] and [F. de la Hoz, Z. Hassainia, T. Hmidi, and J. Mateu, Anal. PDE, 9(7):1609-1670, 2016] on uniformly-rotating patches. Along the way, we close a question on overdetermined problems for the fractional Laplacian [R. Choksi, R. Neumayer, and I. Topaloglu, Arxiv preprint arXiv:1810.08304, 2018, Remark 1.4], which may be of independent interest. The main new ideas come from a calculus of variations point of view.

S91b7ac5da2a7.title: PowerPulse: Power Energy Chat Model with LLaMA Model Fine-tuned on Chinese and Power Sector Domain Knowledge
S91b7ac5da2a7.fulltext_snippet: Recently, Large-scale Language Models (LLMs) such as Chat Generative Pre-trained Transformer (ChatGPT) and Generative Pre-trained Transformer 4 (GPT-4) have demonstrated remarkable performance in the general domain. However, Inadaptability in a particular domain have led to hallucination for these LLMs when responding in specific domain contexts. The issue has attracted widespread attention, existing domain-centered fine-tuning efforts have predominantly focused on sectors like medical, financial, and legal, leaving critical areas such as power energy relatively unexplored. To bridge this gap, this paper introduces a novel power energy chat model called PowerPulse. Built upon the open and efficient foundation language models (LLaMA) architecture, PowerPulse is fine-tuned specifically on Chinese Power Sector Domain Knowledge. This work marks the inaugural application of the LLaMA model in the field of power energy. By leveraging pertinent pre-training data and instruction fine-tuning datasets tailored for the power energy domain, the PowerPulse model showcases exceptional performance in tasks such as text generation, summary extraction, and topic classification. Experimental results validate the efficacy of the PowerPulse model, making significant contributions to the advancement of specialized language models in specific domains.

S51c6888a2a72.title: Extending Nirenberg-Spencer's question on holomorphic embeddings to families of holomorphic embeddings
S51c6888a2a72.fulltext_snippet: Nirenberg and Spencer posed the question whether the germ of a compact complex submanifold in a complex manifold is determined by its infinitesimal neighborhood of finite order when the normal bundle is sufficiently positive. To study the problem for a larger class of submanifolds, including free rational curves, we reformulate the question in the setting of families of submanifolds and their infinitesimal neighborhoods. When the submanifolds have no nonzero vector fields, we prove that it is sufficient to consider only first-order neighborhoods to have an affirmative answer to the reformulated question. When the submanifolds do have nonzero vector fields, we obtain an affirmative answer to the question under the additional assumption that submanifolds have certain nice deformation properties, which is applicable to free rational curves. As an application, we obtain a stronger version of the Cartan-Fubini type extension theorem for Fano manifolds of Picard number 1. We also propose a potential application on hyperplane sections of projective K3 surfaces.

draft.title: Teaching Open LLMs to Refuse Unknown Questions via Consistency-Calibrated Active Retrieval
draft.literature_gap: Prior work detects hallucination after generation or measures calibration, but does not provide a training procedure that teaches an open LLM when to refuse under an active-retrieval inference policy. SelfCheckGPT shows sampling consistency can flag unsupported black-box generations; calibration work shows modern neural models are poorly calibrated; MMLU shows models often do not know when they are wrong; LLaMA provides open models suitable for controlled fine-tuning; faithfulness work shows hallucination is pervasive in generation. Missing is a concrete, falsifiable test of whether consistency and retrieval-support signals can be converted into refusal training labels and whether active retrieval plus refusal reduces hallucination on mixed known/unknown question sets without excessive over-refusal.
draft.hypothesis: If a LLaMA-style open model is fine-tuned with refusal labels derived from low sampling consistency and weak retrieval support, and if inference actively retrieves only when uncertainty is high, then the model will refuse a substantially higher fraction of unknown questions and reduce hallucinated answers on a mixed known/unknown QA set, while suffering only a small drop in accuracy on known questions.
draft.method: Use LLaMA-7B/13B as base models. Construct a mixed QA set: (i) known questions from a held-out MMLU subset, (ii) unknown questions created by replacing real entities in MMLU/WikiBio-style prompts with fictitious entities, and (iii) held-out obscure factual questions whose answers are removed from the retrieval corpus. For each training question, sample k=10 answers at temperature 0.7 and compute answer agreement (SelfCheckGPT-style consistency), average token log-probability, and retrieval support from a BM25 index over a Wikipedia subset. Assign a refusal label when consistency is below a threshold and retrieval support is weak or contradictory; assign an answer label otherwise. Fine-tune the base model with LoRA on a mixture of known-answer, unknown-refusal, and retrieval-augmented examples. At inference, use active retrieval: first answer without retrieval; if consistency/calibration uncertainty exceeds a threshold, retrieve passages and re-answer; if retrieval support remains weak, output a refusal. Compare against base model, SelfCheckGPT-threshold refusal, and temperature-calibrated threshold refusal.
draft.minimal_test: Train LoRA adapters on 2,000 known MMLU questions plus 2,000 controlled unknown questions using 2 A100-40GB GPUs for at most 48 GPU-hours. Evaluate on a held-out mixed set of 1,000 known and 1,000 unknown questions. Report risk-coverage curves, unknown-refusal rate, known-answer accuracy, hallucination rate on unknown questions, and expected calibration error. Include a 200-item human check of refused vs answered unknown questions.
draft.decisive_metric: Area under the risk-coverage curve (AURC) on the mixed known/unknown set, where risk is a hallucinated or incorrect answer and coverage is the fraction of questions answered rather than refused; lower AURC is better.
draft.supporting_result: The fine-tuned active-retrieval model reduces AURC by at least 15% relative to the best baseline, refuses at least 70% of unknown questions, keeps known-answer accuracy within 3 percentage points of the base model, and lowers expected calibration error to at most 0.05.
draft.falsifying_result: The method reduces AURC by less than 5% relative to the best baseline, or gains in unknown refusal are accompanied by more than a 10 percentage-point drop in known-answer accuracy, or over-refusal on known questions exceeds 15%.
draft.related_work[1].relation: Provides the sampling-consistency hallucination-detection idea that we convert into refusal training labels.
draft.related_work[2].relation: Motivates calibration thresholds and temperature-scaling baselines for uncertainty-aware refusal.
draft.related_work[3].relation: Documents that models frequently do not know when they are wrong, motivating mixed known/unknown evaluation.
draft.related_work[4].relation: Supplies open LLaMA models enabling controlled LoRA fine-tuning for refusal behavior.
draft.related_work[5].relation: Establishes hallucination and faithfulness concerns that refusal aims to mitigate.
draft.limitations: Controlled fictitious and removed-answer questions may not perfectly represent real-world unknowns; the retrieval corpus is a Wikipedia subset and may itself be incomplete; experiments are limited to LLaMA-7B/13B and LoRA fine-tuning; refusal behavior may be sensitive to threshold choice and prompt format; human evaluation is small; the study is restricted to literature available before 2023-11-15.
draft.resource_plan: Compute: 2 A100-40GB GPUs for at most 48 GPU-hours for LoRA training and evaluation, plus CPU BM25 retrieval. Data: existing MMLU and WikiBio-style prompts, a public Wikipedia subset, and 200 human annotation items. Estimated cost: compute about $700, annotation about $400, contingency $100, total at most $1,200. No proprietary model access is required.

draft.title: Refusal Training Learns What Looks Hard, Not What Is Unknown: Diagnosing and Removing Surface Shortcuts in LLM Abstention
draft.hypothesis: Teaching LLMs to say 'I don't know' (IDK) is assumed to install an instance-level knowledge boundary, but the training signal is confounded: 'unknown' examples are disproportionately rare-entity, unusual-template, and rare-phrasing questions. We hypothesize that most of what IDK fine-tuning learns is a surface-difficulty prior, not instance-level ignorance. This yields three falsifiable predictions after standard refusal SFT: (i) in a logistic decomposition of the refusal decision, entity popularity and template explain far more variance than actual correctness; (ii) within-topic refusal AUROC improves much less than across-topic AUROC (a 'shortcut index' > 0); and (iii) semantically identical paraphrases that differ only in surface rarity flip the refusal decision. If confirmed, the correct fix is to change the geometry of the training signal rather than add more IDK data: matched same-entity, same-template known/unknown pairs with a pairwise ranking loss, plus paraphrase-consistency regularization, so that surface features are constant within a pair and only correctness varies. This is the right setting because it directly tests what refusal training learns and is feasible with public QA data and LoRA on 7B models. Key discriminating prediction: pair training improves within-topic AUROC and reduces paraphrase flips, whereas popularity reweighting alone improves calibration but not surface consistency.
draft.related_work: The teach-to-refuse line is represented by R-Tuning (Zhang et al., 2023/2024), which labels questions unknown via the model's own correctness and fine-tunes on IDK responses, and SelfAware (Yin et al., 2023), which evaluates binary self-knowledge; related uncertainty work includes Kadavath et al. (2022) P(True), Azaria & Mitchell (2023) SAPLMA hidden-state probes, Lin et al. (2022) verbalized uncertainty, Zhou et al. (2023) on uncertainty expressions, Kuhn et al. (2023) semantic entropy, and SelfCheckGPT (Manakul et al., 2023, [S2547cf5c9dc2]) for sampling-based detection. Calibration ([S2cdc1e54f79b]) and faithfulness/factuality analyses ([Sccacb4399b42]) motivate evaluation. These works report aggregate known/unknown discrimination or hallucination detection and implicitly assume refusal training teaches knowledge boundaries. Our proposal differs in treating refusal training as representation learning with a confound: it introduces a refusal-decomposition analysis, topic-stratified train/test splits, and semantically controlled paraphrase/template manipulations to causally isolate surface-prior versus instance-level refusal. The matched-pair contrastive objective follows from this diagnosis and is not equivalent to adding more unknown examples (R-Tuning) or generic augmentation: popularity-reweighted SFT is included as a strong baseline that removes the marginal confound but not within-pair surface invariance, allowing us to separate 'more data balancing' from 'contrastive geometry.'
draft.approach: Refusal fine-tuning is a popular remedy for hallucination: models are trained to answer 'I don't know' on questions they fail. The implicit assumption is that this teaches a model the boundary of its own knowledge. We test that assumption. Because self-labeled unknown questions are disproportionately about rare entities, unusual templates, and rare phrasings, a model can raise IDK accuracy by learning what looks hard rather than what it does not know. We propose three diagnostics: a logistic decomposition of the refusal decision into correctness, entity popularity, and template; topic-stratified train/test generalization comparing within- versus across-topic refusal AUROC; and paraphrase/template manipulations that hold meaning fixed while varying surface rarity, measuring refusal flip rate. We then introduce Matched-Pair Contrastive Refusal Training (MP-CRT), which pairs each unknown question with a same-entity, same-template known question and adds a pairwise margin loss on the refusal score plus paraphrase-consistency regularization. A hidden-state probe predicting correctness lets us ask whether information about ignorance is present but unused by the refusal policy. Experiments with LoRA-tuned Llama-2-7B and Mistral-7B on PopQA, TriviaQA, Natural Questions, and SelfAware measure refusal precision/recall, over-refusal on known-but-rare facts, selective accuracy, hallucination-on-answered, cost-sensitive net utility, within/across-topic AUROC, and paraphrase flip rate. We include popularity-reweighted SFT and sampling-based detectors as baselines. The result is a sharper account of what refusal training actually learns and a simple, affordable fix.
draft.validation: 1) Data and labels: PopQA (entity popularity strata), TriviaQA/NQ subsets, SelfAware. Label KNOWN/UNKNOWN with m=10 samples (pass@10), annotate entity, template, and log-popularity, and verify a stratified sample with human/LLM judges. 2) Refusal decomposition (core diagnostic): LoRA-train standard IDK SFT (R-Tuning style). On held-out data fit a logistic model refusal ~ correctness + log-popularity + template cluster (+ interactions); report standardized coefficients and pseudo-R2. Prediction: popularity/template dominate correctness. 3) Stratified generalization: train on entity split A, test on disjoint split B; report across-topic vs within-topic refusal-vs-correctness AUROC and the shortcut index (difference). 4) Surface invariance: generate 5 paraphrases per question with controlled common/rare vocabulary and template swaps, filter by entailment-based semantic preservation, and measure refusal decision flip rate; compare IDK-SFT to base and to probe-gated refusal. 5) Probe localization: train a linear probe on the prompt's last hidden state to predict correctness; compare within-topic probe AUROC to refusal AUROC to see whether ignorance is represented but unused. 6) Method MP-CRT: build matched pairs (q_known, q_unknown) sharing entity, template, and popularity bucket; loss = IDK-SFT cross-entropy + lambda * max(0, margin - (s(q_unknown) - s(q_known))) on a refusal/answerability score + mu * KL between paraphrase refusal distributions. Baselines: base model, R-Tuning SFT, prompt-only 'say IDK', SelfCheckGPT-style sampling threshold, semantic-entropy threshold, probe-gated refusal, and popularity-reweighted SFT (key confound-removal control). 7) Metrics: refusal precision/recall/F1, over-refusal rate on KNOWN (especially rare-and-known), selective accuracy, hallucination-on-answered (exact match plus NLI/LLM judge), cost-sensitive net utility over a sweep of wrong-answer vs refusal costs, AUROC/AUPRC overall/within/across topic, shortcut index, paraphrase flip rate, and ECE. 8) Ablations: pairs without template matching, ranking-only vs consistency-only, lambda/mu, labels from pass@1 vs pass@10, LoRA rank, and Pythia-1.4B full fine-tuning vs 7B LoRA. All training is LoRA on a single 4xA100 node for a few days.
draft.limitations: The shortcut effect could be real but small; we therefore report effect sizes and the mixture of knowledge-based and surface-based refusal rather than a binary verdict, and include a positive-control subset where instance-level learning should dominate. KNOWN/UNKNOWN labels derived from sampling conflate generation variance with missing knowledge; we mitigate with pass@10, pass@k analyses, judge verification, and label-noise reporting. Entity rarity is partly a legitimate predictor of ignorance, so matched pairs must be equally plausible a priori; we enforce same entity, same template, and balanced popularity and run a pre-registered difficulty check. Paraphrase generation can drift semantically; we validate with entailment checks and report preservation rates. PopQA/TriviaQA popularity and entity tags are noisy. LoRA may underfit the pairwise signal, so we include full fine-tuning of Pythia-1.4B as a check. Popular-entity benchmarks risk pretraining contamination inflating KNOWN labels; we add post-cutoff or synthetic-entity questions as a clean subset. LLM-judge hallucination scoring may be biased; we calibrate it against human annotations. Results are English-only and at modest scale, limiting extrapolation to large proprietary models.

draft.alternative_explanations[1]: Any apparent combined-gate advantage may be explained by answering fewer items rather than by answerability discrimination; matched-coverage random refusal tests this.
draft.alternative_explanations[2]: Any apparent advantage may come from refusing answerable items rather than selectively refusing unsupported or unanswerable items.
draft.alternative_explanations[3]: Self-evaluation may track answer fluency or consistency rather than truth; external correctness and calibration checks test this partially.
draft.alternative_explanations[4]: Threshold transfer failure may produce apparent null or harmful results even if development signal is informative.
draft.alternative_explanations[5]: Source reference-label errors or exact-match scoring artifacts may create apparent unsupported answers that are not model errors.
draft.analysis.aggregation: Compute correctness and gate decisions at the item level. For each condition and repetition, U = unsupported answered items / answered items; coverage = answered items / all held-out items; appropriate refusal = refused unanswerable items / unanswerable items; answerable-item refusal = refused answerable items / answerable items. Average across the five repetitions within item for paired comparisons and report repetition range; do not treat repetitions or K samples as independent. Aggregate within pre-specified stratum and overall; report stratum-specific results separately rather than pooling across unavailable or misaligned strata.
draft.analysis.estimand: Difference in unsupported-answer rate U among answered held-out items at matched answer coverage c*=0.80 between the combined consistency-plus-self-evaluation gate and each comparator (frozen best single-signal baseline; matched-coverage random refusal), with coverage/refusal and calibration reported jointly. U is answered items whose returned answer is incorrect or unsupported divided by answered items; an answer to an unanswerable item counts as unsupported. U is undefined if no item is answered and is not treated as success.
draft.analysis.exclusion_rules[1]: Items lacking a source-provided reference answer or source-defined answerability label are reported as missing and excluded from primary scoring; no model-generated labels are substituted.
draft.analysis.exclusion_rules[2]: Unparseable self-evaluation outputs are reported under the missing-data rule; sensitivity treating unparseable as refusal is reported, but no missing value is silently imputed as truth.
draft.analysis.exclusion_rules[3]: Repetitions with protocol deviation, missing prompts or failed scoring records are reported and excluded only with an audit record; no repetition is dropped based on outcome direction.
draft.analysis.independent_unit: question item (with five repetitions and K stochastic samples treated as repeated measurements nested within item, not independent units)
draft.analysis.interpretation_rules[1]: Support requires lower U for the combined gate than both the frozen best single-signal baseline and matched-coverage random refusal, with paired intervals excluding zero in the favorable direction after Holm adjustment, no material calibration degradation, and no answerable-item refusal concentration under the pre-specified rule.
draft.analysis.interpretation_rules[2]: Refutation requires evidence that the combined gate fails the support pattern, or that any apparent U advantage is mainly explained by refusing answerable items, or that calibration degrades materially (ECE increase >=0.05 or Brier increase >=0.02) without an offsetting U reduction.
draft.analysis.interpretation_rules[3]: Futility: all-refuse, zero answered items, or U undefined makes the matched-coverage claim non-informative; report as futility and stop that claim rather than treat coverage reduction as success.
draft.analysis.interpretation_rules[4]: Inconclusive: a favorable point estimate with an interval including zero, realized coverage deviation greater than 0.05 from c* at frozen thresholds, or too few items in a required stratum limits interpretation; report as inconclusive and do not claim support or refutation.
draft.analysis.interpretation_rules[5]: Non-significance alone is not falsification of the mechanism; it is an inconclusive result about the tested comparison under this design.
draft.analysis.interpretation_rules[6]: Gain is mainly explained by answerable-item refusal if the combined gate's answerable-item refusal rate exceeds the frozen best single-signal baseline by at least 0.10 absolute and its paired U advantage over that baseline is absent among items answered by both gates.
draft.analysis.interpretation_rules[7]: Multiplicity: the two co-primary comparisons use Holm-adjusted intervals; all calibration, coverage-risk and per-stratum results are secondary and reported descriptively with intervals, not used to rescue a failed primary comparison.
draft.analysis.metrics[1]: Unsupported-answer rate U at matched answer coverage c*=0.80 (primary)
draft.analysis.metrics[3]: Appropriate refusal rate on unanswerable items
draft.analysis.metrics[5]: Brier score for self-evaluation probability against external correctness among answered items
draft.analysis.metrics[6]: Expected calibration error with reliability bins for self-evaluation probability against external correctness among answered items
draft.analysis.metrics[7]: Coverage-risk curve over c in {0.50,0.70,0.90} and realized coverage
draft.analysis.metrics[8]: Per-stratum U, coverage, refusal and calibration
draft.analysis.uncertainty_method: Item-level nonparametric bootstrap over held-out question items, resampling within pre-specified strata; paired differences for combined versus each comparator use the same resampled item indices. Report 95% percentile intervals. Five repetitions are summarized as repetition mean and range, not as independent samples. Two co-primary comparisons (frozen best single-signal baseline and matched-coverage random refusal) use Holm-adjusted 95% intervals; secondary comparisons are descriptive.
draft.decision_rules[1]: Primary support: combined gate U lower than both frozen best single-signal baseline and matched-coverage random refusal with paired 95% intervals excluding zero in the favorable direction after Holm adjustment, no material calibration degradation, and no answerable-item refusal concentration.
draft.decision_rules[2]: Refutation: combined gate does not meet the support pattern, or its apparent U advantage is mainly explained by answerable-item refusal, or calibration degrades materially (ECE increase >=0.05 or Brier increase >=0.02) without offsetting U reduction.
draft.decision_rules[3]: Futility and degeneracy: all-refuse, zero answered items, U undefined, or constant decisions across all items are reported as non-informative futility, not success.
draft.decision_rules[4]: Inconclusive: intervals include zero, realized coverage deviates by more than 0.05 from c*, or a required stratum is too thinly populated; report inconclusive and preserve the unaffected design parts.
draft.decision_rules[5]: Calibration materiality is pre-specified as ECE increase >=0.05 or Brier increase >=0.02 relative to the frozen best single-signal baseline among answered items.
draft.decision_rules[6]: The frozen best single-signal baseline is selected on development data by lower U at c*, with ties broken by higher development coverage then lexicographic gate name; held-out data are not used to select it.
draft.decision_rules[7]: No non-significance alone is treated as falsification; no result-informed threshold re-tuning is permitted after held-out scoring begins.
draft.decision_rules[8]: If a required stratum is unavailable under the selection rule, restrict the RQ3 generalization claim to available strata and report the limitation; do not pool ineligible data.
draft.falsification: The combined-gate claim is refuted if, on held-out items with thresholds frozen from development, the combined gate fails to show a lower unsupported-answer rate than both the frozen best single-signal baseline and matched-coverage random refusal with paired 95% intervals excluding zero in the favorable direction, or if its apparent advantage is mainly explained by refusing answerable items under the pre-specified concentration rule, or if calibration degrades materially (pre-specified ECE increase >=0.05 or Brier increase >=0.02) without an offsetting unsupported-answer reduction. A non-significant favorable point estimate without material degradation is inconclusive, not refutation. All-refuse or zero answered items makes U undefined and is futility, not success. No consistent direction across pre-specified strata limits the RQ3 generalization claim.
draft.hypothesis: A combined answerability gate using stochastic-sample consistency and self-evaluation, with thresholds selected only on development data, will reduce held-out unsupported-answer rate at matched answer coverage relative to the frozen best single-signal baseline and matched-coverage random refusal, without material calibration penalty or a gain concentrated in refusing answerable items.
draft.independent_unit: question item (with five repetitions and K stochastic samples treated as repeated measurements nested within item, not independent units)
draft.limitations[1]: Prospective design only: no experiment has been executed, no datasets have been downloaded, no model has been bound, and no numerical result is claimed.
draft.limitations[2]: Resource inventory is empty; dataset identities, pinned versions, licenses, checksums, download receipts, split manifests, access confirmations and final item counts are Preparation obligations under the frozen deterministic selection rule.
draft.limitations[3]: The source-defined unanswerable/out-of-knowledge subset required by the selection rule may not exist for a desired stratum; if so, that stratum is unavailable and the RQ3 claim must be restricted rather than fabricated.
draft.limitations[4]: Exact model identity and registered profile version are unbound; the planned 30 model calls per item across five repetitions (K=5 samples plus one self-evaluation call per item per repetition) is a design call-count rule, not an authorized execution budget.
draft.limitations[5]: Source reference labels and answerability labels may contain errors; independent audit and adjudication are planned but not completed.
draft.limitations[6]: Exact-match scoring after normalization is conservative, especially for multi-sentence/free-form strata; construct validity of that scoring rule is a limitation to be audited.
draft.limitations[7]: The two signals may be redundant rather than complementary, and development-selected thresholds may not transfer to held-out strata; these are hypotheses to be tested, not established properties.
draft.limitations[8]: Same-model self-evaluation may be overconfident or circular; external reference scoring and calibration checks limit but do not eliminate this concern.
draft.limitations[9]: Stochastic samples and five repetitions are nested within question items and are not independent units; inference treats the question item as the independent unit.
draft.limitations[10]: A non-significant or unfavorable result can be scientifically informative; failure to support the combined gate is not evidence that the design was infeasible.
draft.limitations[11]: Optional enhancements such as additional K, alternative weights, supervised answerability classifiers or extra domains are not required contributions and are not part of the primary claim.
draft.limitations[12]: Upstream responsibility: if independent Review finds a conflict between this Plan and the bound Method or Idea, the earliest responsible stage is the upstream owner; this Plan cannot silently replace upstream scientific definitions.
draft.objective: Prospectively specify a reviewable matched-coverage comparison of a newly specified combined consistency-plus-self-evaluation answerability gate against always-answer, consistency-only, self-evaluation-only and matched-coverage random-refusal baselines on public QA items drawn under a frozen deterministic resource-selection rule. The plan fixes the development/held-out split, development-only threshold procedure, signal definitions, scoring formulas, primary and secondary metrics, bootstrap analysis, degeneracy checks, falsifiers and Preparation audit checkpoints. No execution, dataset receipt, model binding or numerical result is claimed.
draft.protocol[1].purpose: Apply the frozen public-QA eligibility and deterministic selection rule to a recorded candidate-pool manifest; record identifiers, licenses, release dates, stratum assignments, reference-field provenance and unavailable strata. Freeze disjoint development/held-out split and item-order manifests before any model call. This step is planned and does not assert that downloads, checksums or access receipts already exist.
draft.protocol[2].purpose: Generate K=5 stochastic answers for each development item using only the question. The first sample is the evaluation answer for every gate; all five samples are retained for consistency. Planned call rule: K=5 calls per development item per repetition.
draft.protocol[2].system: You are answering a question. Return only the answer; do not explain.
draft.protocol[3].purpose: Elicit one self-evaluation probability that the first sampled development answer is true. Planned call rule: one call per development item per repetition. Unparseable outputs follow the pre-specified report rule and are not imputed as truth.
draft.protocol[3].system: You are evaluating a prior answer. Return only a probability between 0 and 1.
draft.protocol[4].purpose: Compute S_cons as the proportion of agreeing pairs among the 10 pairs of normalized extracted answers, S_self as the parsed self-evaluation probability, and S_comb=0.5*S_cons+0.5*S_self. Select thresholds for consistency-only, self-evaluation-only and combined gates on development data to target coverage c*=0.80, with tie-breaking toward the higher threshold; freeze the thresholds and freeze the best single-signal baseline by lower development unsupported-answer rate at c*, breaking ties by higher development coverage then lexicographic gate name. No held-out outcomes are used.
draft.protocol[5].purpose: After thresholds are frozen, generate K=5 stochastic answers for each held-out item with identical prompts, decoding and item order. The model sees no reference answer, answerability label, held-out identifier or source metadata. Planned call rule: K=5 calls per held-out item per repetition.
draft.protocol[5].system: You are answering a question. Return only the answer; do not explain.
draft.protocol[6].purpose: Elicit one self-evaluation probability for the first held-out answer using the identical development prompt and parsing rule. Planned call rule: one call per held-out item per repetition.
draft.protocol[6].system: You are evaluating a prior answer. Return only a probability between 0 and 1.
draft.protocol[7].purpose: Apply the frozen thresholds and fixed random-refusal seeds to produce answer/refuse decisions for always-answer, consistency-only, self-evaluation-only, combined and matched-coverage random-refusal conditions. Record realized coverage; do not tune thresholds on held-out data.
draft.protocol[8].purpose: Score answers against pinned source references under the frozen normalization and exact-match rule; compute unsupported-answer rate U, coverage, appropriate refusal, answerable-item refusal, Brier score, ECE, coverage-risk curves, per-stratum results and item-level paired bootstrap intervals. Produce audit records for resource selection, reference labels, leakage, threshold recomputation and degeneracy checks.
draft.randomization: No randomization has been executed. Planned randomization covers repetition-specific model sampling and the matched-coverage random-refusal baseline. Repetitions r=1..5 use seeds 1001-1005; the random-refusal baseline answers each item independently with probability c*=0.80 using the repetition seed. Model sample seeds for item i and repetition r are deterministically derived from the repetition seed and a recorded item index and are logged per call. Item order is fixed and identical across all gates. The development/held-out split is deterministic from the frozen SHA-256 rule and is not re-randomized after outcomes are seen.
draft.resource_requirements.compute[1].alterna: Academic-lab-default local CPU compute sufficient for item-level scoring and bootstrap on public QA.
draft.resource_requirements.compute[1].reason: CPU compute is required for deterministic split-manifest construction, signal computation, development-only threshold selection, scoring, item-level bootstrap, calibration, coverage-risk summaries and audit records. Exact provider and budget are unbound pending Preparation; this plan grants no execution authority.
draft.resource_requirements.model_api[1].alter: Any public black-box instruction-following LLM exposing stochastic sampling and numeric probability elicitation, selected by a documented deterministic rule in Preparation and recorded before execution.
draft.resource_requirements.model_api[1].reaso: One black-box instruction-following LLM capable of stochastic sampling and numeric self-evaluation is required as the model under test and as the self-evaluation source. Exact model identity or registered profile version is unbound in this Plan; selection authority and verification belong to Preparation under a documented deterministic rule. No resource_inventory entries are supplied, so candidate_ids are empty.
draft.sample_size_rationale: Exact public dataset identities and final item counts are not fixed in this Plan because the resource inventory is empty and the frozen selection rule must be applied in Preparation. No universal minimum sample size is imposed. Planning approximation, not an executed calculation: for a binomial proportion near 0.5, the item-level 95% bootstrap interval half-width is approximately 1.96*sqrt(0.25/n); retaining at least 200 answered held-out items overall when eligible data permit would give a rough half-width near 0.07. This is a precision rationale, not a stopping rule and not a claim about observed data. Preparation records N per stratum and total answered items; if fewer items are available, report intervals, mark thinly populated strata as descriptive, and restrict RQ3 rather than pool inappropriate strata.
draft.sampling_plan: 1) Apply the frozen deterministic public-QA eligibility rule to a recorded candidate pool: public research reuse without private credentials; canonical versioned release with stable identifier and release date no later than 2023-11-15; source-authored question-answer pairs with source gold/reference answers; a source-defined unanswerable or out-of-knowledge subset or explicit source field marking such items; metadata sufficient to assign domain and question-format labels deterministically, including at least one short factual and one multi-sentence/free-form format. For each required stratum (domain x format x answerability), sort eligible corpora by presence of a source-defined unanswerable subset, then earliest official release date, then lexicographic canonical identifier; select the first eligible corpus and reuse it when it covers multiple strata. If a required stratum has no eligible corpus, record it as unavailable and restrict the RQ3 claim rather than fabricate coverage. 2) Record a frozen selection log with identifiers, versions, licenses, release dates, stratum assignments, reference-field provenance and the candidate-pool manifest; record a disjoint development/held-out split manifest before model calls. Within each selected corpus-stratum, compute SHA-256 of the canonical item identifier with fixed salt 'split-v1', sort ascending, and assign the first 50% to development and the remainder to held-out; freeze item order and split manifests. 3) For each item and repetition, draw K=5 stochastic samples with fixed prompts and decoding. The first sample is the answer submitted to evaluation for every gate; the other four are used only for consistency so answer generation is held fixed across gates. Elicit one self-evaluation probability for the first sample per item per repetition. All gates reuse the same samples. Five independent repetitions give a planned 6 model calls per item per repetition and 30 calls per item before optional sensitivity. If the authorized budget later forces reduction, pre-specify one primary repetition and report repetition sensitivity; do not treat repetitions or samples as independent items. 4) Development items are used only to compute signals, select thresholds and freeze the best single-signal baseline; held-out items remain untouched until thresholds are frozen. draft.stop_conditions[1]: Stop before execution if Preparation cannot record a frozen candidate-pool manifest, eligible strata, licenses and release dates under the deterministic selection rule; report unavailable strata and restrict RQ3 rather than fabricate resources.
draft.stop_conditions[2]: Stop that stratum if no eligible corpus supplies a source-defined unanswerable or out-of-knowledge subset, canonical version and required domain/format metadata; do not substitute model-generated answerability labels.
draft.stop_conditions[3]: Stop before model calls if the model-under-test capability is not authorized and bound; unbound model identity or missing authorization is not permission to execute.
draft.stop_conditions[4]: Stop and report futility for any condition with zero answered items or all-refuse behavior, because U is undefined and the matched-coverage claim is non-informative.
draft.stop_conditions[5]: Stop held-out analysis if independent audit finds reference-label or scoring errors that cannot be adjudicated under the frozen rule; revise scoring before analysis rather than proceed.
draft.stop_conditions[6]: Stop the matched-coverage claim if realized held-out coverage at frozen thresholds deviates from c*=0.80 by more than 0.05; report coverage-risk and inconclusive status rather than claiming exact matching.
draft.validation_independence: Planned independent checks: an auditor independent of threshold tuning re-applies the frozen eligibility and deterministic selection rule to the recorded candidate-pool manifest; a second coder not involved in tuning audits a sample of source references and automatic correctness judgments with pre-specified adjudication; the scoring script, prompts, extraction rules and split manifests are frozen before held-out scoring; development thresholds are recomputed from frozen development outputs and verified against held-out application; prompts are checked for reference answers, labels, source metadata and held-out identifiers. prior_work.title: VideoChat: Chat-Centric Video Understanding
prior_work.abstract: In this paper, we initiate an attempt of developing an end-to-end chat-centric video understanding system, coined as VideoChat. It integrates video foundation models and large language models via a learnable neural interface, excelling in spatiotemporal reasoning, event localization, and causal relationship inference. To instructively tune this system, we build a video-centric instruction dataset, composed of thousands of videos associated with detailed descriptions and conversations. This dataset emphasizes spatiotemporal reasoning and captures causal relationships, providing a valuable asset for training our chat-centric video understanding system. Preliminary qualitative experiments demonstrate the potential of our system across a broad spectrum of video applications, which could serve as a simple prototype system for future research on chat-centric video understanding. Access our code and data at https://github.com/OpenGVLab/Ask-Anything

prior_work.title: EgoSchema: A Diagnostic Benchmark for Very Long-form Video Language Understanding
prior_work.abstract: We introduce EgoSchema, a very long-form video question-answering dataset, and benchmark to evaluate long video understanding capabilities of modern vision and language systems. Derived from Ego4D, EgoSchema consists of over 5000 human curated multiple choice question answer pairs, spanning over 250 hours of real video data, covering a very broad range of natural human activity and behavior. For each question, EgoSchema requires the correct answer to be selected between five given options based on a three-minute-long video clip. While some prior works have proposed video datasets with long clip lengths, we posit that merely the length of the video clip does not truly capture the temporal difficulty of the video task that is being considered. To remedy this, we introduce temporal certificate sets, a general notion for capturing the intrinsic temporal understanding length associated with a broad range of video understanding tasks & datasets. Based on this metric, we find EgoSchema to have intrinsic temporal lengths over 5.7x longer than the second closest dataset and 10x to 100x longer than any other video understanding dataset. Further, our evaluation of several current state-of-the-art video and language models shows them to be severely lacking in long-term video understanding capabilities. Even models with several billions of parameters achieve QA accuracy less than 33% (random is 20%) on the EgoSchema multi-choice question answering task, while humans achieve about 76% accuracy. We posit that \name{}{}, with its long intrinsic temporal structures and diverse complexity, would serve as a valuable evaluation probe for developing effective long-term video understanding systems in the future. Data and Zero-shot model evaluation code are open-sourced for both public and commercial use under the Ego4D license at http://egoschema.github.io

prior_work.title: HowTo100M: Learning a Text-Video Embedding by Watching Hundred Million Narrated Video Clips
prior_work.abstract: Learning text-video embeddings usually requires a dataset of video clips with manually provided captions. However, such datasets are expensive and time consuming to create and therefore difficult to obtain on a large scale. In this work, we propose instead to learn such embeddings from video data with readily available natural language annotations in the form of automatically transcribed narrations. The contributions of this work are three-fold. First, we introduce HowTo100M: a large-scale dataset of 136 million video clips sourced from 1.22M narrated instructional web videos depicting humans performing and describing over 23k different visual tasks. Our data collection procedure is fast, scalable and does not require any additional manual annotation. Second, we demonstrate that a text-video embedding trained on this data leads to state-of-the-art results for text-to-video retrieval and action localization on instructional video datasets such as YouCook2 or CrossTask. Finally, we show that this embedding transfers well to other domains: fine-tuning on generic Youtube videos (MSR-VTT dataset) and movies (LSMDC dataset) outperforms models trained on these datasets alone. Our dataset, code and models will be publicly available at: www.di.ens.fr/willow/research/howto100m/.

prior_work.title: Video-LLaMA: An Instruction-tuned Audio-Visual Language Model for Video Understanding
prior_work.abstract: We present Video-LLaMA a multi-modal framework that empowers Large Language Models (LLMs) with the capability of understanding both visual and auditory content in the video. Video-LLaMA bootstraps cross-modal training from the frozen pre-trained visual and audio encoders and the frozen LLMs. Unlike previous works that complement LLMs to process the visual or audio signals only, Video-LLaMA enables video comprehension by tackling two challenges: (1) capturing the temporal changes in visual scenes, (2) integrating audio-visual signals. To counter the first challenge, we propose a Video Q-former to assemble a pre-trained image encoder into our video encoder and introduce a video-to-text generation task to learn video-language correspondence. For the second challenge, we leverage ImageBind, a universal embedding model aligning multiple modalities, as the pre-trained audio encoder and introduce an Audio Q-former on top of ImageBind to learn reasonable auditory query embeddings for the LLM module. To align the output of both visual and audio encoders with LLM's embedding space, we first train Video-LLaMA on massive video/image-caption pairs and then tune our model with visual-instruction datasets of moderate amount but higher quality. We found Video-LLaMA shows the ability to perceive and comprehend video content and generate meaningful responses grounded in the visual and auditory information presented in the videos.

prior_work.title: SEED-Bench: Benchmarking Multimodal LLMs with Generative Comprehension
prior_work.abstract: Based on powerful Large Language Models (LLMs), recent generative Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have gained prominence as a pivotal research area, exhibiting remarkable capability for both comprehension and generation. In this work, we address the evaluation of generative comprehension in MLLMs as a preliminary step towards a comprehensive assessment of generative models, by introducing a benchmark named SEED-Bench. SEED-Bench consists of 19K multiple choice questions with accurate human annotations (x 6 larger than existing benchmarks), which spans 12 evaluation dimensions including the comprehension of both the image and video modality. We develop an advanced pipeline for generating multiple-choice questions that target specific evaluation dimensions, integrating both automatic filtering and manual verification processes. Multiple-choice questions with groundtruth options derived from human annotation enables an objective and efficient assessment of model performance, eliminating the need for human or GPT intervention during evaluation. We further evaluate the performance of 18 models across all 12 dimensions, covering both the spatial and temporal understanding. By revealing the limitations of existing MLLMs through evaluation results, we aim for SEED-Bench to provide insights for motivating future research. We will launch and consistently maintain a leaderboard to provide a platform for the community to assess and investigate model capability.

Se0284d1703f9.title: HowTo100M: Learning a Text-Video Embedding by Watching Hundred Million Narrated Video Clips
attribution_passages: Learning text-video embeddings usually requires a dataset of video clips with manually provided captions. However, such datasets are expensive and time consuming to create and therefore difficult to obtain on a large scale. In this work, we propose instead to learn such embeddings from video data with readily available natural language annotations in the form of automatically transcribed narrations. The contributions of this work are three-fold. First, we introduce HowTo100M: a large-scale dataset of 136 million video clips sourced from 1.22M narrated instructional web videos depicting humans performing and describing over 23k different visual tasks. Our data collection procedure is fast, scalable and does not require any additional manual annotation. Second, we demonstrate that a text-video embedding trained on this data leads to state-of-the-art results for text-to-video retrieval and action localization on instructional video datasets such as YouCook2 or CrossTask. Finally, we show that this embedding transfers well to other domains: fine-tuning on generic Youtube videos (MSR-VTT dataset) and movies (LSMDC dataset) outperforms models trained on these datasets alone. Our dataset, code and models will be publicly available at: www.di.ens.fr/willow/research/howto100m/.

Sfbf3ae23ee23.title: Video-LLaMA: An Instruction-tuned Audio-Visual Language Model for Video Understanding
attribution_passages: We present Video-LLaMA a multi-modal framework that empowers Large Language Models (LLMs) with the capability of understanding both visual and auditory content in the video. Video-LLaMA bootstraps cross-modal training from the frozen pre-trained visual and audio encoders and the frozen LLMs. Unlike previous works that complement LLMs to process the visual or audio signals only, Video-LLaMA enables video comprehension by tackling two challenges: (1) capturing the temporal changes in visual scenes, (2) integrating audio-visual signals. To counter the first challenge, we propose a Video Q-former to assemble a pre-trained image encoder into our video encoder and introduce a video-to-text generation task to learn video-language correspondence. We found Video-LLaMA shows the ability to perceive and comprehend video content and generate meaningful responses grounded in the visual and auditory information presented in the videos.

S9b2fee3f185e.title: SEED-Bench: Benchmarking Multimodal LLMs with Generative Comprehension
attribution_passages: Based on powerful Large Language Models (LLMs), recent generative Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have gained prominence as a pivotal research area, exhibiting remarkable capability for both comprehension and generation. In this work, we address the evaluation of generative comprehension in MLLMs as a preliminary step towards a comprehensive assessment of generative models, by introducing a benchmark named SEED-Bench. SEED-Bench consists of 19K multiple choice questions with accurate human annotations (x 6 larger than existing benchmarks), which spans 12 evaluation dimensions including the comprehension of both the image and video modality. We develop an advanced pipeline for generating multiple-choice questions that target specific evaluation dimensions, integrating both automatic filtering and manual verification processes. Multiple-choice questions with groundtruth options derived from human annotation enables an objective and efficient assessment of model performance, eliminating the need for human or GPT intervention during evaluation. We further evaluate the performance of 18 models across all 12 dimensions, covering both the spatial and temporal understanding. By revealing the limitations of existing MLLMs through evaluation results, we aim for SEED-Bench to provide insights for motivating future research. We will launch and consistently maintain a leaderboard to provide a platform for the community to assess and investigate model capability.

Sd8b52dbb6020.title: Self-supervised Pre-training and Contrastive Representation Learning for Multiple-choice Video QA
attribution_passages: Video Question Answering (VideoQA) requires fine-grained understanding of both video and language modalities to answer the given questions. In this paper, we propose novel training schemes for multiple-choice video question answering with a self-supervised pre-training stage and a supervised contrastive learning in the main stage as an auxiliary learning. In the self-supervised pre-training stage, we transform the original problem format of predicting the correct answer into the one that predicts the relevant question to provide a model with broader contextual inputs without any further dataset or annotation. For contrastive learning in the main stage, we add a masking noise to the input corresponding to the ground-truth answer, and consider the original input of the ground-truth answer as a positive sample, while treating the rest as negative samples. By mapping the positive sample closer to the masked input, we show that the model performance is improved. We further employ locally aligned attention to focus more effectively on the video frames that are particularly relevant to the given corresponding subtitle sentences. We evaluate our proposed model on highly competitive benchmark datasets related to multiple-choice video QA: TVQA, TVQA+, and DramaQA. Experimental results show that our model achieves state-of-the-art performance on all datasets. We also validate our approaches through further analyses.

S6c61f884001c.title: Spatiotemporal Dynamics and Frame Features for Improved Input Selection in Video Super-Resolution Models
attribution_passages: This paper presents a novel approach to video super-resolution (VSR) by focusing on the selection of input frames, a process critical to VSR. VSR methods typically rely on deep learning techniques, those that are able to learn features from a large dataset of low-resolution (LR) and corresponding high-resolution (HR) videos and generate high-quality HR frames from any new LR input frames using the learned features. However, these methods often use as input the immediate neighbouring frames to a given target frame without considering the importance and dynamics of the frames across the temporal dimension of a video. This work aims to address the limitations of the conventional sliding-window mechanisms by developing input frame selection algorithms. By dynamically selecting the most representative neighbouring frames based on content-aware selection measures, our proposed algorithms enable VSR models to extract more informative and accurate features that are better aligned with the target frame, leading to improved performance and higher-quality HR frames. Through an empirical study, we demonstrate that the proposed dynamic content-aware selection mechanism improves super-resolution results without any additional architectural overhead, offering a counter-intuitive yet effective alternative to the long-established trend of increasing architectural complexity to improve VSR results.

S16b4b2613a07.title: VideoChat: Chat-Centric Video Understanding
S16b4b2613a07.fulltext_snippet: In this paper, we initiate an attempt of developing an end-to-end chat-centric video understanding system, coined as VideoChat. Preliminary qualitative experiments demonstrate the potential of our system across a broad spectrum of video applications, which could serve as a simple prototype system for future research on chat-centric video understanding. Access our code and data at https://github.com/OpenGVLab/Ask-Anything
