draft.title: Question-Conditioned Frame Retrieval for Long Video Understanding in Video-Large Language Models
draft.literature_gap: Current video-LLMs (e.g., VideoChat, Video-LLaMA) process long videos by uniformly sampling a fixed number of frames or using a fixed temporal resolution, which often misses question-relevant segments and leads to poor performance on long-form QA benchmarks like EgoSchema (accuracy <33% vs human 76%). Prior work has not systematically evaluated whether selecting frames based on their relevance to the question—rather than uniform sampling—improves long video understanding at an equal frame budget. This gap is critical because long videos exceed typical context windows, and naive sampling discards informative content.
draft.hypothesis: At a fixed frame budget (e.g., K=8 frames), selecting frames via question-conditioned relevance scoring (using CLIP similarity between the question text and frame embeddings) improves multiple-choice QA accuracy on long videos compared to uniform sampling.
draft.method: Use an open-source video-LLM (Video-LLaMA) with a fixed maximum of K=8 frames. For each video-question pair, compute CLIP embeddings for all frames (sampled at 1 fps) and for the question text. Select the top-K frames by cosine similarity between question and frame embeddings. Feed these selected frames to the video-LLM and obtain the answer. Baseline: uniform sampling of K frames across the video. Evaluate on a subset of the EgoSchema benchmark (500 multiple-choice questions). Control for frame budget and model weights.
draft.minimal_test: Run both uniform sampling and question-conditioned retrieval on 500 EgoSchema questions with the same Video-LLaMA model and K=8. Compute multiple-choice accuracy for each condition.
draft.decisive_metric: Accuracy on EgoSchema multiple-choice QA (percentage of correct answers).
draft.supporting_result: Question-conditioned retrieval achieves at least 5 percentage points higher accuracy than uniform sampling (e.g., 35% vs 30%) with a paired bootstrap test yielding p < 0.05.
draft.falsifying_result: Question-conditioned retrieval shows no significant improvement over uniform sampling (difference ≤ 1 percentage point or p ≥ 0.05), or performs worse.
draft.related_work[1]: VideoChat (2305.06355): chat-centric video understanding with fixed frame sampling; does not address question-conditioned frame selection.
draft.related_work[2]: Video-LLaMA (2306.02858): audio-visual language model with video Q-former; uses uniform frame sampling.
draft.related_work[3]: EgoSchema (2308.09126): long-form video QA benchmark showing poor performance of current models; provides evaluation protocol.
draft.related_work[4]: SEED-Bench (2307.16125): multimodal benchmark including video temporal understanding; supports need for better long video methods.
draft.related_work[5]: HowTo100M (1906.03327): large-scale video-text pretraining; not directly about long video QA but demonstrates relevance of text-video alignment.
draft.limitations: The study uses a single video-LLM and one dataset (EgoSchema); results may not generalize to other models or tasks. CLIP-based retrieval may not capture complex temporal or causal question semantics. The fixed frame budget K=8 may be suboptimal for some questions. The method ignores audio and only uses visual frames.
draft.resource_plan: Use one NVIDIA A100 (40GB) or RTX 3090 GPU for inference. Precompute CLIP embeddings for all frames (offline, ~1 hour). Run 1000 inferences (500 questions × 2 conditions) with Video-LLaMA, estimated 10–20 GPU hours. Total cloud compute cost under $200 (e.g., at $1–2/GPU-hour). All models and datasets are open-source. Timeline: 2 weeks including setup, experiments, and analysis.

draft.title: Look Where the Answer Lives: Answer-Conditioned Active Frame Retrieval for Long-Video vLLMs
draft.hypothesis: Long-video vLLM errors are dominated by temporal evidence allocation rather than visual encoding capacity. If a vLLM's own answer distribution over competing hypotheses is used to retrieve temporally localized evidence that discriminates between those hypotheses, then a fixed frame budget can yield large accuracy gains without retraining. Multiple-choice long-video QA is the cleanest setting to test this because candidate answers provide explicit hypotheses and EgoSchema provides long videos with diagnostic questions.
draft.related_work: VideoChat and Video-LLaMA integrate video encoders with LLMs but typically consume a small, fixed set of uniformly sampled frames or clips, which dilutes sparse evidence in long videos. EgoSchema explicitly shows that long-form video-language understanding is difficult for such systems, while SEED-Bench evaluates generative multimodal comprehension on shorter or less temporally demanding content. HowTo100M popularized large-scale narrated video pretraining but does not address inference-time evidence allocation. Recent long-video systems use memory banks, hierarchical summarization, or LLM-agent pipelines that call captioning/search tools. This proposal differs in three ways: it is training-free at inference; it uses the vLLM's own uncertainty over candidate answers as the retrieval controller; and it retrieves frames to discriminate between competing answer hypotheses rather than merely matching the question or selecting visually salient keyframes. This avoids dense captioning and external agent tooling while directly targeting the failure mode of fixed frame sampling.
draft.approach: Video-language models (vLLMs) have made rapid progress, yet they still struggle on long videos because they can observe only a small frame budget. Existing systems commonly sample frames uniformly or select visually salient keyframes. Both strategies ignore a crucial signal available at inference: the model's uncertainty over candidate answers. We propose Answer-Conditioned Active Retrieval (ACAR), a training-free inference framework that turns a vLLM into its own retrieval controller. Given a long video and a question with candidate answers, ACAR first retrieves a diverse coarse set of segments using question-video similarity. It then queries the vLLM and observes its answer distribution. If the model is uncertain, ACAR treats the top competing answers as hypotheses and retrieves additional segments that are maximally discriminative between them: segments whose visual or audio-text embeddings are strongly aligned with one hypothesis and weakly aligned with the others. The vLLM re-answers with the expanded evidence set, and the loop stops when the answer is stable or a frame budget is reached. This converts frame selection into active hypothesis testing rather than passive sampling. We evaluate ACAR on EgoSchema, NExT-QA, and controlled long-video needle-in-a-haystack benchmarks using open vLLMs such as Video-LLaMA and VideoChat. We measure accuracy at fixed frame budgets, frames consumed, retrieval rounds, latency, and robustness to distractor duration. Ablations isolate the contributions of uncertainty triggering, answer-conditioned retrieval, and diversity. If successful, ACAR offers a simple, general way to improve long-video understanding without retraining the underlying vLLM.
draft.validation: 1. Main long-video QA evaluation: use EgoSchema multiple-choice QA with open vLLMs such as Video-LLaMA and VideoChat. Compare ACAR against uniform sampling, random sampling, CLIP question-only top-k retrieval, and an oracle that uses ground-truth temporal annotations when available, all under the same maximum frame budget. Metrics: accuracy, average frames consumed, number of retrieval rounds, wall-clock latency, and token usage. 2. Adaptive-budget analysis: sweep frame budgets (8, 16, 32, 64) and stopping thresholds. Test whether ACAR improves the accuracy-per-frame frontier and whether uncertain questions receive more frames. 3. Ablation study: remove answer-conditioned retrieval and use question-only retrieval; replace vLLM uncertainty with fixed two-round retrieval; remove temporal diversity; use only top-1 answer versus top-2/top-3 hypotheses; vary the contrastive retrieval weight. 4. Controlled needle-in-a-haystack test: insert a short evidence clip from NExT-QA or ActivityNet into a long distractor video. Ask a question whose answer depends only on the inserted clip. Measure accuracy as distractor duration grows (30s, 1min, 3min, 5min) and report retrieval recall of the evidence clip. 5. Temporal reasoning evaluation: run on NExT-QA temporal and causal subsets to check that gains are not limited to multiple-choice EgoSchema. 6. Robustness and calibration: measure answer stability across retrieval rounds, correlation between vLLM confidence and correctness, and performance when ASR is available versus visual-only retrieval. 7. Implementation details: split videos into 2-4 second segments; encode segments with a frozen CLIP-style video encoder and optional ASR text encoder; retrieve with question and answer-hypothesis text queries; enforce temporal diversity with farthest-point selection; feed time-stamped frames to the vLLM. Use a small held-out dev split only to set the stopping threshold, without training the vLLM.
draft.limitations: CLIP-style retrieval may miss fine-grained actions, small objects, or evidence that is only interpretable through motion. Candidate answers in multiple-choice QA are convenient hypotheses, so the method may transfer less directly to open-ended QA where hypotheses must be generated. vLLM confidence can be miscalibrated, causing unnecessary retrieval rounds or premature stopping. Answer-conditioned retrieval may retrieve visually similar but non-evidential segments, especially when answers are semantically close. The iterative loop adds inference cost and latency; gains must be evaluated at matched frame and compute budgets. Long-video benchmarks are limited, and EgoSchema may not cover all long-video domains. The approach does not improve the underlying visual encoder and may fail when the evidence is absent from the video or requires reasoning over very long temporal dependencies. Finally, results with one or two open vLLMs may not generalize to closed proprietary models.

draft.alternative_explanations[1]: A positive D_i could reflect salience or visual complexity differences between localized and distractor windows rather than temporal-evidence use; equal duration, equal frame count, non-overlap, and baseline comparisons reduce but do not eliminate this explanation.
draft.alternative_explanations[2]: A positive or null D_i could be driven by option-order or first-option bias; deterministic permutation averaging and order-cue audits are designed to detect this.
draft.alternative_explanations[3]: A null D_i could reflect a flat or invalid confidence readout, tokenizer mismatch, or failed multi-frame handling rather than absence of evidence use; readout checks and invalidity rules separate these cases.
draft.alternative_explanations[4]: Cross-benchmark differences in video domain, clip length, question type, and annotation conditions could produce heterogeneity; cross-benchmark claims are limited to the two evaluated benchmarks.
draft.alternative_explanations[5]: Answer leakage in window construction could inflate localized-versus-distractor contrast; blinded construction and a second reviewer audit are required.
draft.analysis.aggregation: Average Yes confidence over P=24 permutations within item before computing D_i; analyze item-level D_i. Do not treat repeated model calls or permutations as independent samples. Report EgoSchema and second benchmark separately; pooled estimates are descriptive only and cannot alone establish cross-benchmark generalization.
draft.analysis.estimand: Within each evaluated benchmark, the item-level primary estimand is mean D_i, where D_i = mean over shuffled permutations of Yes(supported option | localized_evidence_shuffled_order) minus mean over shuffled permutations of Yes(supported option | matched_distractor_shuffled_order); raw QA accuracy is secondary. The pre-specified smallest scientifically meaningful paired effect is delta_min = 0.05 on this D_i scale.
draft.analysis.exclusion_rules[1]: Exclude an item if blinded window audit fails, if required matched-distractor or localized-evidence readout is missing or invalid, or if the item lacks all required primary condition readouts; report exclusion counts per benchmark.
draft.analysis.exclusion_rules[2]: Do not exclude items based on observed outcome, answer correctness, or effect direction.

draft.analysis.independent_unit: One video-question item with its option set, after averaging per-option Yes confidence over deterministic option permutations within item.
draft.analysis.interpretation_rules[1]: Readout validity gate: if Yes token mapping, first-token extraction, or fixed multi-frame per-option confidence checks fail for R*, the confidence readout is invalid and cannot support or refute the hypothesis.
draft.analysis.interpretation_rules[2]: Support for a benchmark: mean D_i is at least delta_min = 0.05, its 95% CI excludes zero in the pre-specified positive direction, readout and audits pass, and baseline comparisons do not show an equivalent contrast without localized evidence; interpret with leakage, permutation, tokenizer, and frame checks, not as proof of temporal reasoning.
draft.analysis.interpretation_rules[3]: Futility for the minimum meaningful effect: if the 95% CI lies entirely below delta_min = 0.05 (upper bound < 0.05) and is not a reversed-direction refutation, report futility for the pre-specified minimum meaningful contrast, not mechanism falsification.
draft.analysis.interpretation_rules[4]: Refutation or disconfirmation for a benchmark: mean D_i is negative with a 95% CI excluding zero in the reversed direction, or first-option/order-cue selection persists regardless of evidence window, or confidence is flat or constant such that localized and matched-distractor windows cannot be distinguished; report as disconfirmed for this setup.
draft.analysis.interpretation_rules[5]: Inconclusive: non-significant result with CI including zero, a positive result below delta_min whose CI is not entirely below delta_min, insufficient N/MDE, missing or invalid readouts, or audit failure; non-significance alone is not falsification and does not support the hypothesis.
draft.analysis.interpretation_rules[6]: Second benchmark: a null or reversed D_i, or interaction heterogeneity, is limited or non-generalization; a positive result is cross-benchmark coverage only for the two evaluated benchmarks under identical conditions, not broad cross-domain or cross-question-type generalization.
draft.analysis.interpretation_rules[7]: Stratified persistence: pool-positive results alone are not persistence; require matching stratum signs and no pre-specified interaction heterogeneity, otherwise report limited or non-persistence.
draft.analysis.interpretation_rules[8]: If no eligible second benchmark exists, report rq-3 cross-benchmark coverage as not achieved and do not substitute within-EgoSchema persistence; the limitation remains for upstream Method/scope decision.

draft.analysis.metrics[3]: mean D_i with 95% CI and sign
draft.analysis.uncertainty_method: Two-sided paired t-test at alpha=0.05 on item-level D_i with 95% CI; Wilcoxon signed-rank as sensitivity; paired effect size reported. The pre-specified smallest scientifically meaningful effect is delta_min = 0.05 on the D_i scale, fixed before pilot or confirmatory readout. Primary contrast is a single pre-specified test within each benchmark. Cross-benchmark uses a pre-specified benchmark-by-evidence-window interaction at alpha=0.05; stratified persistence uses a pre-specified stratum-by-evidence-window interaction at alpha=0.05. Secondary stratified analyses are not confirmatory multiplicity-adjusted claims.

draft.decision_rules[2]: If a second benchmark is selected, apply the identical five conditions and D_i contrast; if none is eligible, record rq-3 cross-benchmark coverage as not achieved and make no cross-benchmark, cross-domain, or cross-question-type generalization.
draft.decision_rules[3]: For each benchmark, support is claimed only when mean D_i is at least delta_min = 0.05 with 95% CI excluding zero, audits pass, and baseline comparisons do not show an equivalent contrast without localized evidence; this supports the measurement for the evaluated setup, not a broad causal ranking of vLLM limitations.
draft.decision_rules[4]: For each benchmark, refutation or futility for the setup is reported when mean D_i is negative with a 95% CI excluding zero in the reversed direction, order cues persist regardless of evidence window, or the readout is flat or constant; a 95% CI entirely below delta_min = 0.05 is futility for the minimum meaningful effect, not mechanism falsification.
draft.decision_rules[5]: A non-significant result with CI including zero, or a positive mean below delta_min whose CI is not entirely below delta_min, is inconclusive for the pre-specified meaningful effect, not falsification; report it and keep unresolved claims unresolved.
draft.decision_rules[6]: If the second-benchmark D_i is null or reversed or its interaction indicates heterogeneity, report limited or non-generalization; a pooled positive estimate alone is not cross-benchmark generalization.
draft.decision_rules[7]: If public metadata strata are absent or non-varying, make no stratified persistence claim; within-EgoSchema persistence is secondary and never substitutes for cross-benchmark coverage.
draft.decision_rules[8]: If readout, tokenizer, frame, leakage, or permutation audit fails, report measurement invalidity or item exclusions as applicable; do not claim support or refutation of the scientific hypothesis from invalid readouts.
draft.falsification: For a benchmark, the design is disconfirmed for this setup if pre-specified D_i is negative with a 95% CI excluding zero in the reversed direction, or if first-option or order-cue selection persists across permutations regardless of evidence window, or if the confidence readout is flat or constant so localized evidence and matched distractor cannot be distinguished. A 95% CI lying entirely below delta_min = 0.05 is futility for the pre-specified minimum meaningful effect, not proof that the mechanism is false. A non-significant result or a CI including zero is inconclusive. A positive mean D_i below delta_min whose CI is not entirely below delta_min is inconclusive for the meaningful-effect claim. A second-benchmark null or reversal, or a pre-specified benchmark-by-evidence-window interaction indicating heterogeneity, is reported as limited or non-generalization rather than erased. Readout, tokenizer, or frame-check failure invalidates the confidence measure rather than supporting or refuting the hypothesis.

prior_work.title: Large Language Models are Few-Shot Clinical Information Extractors
prior_work.abstract: A long-running goal of the clinical NLP community is the extraction of important variables trapped in clinical notes. However, roadblocks have included dataset shift from the general domain and a lack of public clinical corpora and annotations. In this work, we show that large language models, such as InstructGPT, perform well at zero- and few-shot information extraction from clinical text despite not being trained specifically for the clinical domain. Whereas text classification and generation performance have already been studied extensively in such models, here we additionally demonstrate how to leverage them to tackle a diverse set of NLP tasks which require more structured outputs, including span identification, token-level sequence classification, and relation extraction. Further, due to the dearth of available data to evaluate these systems, we introduce new datasets for benchmarking few-shot clinical information extraction based on a manual re-annotation of the CASI dataset for new tasks. On the clinical extraction tasks we studied, the GPT-3 systems significantly outperform existing zero- and few-shot baselines.

prior_work.title: NLICE: Synthetic Medical Record Generation for Effective Primary Healthcare Differential Diagnosis
prior_work.abstract: This paper offers a systematic method for creating medical knowledge-grounded patient records for use in activities involving differential diagnosis. Additionally, an assessment of machine learning models that can differentiate between various conditions based on given symptoms is also provided. We use a public disease-symptom data source called SymCat in combination with Synthea to construct the patients records. In order to increase the expressive nature of the synthetic data, we use a medically-standardized symptom modeling method called NLICE to augment the synthetic data with additional contextual information for each condition. In addition, Naive Bayes and Random Forest models are evaluated and compared on the synthetic data. The paper shows how to successfully construct SymCat-based and NLICE-based datasets. We also show results for the effectiveness of using the datasets to train predictive disease models. The SymCat-based dataset is able to train a Naive Bayes and Random Forest model yielding a 58.8% and 57.1% Top-1 accuracy score, respectively. In contrast, the NLICE-based dataset improves the results, with a Top-1 accuracy of 82.0% and Top-5 accuracy values of more than 90% for both models. Our proposed data generation approach solves a major barrier to the application of artificial intelligence methods in the healthcare domain. Our novel NLICE symptom modeling approach addresses the incomplete and insufficient information problem in the current binary symptom representation approach. The NLICE code is open sourced at https://github.com/guozhuoran918/NLICE.

prior_work.title: EHRXQA: A Multi-Modal Question Answering Dataset for Electronic Health Records with Chest X-ray Images
prior_work.abstract: Electronic Health Records (EHRs), which contain patients' medical histories in various multi-modal formats, often overlook the potential for joint reasoning across imaging and table modalities underexplored in current EHR Question Answering (QA) systems. In this paper, we introduce EHRXQA, a novel multi-modal question answering dataset combining structured EHRs and chest X-ray images. To develop our dataset, we first construct two uni-modal resources: 1) The MIMIC-CXR-VQA dataset, our newly created medical visual question answering (VQA) benchmark, specifically designed to augment the imaging modality in EHR QA, and 2) EHRSQL (MIMIC-IV), a refashioned version of a previously established table-based EHR QA dataset. By integrating these two uni-modal resources, we successfully construct a multi-modal EHR QA dataset that necessitates both uni-modal and cross-modal reasoning. To address the unique challenges of multi-modal questions within EHRs, we propose a NeuralSQL-based strategy equipped with an external VQA API. This pioneering endeavor enhances engagement with multi-modal EHR sources and we believe that our dataset can catalyze advances in real-world medical scenarios such as clinical decision-making and research. EHRXQA is available at https://github.com/baeseongsu/ehrxqa.

prior_work.title: The use of analytic hierarchy process for measuring the complexity of medical diagnosis
prior_work.abstract: Diagnostic complexity is an important contextual factor affecting a variety of medical outcomes. Existing measurements of diagnosis complexity either rely on crude proxies or use fine-grained measures that employ indicators from proprietary data that are not readily available. Hence, the study of this important construct in fields such as medical informatics has been hampered by the difficulty of measuring diagnostic complexity. This article presents a novel approach for conceptualizing and operationalizing diagnostic task complexity as a multi-dimensional construct, which employs the readily available International Classification of Diseases codes from medical encounters in hospitals and uses Analytic Hierarchical Process methodology. We demonstrate the reliability of the proposed approach and show that despite using a relatively simple procedure, it is able to predict readmission rates just as well as (or even better) than some of the sophisticated measures that have been used in recent studies (namely, the LaCE score index).

Existing measurements of diagnosis complexity either rely on crude proxies or use fine-grained measures that employ indicators from proprietary data that are not readily available. Hence, the study of this important construct in fields such as medical informatics has been hampered by the difficulty of measuring diagnostic complexity. This article presents a novel approach for conceptualizing and operationalizing diagnostic task complexity as a multi-dimensional construct, which employs the readily available International Classification of Diseases codes from medical encounters in hospitals and uses Analytic Hierarchical Process methodology. We demonstrate the reliability of the proposed approach and show that despite using a relatively simple procedure, it is able to predict readmission rates just as well as (or even better) than some of the sophisticated measures that have been used in recent studies (namely, the LaCE score index). S7a7d0ae97252.title: Sprague-Grundy values and complexity for LCTR
attribution_passages: Given an integer partition of $n$, we consider the impartial combinatorial game LCTR in which moves consist of removing either the left column or top row of its Young diagram. We show that for both normal and misère play, the optimal strategy can consist mostly of mirroring the opponent's moves. We also establish that both LCTR and Downright are domestic as well as returnable, and on the other hand neither tame nor forced. For both games, those structural observations allow for computing the Sprague-Grundy value any position in $O(\log(n))$ time, assuming that the time unit allows for reading an integer, or performing a basic arithmetic operation. This improves on the previously known bound of $O(n)$ due to Ilić (2019). We also cover some other complexity measures of both games, such as state-space complexity, and number of leaves and nodes in the corresponding game tree.

Sfa0c168ffe47.title: Structured Clinical Interview for DSM Diagnosis
attribution_passages: Abstract The Structured Clinical Interview for DSM Diagnosis is a semistructured interview for making the major DSM‐IV Axis I Disorders (SCID‐I) and Axis II Personality Disorders (SCID‐II) diagnoses. Unlike fully structured clinical interviews that may be administered by lay interviewers (e.g., the Diagnostic Interview Schedule), the SCID is a semistructured interview, and it must be administered by a clinician or trained mental health professional. As the most widely used instrument for assessing Axis I disorders, the SCID‐I has been used in thousands of research studies since its introduction in 1986.

S949b14b4ef67.title:
mCodeGPT: Enhancing Cancer Research through Zero-Shot Information 
Extraction from Clinical Free Text Data
attribution_passages: Abstract The rapidly growing collection of clinical free text data about cancer provides an unprecedented opportunity to harness rich, real-world insights for advancing cancer research and treatment. At the same time, there is a formidable challenge in efficiently extracting, standardizing, and structuring this vast and unstructured information to derive meaningful conclusions. In this paper, we address the problem of information extraction to standardize and structure such free text using Large Language Models (LLMs) following the minimal Common Oncology Data Elements (mCODE™) structure. We propose mCodeGPT, a state-of-the-art data standardization tool Cancer related clinical notes. mCodeGPT ingests Cancer ontology knowledge base, automatically generates prompts in a hierarchical manner to extract information within the ontology from the clinical notes, and outputs results in a structured, tabular format. The pipeline is completely zero-shot, meaning it is annotation-free and does not require model training. Our new tool simplifies the conventional labor-intensive process of data collection, annotating, model training, and fine-tuning. To overcome challenges inherent in common LLMs, such as token size limitations, hallucination, and suboptimal accuracy in information extraction, we have developed three distinct methodologies for hierarchical prompt engineering. We conducted rigorous evaluations of mCodeGPT's efficacy in the domain of Cancer clinical note generation and information extraction. Employing the GPT-3.5-turbo model, we generated a diverse set of 400 simulated clinical notes spanning various Cancer types. The effectiveness of our three proposed prompt generation methods was further assessed using both OpenAI models and a selection of open-source LLM models. The outcomes of our research underscore the proficiency of our pipeline, showcasing an impressive 96% accuracy in information extraction. We published mCodeGPT on GitHub for other researchers to use.

Sc83f0295f251.title: Pengaruh Few-shot Learning pada Kinerja LLM untuk Ekstraksi Entitas Iklan Lowongan Kerja
attribution_passages: Ekstraksi informasi dari teks tidak terstruktur, seperti iklan lowongan kerja, merupakan tantangan besar. Pendekatan tradisional berbasis fine-tuning membutuhkan dataset berlabel masif dan sumber daya komputasi tinggi. Sebagai alternatif, Large Language Model (LLM) dengan In-Context Learning (ICL) menawarkan efisiensi. Penelitian ini menginvestigasi pengaruh few-shot learning, khususnya variasi jumlah contoh (k), terhadap akurasi LLM dalam ekstraksi entitas dari iklan lowongan kerja berbahasa Indonesia. Menggunakan model Gemini, eksperimen dilakukan dengan skenario zero-shot (k=0) hingga few-shot (k=1, 3, 5, 10, 20). Setiap skenario dievaluasi lima kali menggunakan Monte Carlo Cross-Validation, dengan metrik Presisi, Recall, dan F1-Score. Hasil menunjukkan korelasi positif antara jumlah contoh dan akurasi, namun dengan point of diminishing returns. Peningkatan kinerja drastis terjadi pada 1-5 shot, dan performa mencapai kejenuhan setelah 10 shot. Model cenderung memiliki Presisi lebih tinggi daripada Recall, memprioritaskan kebenaran ekstrak. Studi ini menyimpulkan bahwa strategi prompting optimal memerlukan keseimbangan akurasi dan efisiensi, merekomendasikan 5-10 contoh untuk sebagian besar aplikasi. Temuan ini memberikan panduan praktis untuk optimalisasi penggunaan LLM dalam ekstraksi informasi.

S1b1dc91728ee.title: Large Language Models are Few-Shot Clinical Information Extractors
S1b1dc91728ee.fulltext_snippet: A long-running goal of the clinical NLP community is the extraction of important variables trapped in clinical notes. However, roadblocks have included dataset shift from the general domain and a lack of public clinical corpora and annotations. In this work, we show that large language models, such as InstructGPT, perform well at zero- and few-shot information extraction from clinical text despite not being trained specifically for the clinical domain. Whereas text classification and generation performance have already been studied extensively in such models, here we additionally demonstrate how to leverage them to tackle a diverse set of NLP tasks which require more structured outputs, including span identification, token-level sequence classification, and relation extraction. Further, due to the dearth of available data to evaluate these systems, we introduce new datasets for benchmarking few-shot clinical information extraction based on a manual re-annotation of the CASI dataset for new tasks. On the clinical extraction tasks we studied, the GPT-3 systems significantly outperform existing zero- and few-shot baselines.

S6b5ec4980730.title: NLICE: Synthetic Medical Record Generation for Effective Primary Healthcare Differential Diagnosis
S6b5ec4980730.fulltext_snippet: This paper offers a systematic method for creating medical knowledge-grounded patient records for use in activities involving differential diagnosis. Additionally, an assessment of machine learning models that can differentiate between various conditions based on given symptoms is also provided. We use a public disease-symptom data source called SymCat in combination with Synthea to construct the patients records. In order to increase the expressive nature of the synthetic data, we use a medically-standardized symptom modeling method called NLICE to augment the synthetic data with additional contextual information for each condition. In addition, Naive Bayes and Random Forest models are evaluated and compared on the synthetic data. The paper shows how to successfully construct SymCat-based and NLICE-based datasets. We also show results for the effectiveness of using the datasets to train predictive disease models. The SymCat-based dataset is able to train a Naive Bayes and Random Forest model yielding a 58.8% and 57.1% Top-1 accuracy score, respectively. In contrast, the NLICE-based dataset improves the results, with a Top-1 accuracy of 82.0% and Top-5 accuracy values of more than 90% for both models. Our proposed data generation approach solves a major barrier to the application of artificial intelligence methods in the healthcare domain. Our novel NLICE symptom modeling approach addresses the incomplete and insufficient information problem in the current binary symptom representation approach. The NLICE code is open sourced at https://github.com/guozhuoran918/NLICE.

S4c9cba91f131.title: EHRXQA: A Multi-Modal Question Answering Dataset for Electronic Health Records with Chest X-ray Images
S4c9cba91f131.fulltext_snippet: Electronic Health Records (EHRs), which contain patients' medical histories in various multi-modal formats, often overlook the potential for joint reasoning across imaging and table modalities underexplored in current EHR Question Answering (QA) systems. In this paper, we introduce EHRXQA, a novel multi-modal question answering dataset combining structured EHRs and chest X-ray images. To develop our dataset, we first construct two uni-modal resources: 1) The MIMIC-CXR-VQA dataset, our newly created medical visual question answering (VQA) benchmark, specifically designed to augment the imaging modality in EHR QA, and 2) EHRSQL (MIMIC-IV), a refashioned version of a previously established table-based EHR QA dataset. By integrating these two uni-modal resources, we successfully construct a multi-modal EHR QA dataset that necessitates both uni-modal and cross-modal reasoning. To address the unique challenges of multi-modal questions within EHRs, we propose a NeuralSQL-based strategy equipped with an external VQA API. This pioneering endeavor enhances engagement with multi-modal EHR sources and we believe that our dataset can catalyze advances in real-world medical scenarios such as clinical decision-making and research. EHRXQA is available at https://github.com/baeseongsu/ehrxqa.

This article presents a novel approach for conceptualizing and operationalizing diagnostic task complexity as a multi-dimensional construct, which employs the readily available International Classification of Diseases codes from medical encounters in hospitals and uses Analytic Hierarchical Process methodology. We demonstrate the reliability of the proposed approach and show that despite using a relatively simple procedure, it is able to predict readmission rates just as well as (or even better) than some of the sophisticated measures that have been used in recent studies (namely, the LaCE score index).

S7a7d0ae97252.title: Sprague-Grundy values and complexity for LCTR
S7a7d0ae97252.fulltext_snippet: Given an integer partition of $n$, we consider the impartial combinatorial game LCTR in which moves consist of removing either the left column or top row of its Young diagram. We show that for both normal and misère play, the optimal strategy can consist mostly of mirroring the opponent's moves. We also establish that both LCTR and Downright are domestic as well as returnable, and on the other hand neither tame nor forced. For both games, those structural observations allow for computing the Sprague-Grundy value any position in $O(\log(n))$ time, assuming that the time unit allows for reading an integer, or performing a basic arithmetic operation. This improves on the previously known bound of $O(n)$ due to Ilić (2019). We also cover some other complexity measures of both games, such as state-space complexity, and number of leaves and nodes in the corresponding game tree.

S91290c69b985.fulltext_snippet: The paper presents the theoretical foundations and research design of a pre-registered quasi-experimental pilot study examining the structured integration of large language model (LLM) tools — specifically ChatGPT — into Legal English instruction for unde

Sfa0c168ffe47.title: Structured Clinical Interview for DSM Diagnosis
Sfa0c168ffe47.fulltext_snippet: Abstract The Structured Clinical Interview for DSM Diagnosis is a semistructured interview for making the major DSM‐IV Axis I Disorders (SCID‐I) and Axis II Personality Disorders (SCID‐II) diagnoses. Unlike fully structured clinical interviews that may be administered by lay interviewers (e.g., the Diagnostic Interview Schedule), the SCID is a semistructured interview, and it must be administered by a clinician or trained mental health professional. As the most widely used instrument for assessing Axis I disorders, the SCID‐I has been used in thousands of research studies since its introduction in 1986.

S949b14b4ef67.title:
mCodeGPT: Enhancing Cancer Research through Zero-Shot Information 
Extraction from Clinical Free Text Data
S949b14b4ef67.fulltext_snippet: Abstract The rapidly growing collection of clinical free text data about cancer provides an unprecedented opportunity to harness rich, real-world insights for advancing cancer research and treatment. At the same time, there is a formidable challenge in efficiently extracting, standardizing, and structuring this vast and unstructured information to derive meaningful conclusions. In this paper, we address the problem of information extraction to standardize and structure such free text using Large Language Models (LLMs) following the minimal Common Oncology Data Elements (mCODE™) structure. We propose mCodeGPT, a state-of-the-art data standardization tool Cancer related clinical notes. mCodeGPT ingests Cancer ontology knowledge base, automatically generates prompts in a hierarchical manner to extract information within the ontology from the clinical notes, and outputs results in a structured, tabular format. The pipeline is completely zero-shot, meaning it is annotation-free and does not require model training. Our new tool simplifies the conventional labor-intensive process of data collection, annotating, model training, and fine-tuning. To overcome challenges inherent in common LLMs, such as token size limitations, hallucination, and suboptimal accuracy in information extraction, we have developed three distinct methodologies for hierarchical prompt engineering. We conducted rigorous evaluations of mCodeGPT's efficacy in the domain of Cancer clinical note generation and information extraction. Employing the GPT-3.5-turbo model, we generated a diverse set of 400 simulated clinical notes spanning various Cancer types. The effectiveness of our three proposed prompt generation methods was further assessed using both OpenAI models and a selection of open-source LLM models. The outcomes of our research underscore the proficiency of our pipeline, showcasing an impressive 96% accuracy in information extraction. We published mCodeGPT on GitHub for other researchers to use.

Sc83f0295f251.title: Pengaruh Few-shot Learning pada Kinerja LLM untuk Ekstraksi Entitas Iklan Lowongan Kerja
Sc83f0295f251.fulltext_snippet: Ekstraksi informasi dari teks tidak terstruktur, seperti iklan lowongan kerja, merupakan tantangan besar. Pendekatan tradisional berbasis fine-tuning membutuhkan dataset berlabel masif dan sumber daya komputasi tinggi. Sebagai alternatif, Large Language Model (LLM) dengan In-Context Learning (ICL) menawarkan efisiensi. Penelitian ini menginvestigasi pengaruh few-shot learning, khususnya variasi jumlah contoh (k), terhadap akurasi LLM dalam ekstraksi entitas dari iklan lowongan kerja berbahasa Indonesia. Menggunakan model Gemini, eksperimen dilakukan dengan skenario zero-shot (k=0) hingga few-shot (k=1, 3, 5, 10, 20). Setiap skenario dievaluasi lima kali menggunakan Monte Carlo Cross-Validation, dengan metrik Presisi, Recall, dan F1-Score. Hasil menunjukkan korelasi positif antara jumlah contoh dan akurasi, namun dengan point of diminishing returns. Peningkatan kinerja drastis terjadi pada 1-5 shot, dan performa mencapai kejenuhan setelah 10 shot. Model cenderung memiliki Presisi lebih tinggi daripada Recall, memprioritaskan kebenaran ekstrak. Studi ini menyimpulkan bahwa strategi prompting optimal memerlukan keseimbangan akurasi dan efisiensi, merekomendasikan 5-10 contoh untuk sebagian besar aplikasi. Temuan ini memberikan panduan praktis untuk optimalisasi penggunaan LLM dalam ekstraksi informasi.

draft.title: Complexity-Calibrated LLM Collectives for Structured Clinical Diagnosis
draft.literature_gap: Prior work shows LLMs can perform few-shot clinical information extraction (arXiv:2205.12689), synthetic records can improve diagnostic model accuracy (NLICE, arXiv:2401.13756), multi-modal EHR QA remains challenging (EHRXQA, arXiv:2310.18652), physician collectives outperform individuals (JAMA Netw Open 2019), and diagnostic complexity can be operationalized from ICD codes via AHP (Ben-Assuli et al. 2019). No supplied work tests whether LLM diagnostic utility can be improved by combining structured LLM-based extraction, synthetic-record few-shot calibration, and complexity-stratified aggregation of multiple LLM differentials. Existing evaluations also lack a pre-registered falsification threshold for high-complexity cases.
draft.hypothesis: A complexity-calibrated LLM collective that (i) extracts structured clinical variables via few-shot prompting, (ii) generates multiple independent differential diagnoses, and (iii) weights their aggregation by an ICD/AHP-style diagnostic-complexity score will improve top-3 diagnostic accuracy on high-complexity synthetic primary-care cases by at least 5 percentage points over the best single-LLM or unstratified LLM-collective baseline, with a 95% bootstrap CI lower bound above 0.
draft.method: Use the public NLICE/SymCat pipeline to generate 450 synthetic primary-care vignettes with known condition labels. Compute a diagnostic-complexity score from ICD-coded condition features using an AHP-style weighting procedure inspired by Ben-Assuli et al.; split cases into low/medium/high complexity tertiles. On a 150-case development split, calibrate aggregation weights; reserve 300 cases (100 per tertile) for pre-registered testing. For each case, create a raw vignette input and a structured extraction produced by few-shot LLM prompting in the style of arXiv:2205.12689 (symptoms, duration, negatives, risk factors, red flags). Compare four strategies: S0 single zero-shot LLM diagnosis; S1 single LLM diagnosis conditioned on structured extraction; S2 unstratified collective of five diverse diagnostic prompts aggregated by weighted Borda voting; S3 complexity-calibrated collective using the same five prompts but aggregation weights conditioned on AHP complexity tertile and extraction completeness. Use fixed model/API version, temperature, and three stochastic repeats per case; report top-1/top-3 accuracy, Brier score, and calibration by complexity tertile. No human subjects or new clinical data collection.
draft.minimal_test: Pre-register the 300-case test set and S3 aggregation rule before test evaluation. Run S0-S3 on all test cases with three repeats. Primary comparison: S3 vs the better of S1 and S2 on the high-complexity tertile. Secondary comparisons: same delta on all cases and calibration/Brier changes. Use paired bootstrap over cases for 95% CIs.
draft.decisive_metric: Delta in top-3 diagnostic accuracy on high-complexity cases: S3 minus max(S1,S2). Support requires delta >= 0.05 with 95% paired-bootstrap CI lower bound > 0.
draft.supporting_result: S3 achieves top-3 accuracy at least 5 percentage points higher than max(S1,S2) on high-complexity cases, with CI lower bound >0, and does not reduce top-3 accuracy by more than 2 percentage points on low-complexity cases. Secondary support: S3 improves or preserves Brier score versus S2 in the high-complexity tertile.
draft.falsifying_result: S3's high-complexity top-3 accuracy advantage over max(S1,S2) is <2 percentage points, or its 95% CI includes 0, or S3 substantially degrades low-complexity accuracy (>5 percentage-point drop), or complexity-stratified weights fail to outperform unstratified aggregation on the pre-registered test set.
draft.related_work[1].use: Provides basis for few-shot LLM structured clinical information extraction used in S1 and S3.
draft.related_work[2].use: Provides synthetic NLICE/SymCat record-generation pipeline and known labels for feasible testing.
draft.related_work[3].use: Motivates structured EHR/QA-style evaluation and highlights multi-modal/structured clinical reasoning gaps; not directly used as dataset to avoid credentialing.
draft.related_work[4].use: Motivates collective aggregation of multiple diagnostic opinions and top-3 evaluation.
draft.related_work[5].use: Motivates ICD-based AHP diagnostic-complexity operationalization for stratification.
draft.limitations: Synthetic NLICE/SymCat cases may not reflect real EHR note noise or full multi-morbidity. The AHP-style complexity score is an operational proxy, not clinician-rated complexity. LLM API versions may drift, so fixed-version logging is required. The study evaluates diagnostic ranking, not treatment or clinical outcomes, and uses no practicing clinicians for adjudication. Results may not transfer to real-world EHRXQA-style multi-modal records.
draft.resource_plan.budget_envelope_assumed: <= US$750 API/compute only; no new data collection or human annotation
draft.resource_plan.data: NLICE/SymCat synthetic vignettes: 450 cases (150 dev, 300 test); public code and labels
draft.resource_plan.llm_calls: 450 cases x 5 prompts x 3 repeats + S0/S1 calls ~= 8,000-10,000 API calls; cap at US$450
draft.resource_plan.compute: Local scripts for generation, aggregation, bootstrap, and plotting; <= US$100
draft.resource_plan.risk_controls: Pre-register test split and S3 rule; fixed API model/version; log all prompts/outputs; use three repeats to estimate variance; stop if API cost exceeds US$600 before test phase

draft.title: The Disagreement Compass: Inter-LLM Opinion Spread as a Validated Diagnostic-Complexity Meter for Cost-Aware Deliberation and Abstention
draft.hypothesis: The spread of diagnoses across a panel of persona-diverse LLM 'physicians' is a cheap, observable proxy for true diagnostic complexity, and can route expensive multi-agent debate and abstention only to genuinely hard cases. We avoid circular validation against debate-gain; instead we test (a) that disagreement rises monotonically with an injected, ground-truth complexity knob (symptom overlap) in synthetic records, (b) that 'hard-case' rankings agree across independent model families (a signature of real complexity vs model-specific noise), and (c) that disagreement correlates with IRT-estimated latent item difficulty, which prior work shows is recoverable from diverse machine response patterns and correlates with human difficulty. The medical setting is ideal because it offers a controllable complexity axis and a ground-truth notion of collective benefit.
draft.related_work: Multi-agent LLM debate (Du et al. 2023; Liang et al. 2023) improves reasoning but assumes always-on debate, optimizes only final accuracy, and ignores cost. Self-consistency (Wang et al. 2022) samples one model and averages votes, ignoring persona diversity and clinical difficulty. Semantic Entropy (Kuhn et al. 2023) uses single-model meaning-clustering to detect hallucination; we instead use inter-agent persona diversity to measure clinical complexity and drive routing — a different object, signal source, and objective. Selective-prediction work relies on token log-probs/verbalized confidence, miscalibrated in medicine. Collective-intelligence studies (r04) show physician pooling reduces misdiagnosis but do not model when pooling helps. Complexity work (r05) uses proprietary indicators, unconnected to machine deliberation. IRT for NLP (Lalor et al. 2019; Vania et al. 2021) estimates latent item difficulty from response patterns but does not connect it to inter-agent LLM disagreement, routing, or abstention. Adaptive-compute/MoE routing uses token-level or heuristic signals; we route by clinically-grounded inter-agent disagreement. Our contribution closes the loop between complexity measurement (r05), collective intelligence (r04), IRT (Lalor), and LLM panels (r01/r02/r03).
draft.approach: Pooling physicians' diagnoses reduces misdiagnosis, and diagnostic complexity drives outcomes, yet we lack cheap ways to measure complexity or decide when pooling is worth its cost. We ask whether disagreement among a panel of persona-diverse LLM 'physicians' is a practical, validated complexity meter that can route deliberation and abstention. We instantiate panels with diverse specialties and reasoning styles and measure disagreement via predictive entropy, semantic answer-cluster count, and pairwise diagnostic divergence. Rather than validate circularly against the gain from debate, we (i) verify disagreement rises monotonically with an injected symptom-overlap complexity knob in synthetic differential-diagnosis records, (ii) test cross-family consistency — whether hard-case rankings agree across independent model families — and (iii) correlate disagreement with IRT-estimated latent item difficulty, which prior work recovers from diverse machine response patterns with human correlation. We then build a cost-aware router that triggers debate or abstention above a disagreement threshold and evaluate the accuracy-vs-#LLM-calls Pareto frontier, risk-coverage/AURC, and calibration (ECE) against log-prob and semantic-entropy baselines. We expect disagreement-based routing to match always-on deliberation accuracy at a fraction of the cost with better-calibrated abstention, offering a validated, resource-efficient recipe for deploying LLM panels in clinical decision support.
draft.validation: E1 Baselines: on MedQA, MedMCQA, and PubMedQA, compare single LLM, self-consistency (k samples), persona-diverse panel majority vote, full multi-agent debate, plus log-prob and semantic-entropy confidence baselines; use Llama-3-8B, Mistral-7B, and a GPT-3.5-class API model under a fixed call budget. E2 Non-circular signal validation: (a) on Synthea/SymCat-NLICE records, sweep injected overlapping-symptom count and test monotonic increase of disagreement (Spearman rho); (b) cross-family consistency — rank-correlate per-case disagreement between independent model families (expect high rho if it reflects real complexity); (c) correlate disagreement with IRT latent difficulty estimated from a diverse ensemble response matrix. E3 Cost-aware router: threshold disagreement to choose single vs debate; sweep thresholds to trace accuracy-vs-#calls Pareto against always-on debate and random routing. E4 Selective prediction/abstention: risk-coverage curves and AURC using disagreement vs log-prob and semantic entropy; report ECE. E5 Ablations/generalization: panel size, persona diversity (homogeneous vs diverse), mixed-family panels, and an EHRXQA table+image subset to test transfer of the routing signal. Metrics: accuracy, macro-F1, #LLM calls/cost, AURC, coverage@fixed-risk, Spearman rho, ECE.
draft.limitations: (1) Disagreement may reflect linguistic ambiguity rather than clinical complexity; mitigated by the injected-complexity test and cross-family/IRT consistency, though neither proves clinical validity. (2) Cross-family correlation could arise from shared pretraining data rather than true difficulty; we pair it with the synthetic ground-truth test. (3) IRT assumes latent-trait structure and machine-derived difficulty is only partially validated against humans; results are correlational. (4) Multiple-choice benchmarks are imperfect proxies for real diagnosis; synthetic records and EHRXQA add complementary but limited external validity. (5) Personas may lack genuine diversity, collapsing to correlated errors; ablations address this. (6) API cost/stochasticity require fixed budgets and multiple seeds; small panels yield noisy disagreement, limiting rare-disease routing. (7) Debate-gain is used only as a downstream utility metric to avoid circularity, so it cannot itself confirm the complexity claim.

draft.alternative_explanations[1]: An observed difference could reflect LLM pretraining or API-computation differences rather than transferable clinical signal; this design reports that as a limitation and does not claim causal attribution.
draft.alternative_explanations[2]: An observed difference could reflect leakage, contamination or annotation inconsistency; the prespecified audits and negative controls are designed to detect some of these failure modes but cannot exclude non-verbatim contamination.
draft.alternative_explanations[3]: A stronger conventional baseline than the matched few-shot baseline could reduce or reverse any apparent LLM advantage; a full-training baseline, if available, is secondary and cannot replace the matched comparator.
draft.analysis.aggregation: Compute paired case-level differences within each task and stratum. Report task-specific estimates separately. If multiple tasks are admitted and the equal-weight task-level macro-average was frozen at Preparation, report it as a separate prespecified aggregate; otherwise it is descriptive only. Do not pool cases across tasks as independent replications.
draft.analysis.estimand: Within each admitted public clinical task and split, the paired case-level difference in calibration-adjusted decision performance between the LLM-assisted pipeline and the matched conventional clinical NLP baseline, measured by Brier score, net benefit at the prespecified primary threshold, and decision accuracy, with task-level reporting and prespecified stratification.
draft.analysis.exclusion_rules[1]: Exclude a case from paired analysis only when the reference decision or a required pipeline score is missing before audit; report counts and reasons and do not impute outcomes.
draft.analysis.exclusion_rules[2]: Exclude a task from the primary comparison if admission checks fail, if no calibration split disjoint from test exists, or if no implementable matched conventional baseline is available within the academic-lab-default budget.
draft.analysis.exclusion_rules[3]: Report a prespecified sensitivity analysis excluding contaminated cases flagged by the leakage audit; do not silently remove flagged cases from the primary analysis.
draft.analysis.independent_unit: Clinical case or record within a prespecified task and split; clustered by patient or document where identifiers exist. Task is the unit of generalization, not the independent case unit.
draft.analysis.interpretation_rules[1]: Support: after audit gates, the paired LLM-minus-baseline Brier difference is below zero and the net-benefit difference at the primary threshold is above zero in the primary analysis and the lower-complexity in-distribution stratum, with two-sided 95% intervals excluding zero for both co-primary metrics after Holm correction, and decision accuracy is not lower.
draft.analysis.interpretation_rules[2]: Refutation: the two-sided 95% intervals exclude benefit and are consistent with harm or no benefit for the co-primary metrics in the primary analysis and the lower-complexity in-distribution stratum; non-significance alone is not refutation.
draft.analysis.interpretation_rules[3]: Futility or inconclusive: intervals include no benefit and a meaningful benefit or harm, or are too wide to separate the prespecified possibilities; report as inconclusive without claiming support or refutation.
draft.analysis.interpretation_rules[4]: A negative result is valid research and does not by itself indicate execution failure.
draft.analysis.interpretation_rules[5]: Do not interpret gains that appear only in contaminated cases, only after test-outcome threshold changes, or only in descriptive secondary thresholds or strata as support for the primary claim.
draft.analysis.interpretation_rules[6]: If model lineage cannot be documented as InstructGPT-family, relabel all results as generic API-model results and mark the InstructGPT-specific hypothesis untested.
draft.analysis.interpretation_rules[7]: Secondary thresholds, secondary strata and any non-prespecified macro-average are descriptive; they cannot replace the primary analysis.
draft.analysis.metrics[2]: net benefit at prespecified primary threshold p_t
draft.analysis.uncertainty_method: Two-sided percentile 95% intervals from a paired cluster bootstrap at the patient or document level within each task, with 1000 replicates fixed before execution; if clustering or sample size makes this infeasible, fix the exact alternative at Preparation rather than choosing after seeing results. Apply Holm correction across the two co-primary metrics, Brier score and net benefit, for the primary claim; decision accuracy is supportive and is not used to rescue a failed co-primary result.

draft.decision_rules[1]: Admission gate: admit a task only when exact public dataset name, version, license, source, label schema, split definition and split hash are verified, splits are identical across pipelines, a calibration split disjoint from test exists, and a matched conventional baseline is implementable; otherwise exclude the task.
draft.decision_rules[2]: Model-identity gate: proceed with the InstructGPT-specific claim only if the exact API model identifier, snapshot or access date and provider documentation support InstructGPT-family lineage; otherwise relabel as generic API-model and mark the InstructGPT-specific hypothesis untested.
draft.decision_rules[3]: Audit gate: freeze leakage/contamination, label-consistency, negative-control and metric-discrimination outputs before primary analysis; if a control matches the pipeline at the primary threshold, revise the metric or threshold through a prespecified design change or report the result as non-discriminating rather than as support.
draft.decision_rules[4]: Support rule: co-primary Brier and net-benefit differences favor the LLM pipeline with two-sided 95% intervals excluding zero after Holm correction in the primary analysis and lower-complexity in-distribution stratum, and decision accuracy is not lower; report task-specific estimates and any prespecified macro-average.
draft.decision_rules[5]: Refutation rule: co-primary intervals exclude benefit and are consistent with harm or no benefit in the primary analysis and lower-complexity in-distribution stratum; non-significance alone is not refutation.
draft.decision_rules[6]: Futility/inconclusive rule: intervals include both no benefit and meaningful benefit or harm, or are too wide to separate them; report as inconclusive and do not claim support or refutation.
draft.decision_rules[7]: Interpretation boundary: do not use contaminated cases, post hoc thresholds, descriptive secondary strata or non-prespecified aggregation to support the primary claim; a negative result is valid and does not by itself indicate execution failure.
draft.decision_rules[8]: Resource and stopping rule: do not exceed the academic-lab-default budget; if planned calls or compute exceed it, stop and report the exact unmet need rather than substituting unregistered resources or changing the scientific question.
draft.falsification: The primary claim is refuted only if, after prespecified leakage and annotation controls and identical splits, the paired LLM-minus-baseline Brier-score interval excludes benefit and the net-benefit interval at the primary threshold excludes benefit, with decision accuracy showing no advantage, in the primary analysis and the prespecified lower-complexity in-distribution stratum. Non-significance alone is not falsification; intervals including both benefit and harm are inconclusive; a negative result is a valid research outcome.
draft.hypothesis: If zero-/few-shot extraction gains reflect transferable clinical signal rather than leakage or annotation artifacts, a documented OpenAI InstructGPT-family API-assisted clinical decision pipeline will show lower Brier score and higher net benefit and decision accuracy than a matched conventional clinical NLP baseline on identical public task definitions and splits, especially in lower-complexity in-distribution strata, with attenuation under distribution shift.

Upstream responsibility remains with the bound Method/Plan owner for supplying or verifying those identifiers; this Plan does not invent them.
draft.limitations[2]: The admitted evidence is source-specific zero-/few-shot clinical extraction evidence and an assumption that the latest OpenAI API generation is the InstructGPT model set; it does not establish decision-level calibration or utility, and the bridge to decision utility remains unproven.
draft.limitations[3]: No experiment execution or private-resource access is claimed or authorized here; this is a prospective design only.
draft.limitations[4]: Pretraining contamination cannot be fully excluded by public audits; exact and near-duplicate overlap audits bound only observable leakage and may miss non-verbatim contamination.
draft.limitations[5]: Annotation inconsistency may persist even after a blind audit, and a small adjudication sample may not represent all labels or ambiguous cases.

No empirical utility or execution is claimed.

This node produces no empirical result.

draft.protocol[4].system: You are a clinical information extraction system. Return only the requested structured output and a positive-class probability; do not use information outside the supplied case text, label definitions and demonstrations.

draft.randomization: Not a randomized treatment experiment. Conditions are paired deterministically at the case level, with the same cases, task instruction, label schema, K demonstrations, decision mapping, calibration split and thresholds across pipelines. Demonstration selection uses the fixed seed in the seeds field and only training-split cases; bootstrap resampling uses the same fixed seed. draft.sample_size_rationale: No uniform minimum sample size is imposed; each admitted task uses its public split size, with precision reported through paired cluster-bootstrap intervals. The design plans 1000 bootstrap replicates as a reproducible default. For each admitted task, the planned LLM generation call count is cases multiplied by R=5 when provider probabilities are unavailable, plus calibration-set calls; the conventional baseline and bootstrap use local compute. These counts will be reconciled against the academic-lab-default budget at Preparation. If intervals are too wide to separate benefit from harm or no benefit, the result is reported as inconclusive rather than as support or refutation.
draft.sampling_plan: Use only public clinical extraction tasks from the admitted source, including CASI-based few-shot benchmarking datasets where public and obtainable under the supplementary literature cutoff of 2024-04-21 inclusive. prior_work.title: Chain-of-Thought Prompting Elicits Reasoning in Large Language Models
prior_work.abstract: We explore how generating a chain of thought -- a series of intermediate reasoning steps -- significantly improves the ability of large language models to perform complex reasoning. In particular, we show how such reasoning abilities emerge naturally in sufficiently large language models via a simple method called chain of thought prompting, where a few chain of thought demonstrations are provided as exemplars in prompting. Experiments on three large language models show that chain of thought prompting improves performance on a range of arithmetic, commonsense, and symbolic reasoning tasks. The empirical gains can be striking. For instance, prompting a 540B-parameter language model with just eight chain of thought exemplars achieves state of the art accuracy on the GSM8K benchmark of math word problems, surpassing even finetuned GPT-3 with a verifier.

prior_work.title: Tree of Thoughts: Deliberate Problem Solving with Large Language Models
prior_work.abstract: Language models are increasingly being deployed for general problem solving across a wide range of tasks, but are still confined to token-level, left-to-right decision-making processes during inference. This means they can fall short in tasks that require exploration, strategic lookahead, or where initial decisions play a pivotal role. To surmount these challenges, we introduce a new framework for language model inference, Tree of Thoughts (ToT), which generalizes over the popular Chain of Thought approach to prompting language models, and enables exploration over coherent units of text (thoughts) that serve as intermediate steps toward problem solving. ToT allows LMs to perform deliberate decision making by considering multiple different reasoning paths and self-evaluating choices to decide the next course of action, as well as looking ahead or backtracking when necessary to make global choices. Our experiments show that ToT significantly enhances language models' problem-solving abilities on three novel tasks requiring non-trivial planning or search: Game of 24, Creative Writing, and Mini Crosswords. For instance, in Game of 24, while GPT-4 with chain-of-thought prompting only solved 4% of tasks, our method achieved a success rate of 74%. Code repo with all prompts: https://github.com/princeton-nlp/tree-of-thought-llm.

prior_work.title: PAL: Program-aided Language Models
prior_work.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have recently demonstrated an impressive ability to perform arithmetic and symbolic reasoning tasks, when provided with a few examples at test time ("few-shot prompting"). Much of this success can be attributed to prompting methods such as "chain-of-thought'', which employ LLMs for both understanding the problem description by decomposing it into steps, as well as solving each step of the problem. While LLMs seem to be adept at this sort of step-by-step decomposition, LLMs often make logical and arithmetic mistakes in the solution part, even when the problem is decomposed correctly. In this paper, we present Program-Aided Language models (PAL): a novel approach that uses the LLM to read natural language problems and generate programs as the intermediate reasoning steps, but offloads the solution step to a runtime such as a Python interpreter. With PAL, decomposing the natural language problem into runnable steps remains the only learning task for the LLM, while solving is delegated to the interpreter. We demonstrate this synergy between a neural LLM and a symbolic interpreter across 13 mathematical, symbolic, and algorithmic reasoning tasks from BIG-Bench Hard and other benchmarks. In all these natural language reasoning tasks, generating code using an LLM and reasoning using a Python interpreter leads to more accurate results than much larger models. For example, PAL using Codex achieves state-of-the-art few-shot accuracy on the GSM8K benchmark of math word problems, surpassing PaLM-540B which uses chain-of-thought by absolute 15% top-1. Our code and data are publicly available at http://reasonwithpal.com/ .

S3c0bad8b0e36.title: A Step-By-Step Guide to the Black-Litterman Model Incorporating User-specified Confidence Levels
attribution_passages: The Black-Litterman model enables investors to combine their unique views regarding the performance of various assets with the market equilibrium in a manner that results in intuitive, diversified portfolios. This paper consolidates insights from the relatively few works on the model and provides step-by-step instructions that enable the reader to implement this complex model. A new method for controlling the tilts and the final portfolio weights caused by views is introduced. The new method asserts that the magnitude of the tilts should be controlled by the user-specified confidence level based on an intuitive 0% to 100% confidence level. This is an intuitive technique for specifying one of most abstract mathematical parameters of the Black-Litterman model.

S90bfd9c3cb81.title: Collective Action and Intra-group Conflict with Fixed Budgets
attribution_passages: We study collective action under adverse incentives: each member of the group has a given budget ('use-it-or-lose-it') that is his private information and that can be used for contributions to make the group win a prize and for internal fights about this very prize. Even in the face of such rivalry in resource use, the group often succeeds to overcome the collective action problem in non-cooperative equilibrium. In one type of equilibrium, all group members jointly contribute; in the other type of equilibrium volunteers make full stand-alone contributions. Both types of equilibrium exist for larger and partially overlapping parameter ranges.

S681784dfc5b5.title: Retrieval-augmented Knowledge Graph Reasoning for Commonsense Question Answering
attribution_passages: Existing Knowledge Graph (KG) models for commonsense question answering present two challenges: (i) existing methods retrieved entities related to questions from the knowledge graph, which may extract noise and irrelevant nodes, and (ii) lack of interaction representation between questions and graph entities. However, current methods mainly focus on retrieving relevant entities with some noisy and irrelevant nodes. In this paper, we propose a novel Retrieval-augmented Knowledge Graph (RAKG) model, which solves the above issues through two key innovations. First, we leverage the density matrix to make the model reason along the corrected knowledge path and extract an enhanced knowledge graph subgraph. Second, we fuse representations of questions and graph entities through a bidirectional attention strategy, in which two representations fuse and update by Graph Convolutional Network (GCN). To evaluate the performance of our method, we conduct experiments on two widely-used benchmark datasets CommonsenseQA and OpenBookQA. The case study gives insight into findings that the augmented subgraph provides reasoning along the corrected knowledge path for question answering.

Se443d33d866d.title: Rings of Siegel-Jacobi forms of bounded relative index are not finitely generated
attribution_passages: We show that the ring of Siegel-Jacobi forms of fixed degree and of fixed or bounded ratio between weight and index is not finitely generated. Our main tool is the theory of toroidal b-divisors and their relation to convex geometry. As a byproduct of our methods, we prove a conjecture of Kramer about the representation of all Siegel-Jacobi forms as sections of certain line bundles and we recover a formula due to Tai for the asymptotic dimension of the space of Siegel-Jacobi forms of given ratio between weight and index.

Chain-of-thought prompting combined with pre-trained large language models has achieved encouraging results on complex reasoning tasks. In this paper, we propose a new decoding strategy, self-consistency, to replace the naive greedy decoding used in chain-of-thought prompting. It first samples a diverse set of reasoning paths instead of only taking the greedy one, and then selects the most consistent answer by marginalizing out the sampled reasoning paths.
