In this paper, we propose a novel Retrieval-augmented Knowledge Graph (RAKG) model, which solves the above issues through two key innovations. First, we leverage the density matrix to make the model reason along the corrected knowledge path and extract an enhanced knowledge graph subgraph. Second, we fuse representations of questions and graph entities through a bidirectional attention strategy, in which two representations fuse and update by Graph Convolutional Network (GCN). To evaluate the performance of our method, we conduct experiments on two widely-used benchmark datasets CommonsenseQA and OpenBookQA. The case study gives insight into findings that the augmented subgraph provides reasoning along the corrected knowledge path for question answering.

Se443d33d866d.title: Rings of Siegel-Jacobi forms of bounded relative index are not finitely generated
Se443d33d866d.fulltext_snippet: We show that the ring of Siegel-Jacobi forms of fixed degree and of fixed or bounded ratio between weight and index is not finitely generated. Our main tool is the theory of toroidal b-divisors and their relation to convex geometry. As a byproduct of our methods, we prove a conjecture of Kramer about the representation of all Siegel-Jacobi forms as sections of certain line bundles and we recover a formula due to Tai for the asymptotic dimension of the space of Siegel-Jacobi forms of given ratio between weight and index.

Sb8747b9e31a3.title: Self-Consistency Improves Chain of Thought Reasoning in Language Models
Sb8747b9e31a3.fulltext_snippet: Chain-of-thought prompting combined with pre-trained large language models has achieved encouraging results on complex reasoning tasks. In this paper, we propose a new decoding strategy, self-consistency, to replace the naive greedy decoding used in chain-of-thought prompting. It first samples a diverse set of reasoning paths instead of only taking the greedy one, and then selects the most consistent answer by marginalizing out the sampled reasoning paths. Self-consistency leverages the intuition that a complex reasoning problem typically admits multiple different ways of thinking leading to its unique correct answer. Our extensive empirical evaluation shows that self-consistency boosts the performance of chain-of-thought prompting with a striking margin on a range of popular arithmetic and commonsense reasoning benchmarks, including GSM8K (+17.9%), SVAMP (+11.0%), AQuA (+12.2%), StrategyQA (+6.4%) and ARC-challenge (+3.9%).

draft.title: Active Retrieval-Augmented Chain-of-Thought for Enhancing Reasoning in Large Language Models
draft.literature_gap: Existing methods such as Chain-of-Thought (CoT), Tree of Thoughts (ToT), and Program-Aided Language Models (PAL) improve reasoning by generating intermediate steps, exploring multiple paths, or offloading computation. However, they rely on static knowledge encoded in the model and do not actively seek external information or tools when the model is uncertain. This can lead to hallucinations or errors when the required knowledge is missing or outdated. There is a gap in dynamically retrieving relevant external knowledge or invoking tools at each reasoning step based on the model's confidence.
draft.hypothesis: Dynamically retrieving relevant external knowledge or tools at each reasoning step when the model's confidence is low will improve reasoning accuracy compared to static chain-of-thought prompting.
draft.method: We propose Active Retrieval-Augmented Reasoning (ARAR). At each reasoning step, the model generates a thought and a confidence score (via a lightweight calibration head or self-evaluation prompt). If confidence is below a threshold (e.g., 0.7), it triggers a retrieval query to a knowledge base (e.g., Wikipedia) or a tool (e.g., calculator) and incorporates the retrieved information into the next step. We compare against CoT, PAL, and ToT baselines on reasoning benchmarks using GPT-3.5 and Llama-2-13B.
draft.minimal_test: Evaluate on GSM8K (math word problems) and HotpotQA (multi-hop reasoning) using a subset of 100 examples each. Use GPT-3.5 via API and Llama-2-13B on a single GPU. Implement retrieval from Wikipedia using BM25 (or DPR) and a calculator tool. Measure exact match accuracy on GSM8K and F1 on HotpotQA.
draft.decisive_metric: Exact match accuracy on GSM8K and F1 on HotpotQA. We expect ARAR to improve accuracy by at least 5% absolute over CoT.
draft.supporting_result: ARAR achieves higher accuracy than CoT and PAL on both datasets, with statistically significant improvement (p<0.05) and at least 5% absolute gain over CoT on GSM8K.
draft.falsifying_result: No significant improvement or a degradation in accuracy compared to CoT on either dataset.
draft.related_work: Chain-of-Thought (Wei et al., 2023) shows that generating intermediate reasoning steps improves performance. Tree of Thoughts (Yao et al., 2023) generalizes CoT by exploring multiple reasoning paths with lookahead and backtracking. PAL (Gao et al., 2023) offloads computation to a Python interpreter by generating programs as intermediate steps. Our work builds on these by adding active retrieval to address knowledge gaps during reasoning.
draft.limitations: Retrieval latency and cost may limit real-time applications. Confidence calibration may be imperfect, leading to unnecessary or missed retrievals. Only tested on two datasets and two models; generalization to other reasoning tasks and larger models is uncertain. Retrieval quality depends on the external knowledge base.
draft.resource_plan: Use OpenAI API for GPT-3.5 (cost ~$0.002 per 1K tokens, 200 examples * ~500 tokens = ~$0.20). Use Llama-2-13B on a single A100 GPU for ~10 hours (cloud cost ~$30). Retrieval from Wikipedia using BM25 (open-source, no cost) and a simple calculator tool. Total budget under $500. Timeline: 2 weeks for implementation and experiments.

draft.title: Does Your Chain Predict a Difference? Counterfactual Predictive Consistency for Selecting LLM Reasoning
draft.hypothesis: A reasoning chain is trustworthy iff it is *predictive*: if it truly explains why the answer is A, then it should also license a specific, falsifiable prediction about what the answer would become under a minimal, chain-derived edit of the problem. We hypothesize that (1) correctness is better separated by this *counterfactual predictive accuracy* than by answer-space voting, and (2) selecting reasoning chains by whether their own predicted answer-flips actually materialize yields a decoding-time boost that self-consistency and unfreeze self-correction cannot obtain. The setting is uniquely suited because the generated counterfactual is executed as a fresh query, giving free, automatically checkable supervision with no ground-truth labels and no human feedback.
draft.related_work: Self-Consistency (Wang et al., 2022) marginalizes over sampled reasoning paths but uses only *final-answer agreement* as the signal; it ignores the chain's internal mechanics and is fragile when multiple wrong chains share the same wrong answer. Chain-of-Verification (Dhuliawala et al.) and Self-Refine/Reflexion (Madaan et al.; Shinn et al.) generate free-text self-feedback, which has been shown to fail or degrade reasoning without external grounding (Huang et al., 2023, 'LLMs Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet'). Our feedback is not a model opinion: it is an executed intervention that either matches or contradicts the chain's stated prediction. Counterfactual Simulatability (Chen et al., 2023) also probes counterfactuals of explanations but is an *evaluation framework* that relies on human inferences of counterfactuals and scores explanation precision; it is neither an inference-time selector nor automatically verified. Thought Experiments (Ma et al., 2023) merely scaffolding counterfactual prompting for moral MMLU, not verifying the model's predicted flips. Metamorphic testing for LLMs uses hand-authored per-task input-output relations; we instead have each chain *derive its own* relation and then hold it accountable for that relation, which makes the signal chain-specific and domain-general. To our knowledge, no prior work uses the *verified accuracy of a chain's own counterfactual predictions* as the selection criterion at inference time.
draft.approach: Large language models reason fluently, but a sampled chain-of-thought can arrive at the right answer for the wrong reasons, or the wrong answer while looking coherent; Self-Consistency mitigates this by majority-voting final answers, which discards everything the chains say about mechanism. We propose Flip-Consistency, an inference-time selector built on a simple asymmetry: a chain that genuinely explains an answer should be able to make a falsifiable prediction about a *different but related* input. Concretely, for each sampled chain we ask the model to propose a small set of minimal edits to the problem that, according to its own reasoning, must change the answer in a stated way (e.g., renaming entities leaves the answer unchanged; decrementing a quantity lowers a count by one; negating a premise flips a label). Each proposed counterfactual is then actually executed as a fresh query, and the chain is scored by the fraction of its predictions that materialize. Chains whose counterfactual predictions hold are selected; ties are broken by answer frequency. This creates automatically checkable, label-free feedback grounded in execution rather than self-opinion, at a compute cost comparable to Self-Consistency. We will test the core scientific claim—that counterfactual predictive accuracy separates correct from incorrect chains—on GSM8K/SVAMP/ASDiv, BBH logical deduction, and multi-hop QA, and evaluate accuracy-at-matched-query-budget against greedy CoT, Self-Consistency, Self-Refine, Chain-of-Verification, and a crucial ablation that executes the same perturbations but drops the prediction-matching step.
draft.validation:
Core diagnostic (falsifiable test of the hypothesis). Sample 1,000 problems from GSM8K and 500 from SVAMP/ASDiv; for each, sample K=5 CoT chains at T=0.7 with Llama-3-8B-Instruct and Qwen2-7B-Instruct (and one API model, GPT-4o-mini). Label each chain correct/incorrect by final-answer match. For every chain, elicit m=3 JSON-structured minimal edits, each with (perturbation type, edited problem, predicted answer). Execute each edited problem with the same model (T=0) and compute Flip Prediction Accuracy (FPA) = fraction of predictions matching the executed answer. Report the paired separation: mean FPA of correct vs. incorrect chains, AUROC of FPA as a correctness classifier at the chain level, and per-problem Spearman correlation between FPA and whether the majority answer is correct. A null result here falsifies the proposal; we budget this as experiment 1 because it is ~1 day of inference.

Main accuracy results. On GSM8K, SVAMP, ASDiv, MultiArith, BBH logical-deduction (3- and 5-object), and HotpotQA/StrategyQA: compare (a) greedy CoT, (b) Self-Consistency at K=5,10,20,40, (c) Self-Refine (1 and 2 rounds), (d) Chain-of-Verification, (e) Flip-Consistency with K=5,m=1..3, (f) Flip-Consistency + answer-frequency tie-break, and (g) an Ablation-Execute baseline that performs the identical extra queries but *discards* the predicted answers and simply votes across all original+perturbed runs. Plot accuracy vs. number of model queries so that all methods are compared at matched budget; (g) is the decisive control showing the gain comes from prediction verification, not from extra samples.

Chain-blind control. Repeat FPA with the reasoning chain removed from the prompt (only question + candidate perturbation). If chain-blind FPA is as high as chain-informed FPA, the signal is a generic property of the problem, not of the chain; report the gap.

Perturbation-validity audit. Manually annotate 100 perturbations for validity (is the edit genuinely answer-preserving/answer-changing as claimed?) and report the fraction that are ill-posed; also run a 'type-ablated' variant restricted to entity-renaming edits (answer invariance), which are hardest to fake, as a robustness check. Additionally test a 'negation' edit family on BBH and a 'numeric-decrement' family on GSM8K to see which perturbation type carries most signal.

Failure analysis and faithfulness. Stratify gains by problem difficulty, by the number of reasoning steps, and by whether the model's chains agree on the final answer (low vs. high self-consistency). Report the 'right-answer-wrong-reasoning' rate: problems where the majority answer is correct but the highest-FPA chain differs, and vice versa, with 50 hand-inspected chains.

Metrics: task accuracy, FPA, AUROC, accuracy-per-query (query efficiency), and calibration of predicted flips (Brier score). All experiments use open-weight models plus one cheap API model, within a single A100 node.
draft.limitations: (1) The core risk is that FPA is merely another form of self-consistency: a model may be consistently wrong and thus confidently predict flips that agree with its own wrong reasoning. Our mitigation is the Ablation-Execute and chain-blind controls, but a null separation on the diagnostic would invalidate the premise. (2) Self-generated perturbations may be ill-posed (ambiguous, invalid, or trivially easy, e.g., 'set the number to 0'), creating a shortcut signal; the 100-example validity audit and type-ablated variants address this but cannot eliminate it. (3) Exact answer-matching is required for automatic verification, so the method is best suited to closed-form tasks (math, logic, multiple choice); extending to free-form generation would need fuzzy equivalence or a judge model, which reintroduces the unfreeze-feedback problem we are trying to escape. (4) The method costs m extra queries per chain; if m must be large, savings over Self-Consistency vanish. (5) The perturbation elicitation prompt is a design choice; results may be sensitive to phrasing, and we risk over-tuning it on GSM8K. (6) A related risk is 'prediction leakage': asking for a predicted answer may let the model use a shallow heuristic (e.g., 'negation flips yes/no') without consulting the chain—hence the chain-blind control. (7) Gains may be small on tasks where chains are short and self-consistency already saturates (e.g., easy arithmetic).

draft.claims[1].text: The supplied source evidence describes self-consistency as replacing greedy decoding in chain-of-thought prompting by sampling diverse reasoning paths and selecting the most consistent answer, and states that it applies only when the final answer comes from a fixed answer set. These are source-specific conditions, not results of the prospective design.
draft.claims[2].text: The supplied source reports that self-consistency outperforms beam search on UL2-20B when compared with the same number of beams and reasoning paths, and reports benchmark accuracy gains on GSM8K, SVAMP, AQuA, StrategyQA, and ARC-challenge. These are reported source findings; the present Proposal does not claim to have reproduced them.
draft.claims[3].text: The supplied source reports model-specific sampling parameters, including T=0.5 or T=0.7 with top-k=40 and GPT-3 without top-k truncation. The planned fixed T=0.7 and top-k=40 manipulation across models is therefore newly specified and is not a faithful replication of the source's model-specific protocol.
draft.claims[4].section: Source hypotheses and planned attribution test
draft.claims[4].text: The supplied source hypothesizes that correct reasoning processes tend to agree more on final answers than incorrect processes and attributes self-consistency's advantage over beam search to diverse sampled paths. The proposed trace-validity and trace-consistency audits and the aggregation-only low-diversity control are planned tests of that attribution; their outcomes remain unknown.
draft.claims[5].section: Source candidate-count claim and planned compute curve
draft.claims[5].text: The supplied source reports that increasing the number of sampled reasoning paths improves accuracy in its setting. The proposed N in {2,4,8} candidate-count cost-accuracy analysis is a planned prospective computation and is not an executed result or a transfer of that source finding to the planned checkpoints.
draft.gap: Supplied source evidence reports self-consistency performance comparisons and attributes advantages to diverse sampling, but it does not isolate trace validity and trace consistency from answer aggregation and sampling artifacts. Exact public checkpoint identities, few-shot exemplar identities, the audit codebook, and feasibility of N=4 remain unresolved. The gap is therefore an attribution and compute-robustness question, not evidence that the intervention works. The bound Method designates rq-2 as primary and rq-1/rq-3 as secondary; if that designation is intended to change, the repair belongs to the upstream Method owner. The bound Method also does not specify an unprompted baseline, so this Proposal does not silently add one.
draft.idea: The bound Idea is a matched candidate-generation by answer-aggregation factorial boundary test. Its testable prediction is that if valid and consistent diverse traces drive gains, diverse temperature sampling plus majority vote should outperform matched greedy and beam references and an aggregation-only low-diversity control, with trace-validity and trace-consistency indicators distinguishing conditions in the same direction as accuracy. If aggregation alone drives the gain, low-diversity sampling plus majority vote should match diverse sampling plus majority vote after frozen answer extraction. The bound falsifier is preserved as the planned disconfirming pattern; its outcome remains unknown.
draft.method[1]: Scope and claim status: this is a prospective design, not an executed experiment, and it reports no numerical result. It preserves the bound Method designation of rq-2 as primary and rq-1/rq-3 as secondary. The bound Method does not specify an unprompted baseline; this Proposal does not silently add one, so full coverage of an unprompted component of rq-1 would require an upstream Method repair if that baseline is mandatory.
draft.method[2]: Main attribution conditions at N=8 for every model-benchmark pair: (1) greedy single path, N=1, deterministic argmax, no aggregation; (2) beam search with beam width N=8, no aggregation, answer from top beam; (3) diverse temperature sampling, N=8, T=0.7, top-k=40, no aggregation, answer from the first sampled candidate in fixed generation order; (4) diverse temperature sampling, N=8, T=0.7, top-k=40, majority vote after frozen extraction; (5) low-diversity repeated sampling, N=8, T=0.1, top-k=5, no aggregation, answer from the first sampled candidate; (6) low-diversity repeated sampling, N=8, T=0.1, top-k=5, majority vote after frozen extraction. Majority-vote ties are broken by the earliest candidate in fixed generation order. Candidate order, seeds, token counts, stop reasons, and raw generations are saved. Greedy is a lower-compute reference and is not treated as compute-matched to the N=8 conditions.
draft.method[3]: Compute-budget factor for rq-3: a pre-specified candidate-count factor N in {2,4,8} is run on a deterministic 50-item subset per benchmark using the same frozen prompts, stopping rule, extraction code, and three repetitions. The planned compute-budget curves cover diverse sampling plus majority vote, low-diversity sampling plus majority vote, and beam search with no aggregation; greedy N=1 on the same 50-item subset is retained only as a lower-compute reference. The N=8 points on the 50-item subset are run separately from the 100-item main factorial so that all compute levels use identical items. This adds no benchmarks or models. If N=4 is infeasible on all model-benchmark pairs, that reduction must be recorded as an explicit scoped limitation with an accountable decision before execution, not as silent narrowing.
draft.method[4]: Model-selection rule: the planned set is three publicly downloadable open-weight decoder-only checkpoints from one model family under a license permitting academic research, selected as the smallest, median, and largest parameter-count checkpoints available in that family at the time of freezing. Exact repository identifiers, commits, tokenizer revisions, and parameter counts are to be frozen in a resource manifest before Plan or execution. If the family exposes fewer than three public checkpoints, all available checkpoints are used and the rq-3 scale conclusion is explicitly limited. Private and API-only models are excluded because they are outside the public-resource envelope.
draft.method[5]: Benchmark item selection: fixed-answer-set tasks are GSM8K, SVAMP, AQuA, StrategyQA, and ARC-challenge from the supplied packet. For each benchmark, eligible items must come only from official public evaluation splits and must have a single extractable fixed answer. A deterministic SHA-256 ordering of benchmark name plus item identifier selects 100 items per benchmark, stratified by answer label where labels are available; if fewer than 100 eligible items exist, all are used and the shortfall is reported. The 50-item compute-budget subset is the first 50 items in the same frozen hash order. Selected item identifiers are frozen before runs. Few-shot exemplars come only from disjoint training material and never from selected evaluation items; evaluation answers are not placed in prompts.
draft.method[6]: Prompt, generation, and stopping rule: a single frozen few-shot chain-of-thought prompt per benchmark, with four exemplars selected by deterministic hash from training material, is used identically across models, conditions, and candidate counts. No per-condition prompt changes, formatting changes, or exemplar changes are allowed. Each candidate path has a maximum of 256 new tokens and stops at the pre-specified final-answer delimiter or at the token limit. Greedy uses the same prompt and token limit. All candidate paths, seeds, token counts, and stop reasons are stored.
draft.method[7]: Answer extraction: extraction code is frozen before runs and is identical across conditions. GSM8K and SVAMP take the final numeric value after the last answer marker, or the last numeric value if no marker is present; signs, commas, and dataset-defined equivalent fractions are normalized. AQuA and ARC-challenge take the final multiple-choice letter after the answer marker, or the last standalone choice letter. StrategyQA takes the final yes or no after the answer marker. Unparseable or multiple conflicting final answers are coded incorrect and flagged; no manual rescoring after seeing results. Majority vote is computed over normalized extracted answers with the earliest-candidate tie-break.
draft.method[8]: Compute and information matching: all N=8 main conditions use the same model, prompt, item, maximum new-token count, stopping rule, and candidate count. Beam search and both sampling families are matched on candidate count and maximum token budget at each N level; majority vote adds only the fixed extraction-and-counting operation. Generated tokens, stop reasons, and a documented FLOP proxy are recorded per question and candidate for every run. Observed compute differences among same-N conditions are reported rather than claimed to be exactly equal. The primary mechanism contrast is diverse sampling plus majority vote versus low-diversity sampling plus majority vote at N=8, with beam search same-candidate no-aggregation and greedy no-aggregation as references.
draft.method[9]: Degeneracy and extreme-value checks before execution: the analysis specification flags benchmarks where a constant answer policy or the label marginal alone attains accuracy comparable to intended conditions; such benchmarks cannot discriminate the mechanism and the associated claim is limited accordingly. At N=2, majority vote is tie-degenerate on split votes; tie rate is recorded and N=2 is interpreted only as a low-compute reference for the cost curve, not as a strong aggregation test. The low-diversity condition is the removal-of-diversity control: if it matches diverse plus majority vote, the design limits the claim to aggregation or sampling artifacts rather than valid diverse traces. These are design checks, not experimental results.
draft.method[10]: Repetitions and design allocation: each model-benchmark-condition cell in the N=8 main factorial is repeated three times with pre-specified seeds and independent generation order. The compute-budget subdesign uses the same three repetitions and seed set for N in {2,4,8} on the 50-item subset. The same selected items are used across conditions, models, N levels, and repetitions so that item-level paired comparisons are possible. All six main conditions are run for every model-benchmark pair; no condition is dropped after inspection of results.
draft.method[11]: Primary outcome and planned disconfirming pattern for rq-2: the primary outcome is paired answer accuracy after the frozen extraction rule. The decisive contrast is diverse sampling plus majority vote minus low-diversity sampling plus majority vote at N=8, paired by item within model and repetition. The diverse-trace attribution is disconfirmed if the pre-specified 95% paired bootstrap confidence interval for that difference includes zero or is negative after extraction controls, or if the trace-validity and trace-consistency indicators fail to distinguish the conditions in the same direction as accuracy. This is a planned analysis definition, not a result.
draft.method[12]: Planned compute-budget analysis for rq-3: for each model and condition, report item-level accuracy plus generated-token and FLOP-proxy cost; estimate cost-accuracy curves over N in {2,4,8} with paired bootstrap intervals. The pre-specified descriptive question is whether the diverse-plus-majority advantage over low-diversity-plus-majority and beam search changes in magnitude or sign across N and models. If the N=8 advantage is absent at N=2 and N=4 with intervals including zero, the rq-3 conclusion is limited to compute-dependent effects; if the curve is flat or reverses, that pattern is reported without treating it as support for the mechanism. No numerical outcome is claimed in this Proposal.
draft.method[13]: Trace-validity and trace-consistency coding: trace validity is human-coded on 20 candidate traces per model-benchmark-condition, sampled by deterministic hash across repetitions and candidate ranks. Two coders blind to condition assign each trace binary valid or invalid using a pre-specified codebook: valid requires every arithmetic, symbolic, or logical operation in the trace to be correct and the final conclusion to follow from those steps; ambiguous or unparseable traces are invalid but flagged separately. Disagreements are adjudicated by a third coder, and agreement is reported. Trace consistency is computed as the fraction of the N extracted candidate answers that equal the modal extracted answer, using saved generations and not accuracy labels; a separate human audit of five question groups per model-benchmark-condition checks that modal agreement is not created by extraction collisions.
draft.method[14]: Analysis freezing and reporting: before Plan, freeze the extraction code hash, audit codebook, item manifest, compute-subset manifest, prompt manifest, seed manifest, FLOP-proxy definition, and analysis script. Report all conditions, including null or negative results, with item-level paired summaries and the pre-specified confidence intervals. Optional larger candidate counts, additional benchmarks, or extra model scales are enhancements and are not mandatory contributions. No simulation, experiment, or numerical result is claimed as executed.
draft.problem: The proposal addresses whether inference-time reasoning interventions yield reliable multi-step reasoning gains relative to matched no-aggregation and simple-prompting references (rq-1); whether observed gains are explained by valid and consistent reasoning traces rather than answer selection, formatting, or sampling artifacts (rq-2); and how gain magnitude and robustness vary across task types, model scales, and compute budgets under public-resource constraints (rq-3). This is a prospective design. It reports no executed simulation, experiment, or numerical result, and it does not claim that the bound Method has been shown adequate by this drafting.
draft.risks[1]: The bound Method designates rq-2 as primary and rq-1/rq-3 as secondary. If the intended deliverable requires rq-1/rq-3 as primary claims, that is an upstream definition change requiring separate review, not a silent Proposal redesign.
draft.risks[2]: The bound Method does not specify an unprompted baseline. This Proposal preserves greedy single-path no-aggregation and same-candidate beam no-aggregation references but does not relabel them as an unprompted baseline; full coverage of the unprompted component of rq-1 remains unresolved upstream.
draft.risks[3]: Exact public model identities, revisions, and three-scale availability are not fixed by the supplied material; if three public scales are unavailable, rq-3 scale conclusions are limited.
draft.risks[4]: The fixed T=0.7 and top-k=40 setting is a newly specified manipulation and does not faithfully replicate the source's model-specific sampling parameters.
draft.risks[5]: The low-diversity T=0.1 and top-k=5 condition may be too deterministic or may retain enough diversity to weaken its role as an aggregation-only control; this affects attribution to aggregation artifacts.
draft.risks[6]: Trace-validity coding is subjective and the audit sample may miss rare reasoning errors; coder agreement and adjudication reduce but do not remove this limitation.
draft.risks[7]: Compute matching is approximate because beam search, early stopping, and sampling can produce different token use and FLOP proxies even with equal candidate counts.
draft.risks[8]: Public benchmark contamination, answer-extraction ambiguity, and parse failures coded as incorrect may bias or limit interpretation of accuracy differences.
draft.risks[9]: The rq-3 compute-budget conclusion is limited to candidate-count variation over three conditions on a 50-item subset; N=2 is tie-degenerate for majority vote, and if N=4 is not feasible the affected claim must be scoped explicitly at Proposal or Plan.
draft.risks[10]: Optional larger candidate counts or extra benchmarks are enhancements and are not required; treating them as requirements would change the public-resource envelope without a separate scientific decision.
draft.title: Prospective matched factorial proposal for diverse-trace versus aggregation attribution in self-consistency, with a candidate-count compute-budget analysis
draft.unknowns[1]: Exact public checkpoint repository identifiers, commits, tokenizer revisions, parameter counts, and whether three public scales in one family are available remain to be frozen and checked.
draft.unknowns[2]: Exact few-shot exemplar identities and the final trace-validity codebook are not fixed by the supplied material and require versioned manifests before Plan.
draft.unknowns[3]: Feasibility of N=4 on all model-benchmark pairs under the academic-lab public-resource envelope remains unknown and may require an explicitly scoped limitation.
draft.unknowns[4]: Whether the low-diversity aggregation control retains enough candidate variation to be informative remains a testable design risk, not a known result.
draft.unknowns[5]: Whether an unprompted baseline is mandatory for rq-1 remains an upstream Method question; this Proposal does not add that condition.
draft.unknowns[6]: Adequacy of the bound Method, including the primary/secondary RQ designation and the low-diversity control, must be decided by independent Review; this Proposal does not assert that review has accepted it.
draft.unknowns[7]: Public benchmark contamination and answer-extraction ambiguity remain unresolved limitations to be addressed in the Plan and result reporting.
draft.validation[1]: An independent analyst re-extracts answers from hash-manifested raw generations using the frozen extraction code and independently recomputes accuracy, modal-answer consistency, paired differences, and cost-accuracy curves from recorded token and FLOP-proxy logs; disagreements are adjudicated and both computations are reported.
draft.validation[2]: Two coders blind to condition apply the frozen trace-validity codebook to the pre-specified audit sample; agreement and adjudication are reported, and no author self-assessment is used as the sole validity reference.
draft.validation[3]: A separate reviewer checks candidate counts, N levels, seeds, prompts, stopping rules, token budgets, and the shared 50-item compute subset against the Method manifest to verify that same-N conditions are matched and that greedy is reported as a lower-compute reference.
draft.validation[4]: A leakage check verifies that selected evaluation items do not appear as few-shot exemplars and that evaluation answers are absent from prompts; item identifiers, compute-subset identifiers, and prompt exemplars are frozen and auditable.
draft.validation[5]: The pre-specified analysis is checked for the disconfirming pattern, including the diverse-plus-majority versus low-diversity-plus-majority paired contrast at N=8 and the N in {2,4,8} cost-accuracy curves; all conditions are reported regardless of direction.
draft.validation[6]: No success claim is based on a job status, output hash, or producer self-report; validation covers independent recomputation and coding review only and does not assert that the scientific hypothesis is true.

This restricted form of supervision limits their generality and usability since additional labeled data is needed to specify any other visual concept. Learning directly from raw text about images is a promising alternative which leverages a much broader source of supervision. We demonstrate that the simple pre-training task of predicting which caption goes with which image is an efficient and scalable way to learn SOTA image representations from scratch on a dataset of 400 million (image, text) pairs collected from the internet. prior_work.title: Learning Transferable Visual Models From Natural Language Supervision
prior_work.abstract: State-of-the-art computer vision systems are trained to predict a fixed set of predetermined object categories. This restricted form of supervision limits their generality and usability since additional labeled data is needed to specify any other visual concept. Learning directly from raw text about images is a promising alternative which leverages a much broader source of supervision. We demonstrate that the simple pre-training task of predicting which caption goes with which image is an efficient and scalable way to learn SOTA image representations from scratch on a dataset of 400 million (image, text) pairs collected from the internet. After pre-training, natural language is used to reference learned visual concepts (or describe new ones) enabling zero-shot transfer of the model to downstream tasks. We study the performance of this approach by benchmarking on over 30 different existing computer vision datasets, spanning tasks such as OCR, action recognition in videos, geo-localization, and many types of fine-grained object classification. The model transfers non-trivially to most tasks and is often competitive with a fully supervised baseline without the need for any dataset specific training. For instance, we match the accuracy of the original ResNet-50 on ImageNet zero-shot without needing to use any of the 1.28 million training examples it was trained on. We release our code and pre-trained model weights at https://github.com/OpenAI/CLIP.

prior_work.title: EV-SegNet: Semantic Segmentation for Event-based Cameras
prior_work.abstract: Event cameras, or Dynamic Vision Sensor (DVS), are very promising sensors which have shown several advantages over frame based cameras. However, most recent work on real applications of these cameras is focused on 3D reconstruction and 6-DOF camera tracking. Deep learning based approaches, which are leading the state-of-the-art in visual recognition tasks, could potentially take advantage of the benefits of DVS, but some adaptations are needed still needed in order to effectively work on these cameras. This work introduces a first baseline for semantic segmentation with this kind of data. We build a semantic segmentation CNN based on state-of-the-art techniques which takes event information as the only input. Besides, we propose a novel representation for DVS data that outperforms previously used event representations for related tasks. Since there is no existing labeled dataset for this task, we propose how to automatically generate approximated semantic segmentation labels for some sequences of the DDD17 dataset, which we publish together with the model, and demonstrate they are valid to train a model for DVS data only. We compare our results on semantic segmentation from DVS data with results using corresponding grayscale images, demonstrating how they are complementary and worth combining.

prior_work.title: Event-based Vision: A Survey
prior_work.abstract: Event cameras are bio-inspired sensors that differ from conventional frame cameras: Instead of capturing images at a fixed rate, they asynchronously measure per-pixel brightness changes, and output a stream of events that encode the time, location and sign of the brightness changes. Event cameras offer attractive properties compared to traditional cameras: high temporal resolution (in the order of microseconds), very high dynamic range (140 dB vs. 60 dB), low power consumption, and high pixel bandwidth (on the order of kHz) resulting in reduced motion blur. Hence, event cameras have a large potential for robotics and computer vision in challenging scenarios for traditional cameras, such as low-latency, high speed, and high dynamic range. However, novel methods are required to process the unconventional output of these sensors in order to unlock their potential. This paper provides a comprehensive overview of the emerging field of event-based vision, with a focus on the applications and the algorithms developed to unlock the outstanding properties of event cameras. We present event cameras from their working principle, the actual sensors that are available and the tasks that they have been used for, from low-level vision (feature detection and tracking, optic flow, etc.) to high-level vision (reconstruction, segmentation, recognition). We also discuss the techniques developed to process events, including learning-based techniques, as well as specialized processors for these novel sensors, such as spiking neural networks. Additionally, we highlight the challenges that remain to be tackled and the opportunities that lie ahead in the search for a more efficient, bio-inspired way for machines to perceive and interact with the world.

prior_work.title: ESS: Learning Event-based Semantic Segmentation from Still Images
prior_work.abstract: Retrieving accurate semantic information in challenging high dynamic range (HDR) and high-speed conditions remains an open challenge for image-based algorithms due to severe image degradations. Event cameras promise to address these challenges since they feature a much higher dynamic range and are resilient to motion blur. Nonetheless, semantic segmentation with event cameras is still in its infancy which is chiefly due to the lack of high-quality, labeled datasets. In this work, we introduce ESS (Event-based Semantic Segmentation), which tackles this problem by directly transferring the semantic segmentation task from existing labeled image datasets to unlabeled events via unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA). Compared to existing UDA methods, our approach aligns recurrent, motion-invariant event embeddings with image embeddings. For this reason, our method neither requires video data nor per-pixel alignment between images and events and, crucially, does not need to hallucinate motion from still images. Additionally, we introduce DSEC-Semantic, the first large-scale event-based dataset with fine-grained labels. We show that using image labels alone, ESS outperforms existing UDA approaches, and when combined with event labels, it even outperforms state-of-the-art supervised approaches on both DDD17 and DSEC-Semantic. Finally, ESS is general-purpose, which unlocks the vast amount of existing labeled image datasets and paves the way for new and exciting research directions in new fields previously inaccessible for event cameras.

Sb1b857b990c6.title: Text organization via projection from researcher‐space onto text‐space
attribution_passages: Purpose The purpose of this paper is to propose a new approach for organizing texts for researchers based on projection from researcher space (consisting of reasoning ability and research ability) onto text space (consisting of text features). Design/methodology/approach The projection from researcher space onto text space is performed on the grounds of the differences between the sets of essential text features which are consistent, respectively, for the reasoning ability (as researcher's existing ability) and the research ability (as researcher's desired ability) using the concept of a dependency graph. Findings Through the projection from researcher space onto text space, one can expect to find an effective text which can help a person with certain reasoning ability acquire a certain research ability in the related domain. Research limitations/implications Acquisition of reasoning ability (ies) may call for a comprehensive questionnaire or test protocol whose validation by the expert may not necessarily be convenient. Appropriate questionnaires/test protocols, as well as knowledge‐based models for the text features at different layers (to assure derivation of more reliable features), is suggested as future work. Practical implications A salient benefit of the proposed approach is its flexibility in responding to a wide range of users with different models. It thus can be used as an efficient tool for online e‐learning and e‐research purposes in cyber‐learning environment. Originality/value The originality of the paper mostly lies in the concept of projection from researcher space onto text space as an approach for provision of appropriate text features; and the application of dependency graph as a potential means for identifying those text features whose prerequisites exist in the research abilities of the researcher.

However, due to the modal divide and semantic differences, existing unsupervised methods cannot adequately bridge the modal differences, leading to suboptimal retrieval results. In this paper, we propose CLIPbased Cycle Alignment Hashing for unsupervised vision-text retrieval (CCAH), which aims to exploit the semantic link between the original features of modalities and the reconstructed features. Firstly we design a modal cyclic interaction method that aligns semantically within intramodality, where one modal feature reconstructs another modal feature, thus taking full account of the semantic similarity between intra-modal and inter-modal relationships. Secondly, introducing GAT into crossmodal retrieval tasks. Consider the influence of text neighbour nodes and add attention mechanisms to capture the global features of text modalities. Thirdly, Fine-grained extraction of image features using the CLIP visual coder. Finally, hash encoding is learning through hash functions. The experiments demonstrate on three widely used datasets that our proposed CCAH achieves satisfactory results in total retrieval accuracy. S41ec9dbf3834.title: Parrot Captions Teach CLIP to Spot Text
attribution_passages: These samples break the assumption that the CLIP models leverage text supervision to align the visual and language concepts.

Despite CLIP being the foundation model in numerous vision-language applications, the CLIP suffers from a severe text spotting bias. Such bias causes CLIP models to `Parrot' the visual text embedded within images while disregarding the authentic visual semantics. We uncover that in the most popular image-text dataset LAION-2B, the captions also densely parrot (spell) the text embedded in images. Our analysis shows that around 50% of images are embedded with visual text content, and around 30% of captions words are in these embedded visual content. Based on such observation, we thoroughly inspect the different released versions of CLIP models and verify that the visual text is the dominant factor in measuring the LAION-style image-text similarity for these models. To examine whether these parrot captions shape the text spotting bias, we train a series of CLIP models with LAION subsets curated by different parrot-caption-oriented criteria. We show that training with parrot captions easily shapes such bias but harms the expected visual-language representation learning in CLIP models. This suggests that it is urgent to revisit either the design of CLIP-like models or the existing image-text dataset curation pipeline built on CLIP score filtering.
