prior_work.title: A Closer Look at Machine Unlearning for Large Language Models
prior_work.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) may memorize sensitive or copyrighted content, raising privacy and legal concerns. Due to the high cost of retraining from scratch, researchers attempt to employ machine unlearning to remove specific content from LLMs while preserving the overall performance. In this paper, we discuss several issues in machine unlearning for LLMs and provide our insights on possible approaches. To address the issue of inadequate evaluation of model outputs after unlearning, we introduce three additional metrics to evaluate token diversity, sentence semantics, and factual correctness. We then categorize unlearning methods into untargeted and targeted, and discuss their issues respectively. Specifically, the behavior that untargeted unlearning attempts to approximate is unpredictable and may involve hallucinations, and existing regularization is insufficient for targeted unlearning. To alleviate these issues, we propose using the objective of maximizing entropy (ME) for untargeted unlearning and incorporate answer preservation (AP) loss as regularization for targeted unlearning. Experimental results across three scenarios, i.e., fictitious unlearning, continual unlearning, and real-world unlearning, demonstrate the effectiveness of our approaches. The code is available at https://github.com/sail-sg/closer-look-LLM-unlearning.

prior_work.title: Evaluating Deep Unlearning in Large Language Models
prior_work.abstract: Machine unlearning has emerged as an important component in developing safe and trustworthy models. Prior work on fact unlearning in LLMs has mostly focused on removing a specified target fact robustly, but often overlooks its deductive connections to other knowledge. We propose a new setting for fact unlearning, deep unlearning, where the goal is not only to remove a target fact but also to prevent it from being deduced via retained knowledge in the LLM and logical reasoning. We propose three novel metrics: Success-DU and Recall to measure unlearning efficacy, and Accuracy to measure the remainder model utility. To benchmark this setting, we leverage both (1) an existing real-world knowledge dataset, MQuAKE, that provides one-step deduction instances, and (2) newly construct a novel semi-synthetic dataset, Eval-DU, that allows multiple steps of realistic deductions among synthetic facts. Experiments reveal that current methods struggle with deep unlearning: they either fail to deeply unlearn, or excessively remove unrelated facts. Our results suggest that targeted algorithms may have to be developed for robust/deep fact unlearning in LLMs.

prior_work.title: Adversarial Machine Unlearning
prior_work.abstract: This paper focuses on the challenge of machine unlearning, aiming to remove the influence of specific training data on machine learning models. Traditionally, the development of unlearning algorithms runs parallel with that of membership inference attacks (MIA), a type of privacy threat to determine whether a data instance was used for training. However, the two strands are intimately connected: one can view machine unlearning through the lens of MIA success with respect to removed data. Recognizing this connection, we propose a game-theoretic framework that integrates MIAs into the design of unlearning algorithms. Specifically, we model the unlearning problem as a Stackelberg game in which an unlearner strives to unlearn specific training data from a model, while an auditor employs MIAs to detect the traces of the ostensibly removed data. Adopting this adversarial perspective allows the utilization of new attack advancements, facilitating the design of unlearning algorithms. Our framework stands out in two ways. First, it takes an adversarial approach and proactively incorporates the attacks into the design of unlearning algorithms. Secondly, it uses implicit differentiation to obtain the gradients that limit the attacker's success, thus benefiting the process of unlearning. We present empirical results to demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach for machine unlearning.

prior_work.title: System-Aware Unlearning Algorithms: Use Lesser, Forget Faster
prior_work.abstract: Machine unlearning addresses the problem of updating a machine learning model/system trained on a dataset $S$ so that the influence of a set of deletion requests $U \subseteq S$ on the unlearned model is minimized. The gold standard definition of unlearning demands that the updated model, after deletion, be nearly identical to the model obtained by retraining. This definition is designed for a worst-case attacker (one who can recover not only the unlearned model but also the remaining data samples, i.e., $S \setminus U$). Such a stringent definition has made developing efficient unlearning algorithms challenging. However, such strong attackers are also unrealistic. In this work, we propose a new definition, system-aware unlearning, which aims to provide unlearning guarantees against an attacker that can at best only gain access to the data stored in the system for learning/unlearning requests and not all of $S\setminus U$. With this new definition, we use the simple intuition that if a system can store less to make its learning/unlearning updates, it can be more secure and update more efficiently against a system-aware attacker. Towards that end, we present an exact system-aware unlearning algorithm for linear classification using a selective sampling-based approach, and we generalize the method for classification with general function classes. We theoretically analyze the tradeoffs between deletion capacity, accuracy, memory, and computation time.

Sd9af516ee832.title: Partially Blinded Unlearning: Class Unlearning for Deep Networks from Bayesian Perspective
attribution_passages: To follow regulations on individual data privacy and safety, machine learning models must systematically remove information learned from specific subsets of a user's training data that can no longer be utilized. To address this problem, machine unlearning has emerged as an important area of research, that helps remove information learned from specific subsets of training data from a pre-trained model without needing to retrain the whole model from scratch. The principal aim of this study is to formulate a methodology aimed for the purposeful elimination of information linked to a specific class of data from a pre-trained classification network. This intentional removal decreases the model's performance specifically concerning the unlearned data class while simultaneously minimizing any detrimental impacts on the model's performance in other classes. To achieve this goal, we frame the class unlearning problem from a Bayesian perspective, which yields a loss function that minimizes the log-likelihood associated with the unlearned data with a stability regularization in parameter space. This stability regularization incorporates Mohalanobis distance with respect to the Fisher Information matrix and L2 distance from the pre-trained model parameters. Our novel approach, termed Partially-Blinded Unlearning (PBU), surpasses existing state-of-the-art class unlearning methods, demonstrating superior effectiveness. Notably, PBU achieves this efficacy without requiring information about the entire training dataset but only of the unlearned data points, marking a distinctive feature of its performance.

S0ed27a6ea74c.title: A Multi-Hop Localization Algorithm Based on Path Tortuosity Correction and Hierarchical Anchor Extension for Wireless Sensor Networks
attribution_passages: In wireless sensor networks (WSNs), node localization technology serves as a critical foundation for Internet of Things (IoT) applications such as environmental monitoring and ecological protection. High-precision localization has long been a key challenge in IoT applications. However, traditional multi-hop localization algorithms suffer from insufficient localization accuracy in complex environments due to path tortuosity and error accumulation. To address this issue, this paper proposes DV-Hop-HLPT, a multi-hop localization algorithm based on a tortuosity model and a hierarchical strategy for reliable anchor nodes. The algorithm employs a hierarchical localization strategy to expand the anchor node set, incorporating high-precision localized nodes into the anchor node collection through received signal strength indication (RSSI) calibration and evaluating their reliability. To address the multi-hop path tortuosity problem, the algorithm constructs a tortuosity weight model by analyzing path information between anchor nodes, enabling dynamic correction of multi-hop path lengths. Combined with an incremental shortest path first (ISPF) algorithm to limit search depth, the approach enhances adaptability to dynamic networks. Finally, utilizing the tortuosity model and anchor node reliability, the unknown node coordinates are solved through regularized weighted least squares method. Experimental results demonstrate that under square and C-shaped network topologies, DV-Hop-HLPT reduces average normalized localization error by 50.15% and 70.95%, respectively, compared with DV-Hop, and shows significant improvements over other enhanced algorithms, effectively addressing the localization accuracy degradation problem caused by sparse anchor nodes in complex environments.

S5d98dc1fe6f6.title: Deep Learning-Based Unlearning of Dataset Bias for MRI Harmonisation and Confound Removal
attribution_passages: Abstract Increasingly large MRI neuroimaging datasets are becoming available, including many highly multi-site multi-scanner datasets. Combining the data from the different scanners is vital for increased statistical power; however, this leads to an increase in variance due to nonbiological factors such as the differences in acquisition protocols and hardware, which can mask signals of interest. We propose a deep learning based training scheme, inspired by domain adaptation techniques, which uses an iterative update approach to aim to create scanner-invariant features while simultaneously maintaining performance on the main task of interest, thus reducing the influence of scanner on network predictions. We demonstrate the framework for regression, classification and segmentation tasks with two different network architectures. We show that not only can the framework harmonise many-site datasets but it can also adapt to many data scenarios, including biased datasets and limited training labels. Finally, we show that the framework can be extended for the removal of other known confounds in addition to scanner. The overall framework is therefore flexible and should be applicable to a wide range of neuroimaging studies. 1. Highlights We demonstrate a flexible deep-learning-based harmonisation framework Applied to age prediction and segmentation tasks in a range of datasets Scanner information is removed, maintaining performance and improving generalisability The framework can be used with any feedforward network architecture It successfully removes additional confounds and works with varied distributions

S47e780699569.title: A Closer Look at Machine Unlearning for Large Language Models
S47e780699569.fulltext_snippet: Large language models (LLMs) may memorize sensitive or copyrighted content, raising privacy and legal concerns. Due to the high cost of retraining from scratch, researchers attempt to employ machine unlearning to remove specific content from LLMs while preserving the overall performance. In this paper, we discuss several issues in machine unlearning for LLMs and provide our insights on possible approaches. To address the issue of inadequate evaluation of model outputs after unlearning, we introduce three additional metrics to evaluate token diversity, sentence semantics, and factual correctness. We then categorize unlearning methods into untargeted and targeted, and discuss their issues respectively. Specifically, the behavior that untargeted unlearning attempts to approximate is unpredictable and may involve hallucinations, and existing regularization is insufficient for targeted unlearning. To alleviate these issues, we propose using the objective of maximizing entropy (ME) for untargeted unlearning and incorporate answer preservation (AP) loss as regularization for targeted unlearning. Experimental results across three scenarios, i.e., fictitious unlearning, continual unlearning, and real-world unlearning, demonstrate the effectiveness of our approaches. The code is available at https://github.com/sail-sg/closer-look-LLM-unlearning.

S10431739484a.title: Evaluating Deep Unlearning in Large Language Models
S10431739484a.fulltext_snippet: Machine unlearning has emerged as an important component in developing safe and trustworthy models. Prior work on fact unlearning in LLMs has mostly focused on removing a specified target fact robustly, but often overlooks its deductive connections to other knowledge. We propose a new setting for fact unlearning, deep unlearning, where the goal is not only to remove a target fact but also to prevent it from being deduced via retained knowledge in the LLM and logical reasoning. We propose three novel metrics: Success-DU and Recall to measure unlearning efficacy, and Accuracy to measure the remainder model utility. To benchmark this setting, we leverage both (1) an existing real-world knowledge dataset, MQuAKE, that provides one-step deduction instances, and (2) newly construct a novel semi-synthetic dataset, Eval-DU, that allows multiple steps of realistic deductions among synthetic facts. Experiments reveal that current methods struggle with deep unlearning: they either fail to deeply unlearn, or excessively remove unrelated facts. Our results suggest that targeted algorithms may have to be developed for robust/deep fact unlearning in LLMs.

S3e11af705b7b.title: Adversarial Machine Unlearning
S3e11af705b7b.fulltext_snippet: This paper focuses on the challenge of machine unlearning, aiming to remove the influence of specific training data on machine learning models. Traditionally, the development of unlearning algorithms runs parallel with that of membership inference attacks (MIA), a type of privacy threat to determine whether a data instance was used for training. However, the two strands are intimately connected: one can view machine unlearning through the lens of MIA success with respect to removed data. Recognizing this connection, we propose a game-theoretic framework that integrates MIAs into the design of unlearning algorithms. Specifically, we model the unlearning problem as a Stackelberg game in which an unlearner strives to unlearn specific training data from a model, while an auditor employs MIAs to detect the traces of the ostensibly removed data. Adopting this adversarial perspective allows the utilization of new attack advancements, facilitating the design of unlearning algorithms. Our framework stands out in two ways. First, it takes an adversarial approach and proactively incorporates the attacks into the design of unlearning algorithms. Secondly, it uses implicit differentiation to obtain the gradients that limit the attacker's success, thus benefiting the process of unlearning. We present empirical results to demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach for machine unlearning.

Sb3ebb664279a.title: System-Aware Unlearning Algorithms: Use Lesser, Forget Faster
Sb3ebb664279a.fulltext_snippet: Machine unlearning addresses the problem of updating a machine learning model/system trained on a dataset $S$ so that the influence of a set of deletion requests $U \subseteq S$ on the unlearned model is minimized. The gold standard definition of unlearning demands that the updated model, after deletion, be nearly identical to the model obtained by retraining. This definition is designed for a worst-case attacker (one who can recover not only the unlearned model but also the remaining data samples, i.e., $S \setminus U$). Such a stringent definition has made developing efficient unlearning algorithms challenging. However, such strong attackers are also unrealistic. In this work, we propose a new definition, system-aware unlearning, which aims to provide unlearning guarantees against an attacker that can at best only gain access to the data stored in the system for learning/unlearning requests and not all of $S\setminus U$. With this new definition, we use the simple intuition that if a system can store less to make its learning/unlearning updates, it can be more secure and update more efficiently against a system-aware attacker. Towards that end, we present an exact system-aware unlearning algorithm for linear classification using a selective sampling-based approach, and we generalize the method for classification with general function classes. We theoretically analyze the tradeoffs between deletion capacity, accuracy, memory, and computation time.

Sd9af516ee832.title: Partially Blinded Unlearning: Class Unlearning for Deep Networks from Bayesian Perspective
Sd9af516ee832.fulltext_snippet: To follow regulations on individual data privacy and safety, machine learning models must systematically remove information learned from specific subsets of a user's training data that can no longer be utilized. To address this problem, machine unlearning has emerged as an important area of research, that helps remove information learned from specific subsets of training data from a pre-trained model without needing to retrain the whole model from scratch. The principal aim of this study is to formulate a methodology aimed for the purposeful elimination of information linked to a specific class of data from a pre-trained classification network. This intentional removal decreases the model's performance specifically concerning the unlearned data class while simultaneously minimizing any detrimental impacts on the model's performance in other classes. To achieve this goal, we frame the class unlearning problem from a Bayesian perspective, which yields a loss function that minimizes the log-likelihood associated with the unlearned data with a stability regularization in parameter space. This stability regularization incorporates Mohalanobis distance with respect to the Fisher Information matrix and L2 distance from the pre-trained model parameters. Our novel approach, termed Partially-Blinded Unlearning (PBU), surpasses existing state-of-the-art class unlearning methods, demonstrating superior effectiveness. Notably, PBU achieves this efficacy without requiring information about the entire training dataset but only of the unlearned data points, marking a distinctive feature of its performance.

draft.title: Deep-Unlearning Audit: Testing Whether Targeted LLM Unlearning Survives Multi-Hop Deduction and Membership-Inference Auditing
draft.literature_gap: The supplied cluster exposes a specific evaluation gap: unlearning methods are scored mainly on direct target-fact removal (with token-diversity/semantics/factual-correctness additions in 2410.08109) and on one-step deduction in 2410.15153, while adversarial auditing via MIA is treated as a design tool in 2406.07687 and system-aware guarantees in 2506.06073 relax the threat model. No supplied paper jointly tests (i) whether an AP-regularized targeted unlearner from 2410.08109 actually blocks multi-step deductive recovery, and (ii) whether a cheap MIA auditor can predict that leakage. The gap is a missing falsifiable cross-evaluation: direct removal vs deep deductive removal vs auditor-detectable traces, with a retrain reference and a collateral-deletion diagnostic.
draft.hypothesis: H1: On synthetic multi-hop facts, the ME+AP targeted unlearning baseline from 2410.08109 removes the direct target fact but leaves one-/two-hop deductive recovery above the retrain reference, because AP preserves bridge facts that logically entail the deleted target. H1 predicts: retrain Deep Leakage Rate (DLR) <=5%, ME+AP baseline DLR >=25%, and a loss-based MIA auditor distinguishes deleted from retained facts with AUC >=0.65. H0: baseline DLR <=10% or near retrain, which would falsify the claimed deep-unlearning gap for this baseline.
draft.method: Build a controlled deletion set from Eval-DU (multi-step synthetic deduction chains, as used in 2410.15153) and MQuAKE one-step instances. Select K=200 target facts D with retained bridge sets B that entail D. Use open-weight Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct with LoRA (r=16) to create two reference models: M_all (trained on all facts) and M_retrain (identical recipe excluding D), giving an approximate gold standard. On M_all, run: (a) baseline ME+AP targeted unlearning from 2410.08109; (b) diagnostic ablation ME without AP; (c) an intervention adding an adversarial deduction-suppression loss on auditor-generated deduction prompts while applying AP only to bridges B. Evaluate with temperature 0 and deterministic answer extraction: direct target queries, one-hop and two-hop deduction queries constructed from B, plus retained-fact utility and MMLU-subset utility. Independently, train a loss/perplexity-threshold MIA auditor on D versus matched retained facts, following the adversarial MIA viewpoint of 2406.07687, and report AUC. Run 3 seeds; 100-item human spot-check for answer extraction.
draft.minimal_test: One model family, one deletion set, three seeds, two reference models, three unlearning variants, and one auditor. The test is a single pre-registered comparison of deep leakage and collateral utility between ME+AP baseline and the bridge-preserving adversarial intervention, with M_retrain as the floor and M_all as the ceiling. No proprietary weights; no future-paper answer keys.
draft.decisive_metric: Primary: Deep Leakage Rate (DLR), the fraction of deleted targets recoverable directly or by 1-/2-hop deduction at temperature 0. Support requires: M_retrain DLR <=5%; ME+AP baseline DLR >=25%; intervention DLR <=10% while retained-fact accuracy and MMLU-subset accuracy drop <=2 points versus ME+AP and MIA AUC falls to <=0.55. The hypothesis is falsified if baseline DLR <=10% or if the intervention cannot achieve a >=10 percentage-point DLR reduction without >2-point utility loss; auditor predictability is falsified if baseline MIA AUC <0.60 despite DLR >=25%.
draft.supporting_result: ME+AP baseline yields DLR about 0.28 (direct 0.04, one-hop 0.15, two-hop 0.09), M_retrain DLR 0.03, and MIA AUC 0.71. The bridge-preserving adversarial intervention reduces DLR to about 0.08 with retained-fact/MMLU accuracy within 1.2 points of ME+AP and MIA AUC 0.53. The no-AP ablation shows higher direct removal but DLR about 0.18 with a 6-point utility drop, confirming the over-removal failure mode.
draft.falsifying_result: Either the ME+AP baseline already achieves DLR <=0.10 (near M_retrain), showing that the deep-leakage gap does not apply to this baseline, or the intervention leaves DLR >=0.22 or requires >2-point utility loss to reach <=0.10, showing that bridge-preserving adversarial unlearning does not resolve the deductive-leakage tradeoff at this scale. A baseline MIA AUC <0.60 with high DLR would separately falsify the auditor-predicts-leakage claim.

draft.title: The Entailment Shadow: Auditing LLM Unlearning on Deductive Closures Instead of Seed Facts
draft.hypothesis: Current LLM unlearning methods suppress the literal forget fact but leave an 'entailment shadow': paraphrases, negations, and one-hop deductions of the same fact remain recoverable. We hypothesize that under the system-aware indistinguishability definition of unlearning, these models are still distinguishable from a model that never saw the fact, and that the size of this leakage scales monotonically with the fact's entailment-graph degree. A single minimal test can falsify this: if a cheap auditor cannot beat chance at separating an unlearned model from a never-trained model using only closure probes, the shadow does not exist and current seed-level evaluations are adequate.
draft.related_work: Q1MHvGmhyT (A Closer Look at Machine Unlearning for LLMs) explicitly flags that its newly introduced evaluation metrics are a point of concern, but evaluates primarily at the level of the seed fact and general utility. CIN2VRxPKU (Evaluating Deep Unlearning) is the closest work: it shows that logically deducible related facts survive unlearning, but it stops at measuring recall of related facts and does not connect this to an adversarial indistinguishability criterion. swWF948IiC (Adversarial Machine Unlearning) formalizes unlearning as a Stackelberg game with an MIA auditor, but only demonstrates on ResNet-18 image tasks, leaving the LLM/language regime untested. dYTjB86pcT (System Aware Unlearning) supplies the clean indistinguishability definition (observer cannot distinguish from a model trained on the smaller dataset without the deleted points) but provides no LLM empirical instantiation. This proposal distinguishes itself by (i) fusing closure-based evaluation with an auditor-based indistinguishability criterion into one metric (Closure-Auditor AUC), (ii) testing it on open-weight LLMs rather than ResNets, and (iii) testing a quantitative scaling prediction between entailment degree and leakage, which is not a trivial extension of any single supplied paper.
draft.approach: Machine unlearning for LLMs is typically evaluated by whether the model can no longer reproduce the exact forget fact. Recent work shows that logically related facts often survive, yet it remains unclear whether such 'entailment shadows' actually invalidate the unlearning claim under a rigorous definition. We propose a minimal falsifiable test that operationalizes the system-aware indistinguishability definition of unlearning for LLMs: an unlearned model should be indistinguishable from a model that never saw the fact, as judged by a cheap auditor restricted to deductive-closure probes (paraphrases, negations, and one-hop multi-hop deductions). Using public fact corpora and open-weight 7B models, we build per-fact entailment closures with an open NLI model, apply three published unlearning baselines (GA, NPO, WHP), and compute Closure-Auditor AUC (CA-AUC) using a logistic probe on hidden states plus a local LLM judge. We predict that CA-AUC stays well above chance even when seed-fact recall is near zero, and that CA-AUC increases with entailment-graph degree. Ablations replace entailment closures with random distractor facts (expect chance-level CA-AUC) and include a never-trained reference model. If confirmed, the result shows seed-level unlearning metrics are unsound and provides a cheap, reproducible audit that the community can adopt.
draft.validation: Setup: open-weight Llama-3-8B-Instruct and Phi-3-mini; public ToFU fictitious-author biographies (200 profiles) plus a real-fact subset from a public QA dataset; <=8 A100 GPU-days. (1) Closure construction: for each seed fact f, generate 5 paraphrase, 5 negation, and 5 one-hop multi-hop probes with the base model, keep only probes whose entailment is confirmed by an open NLI model (e.g., DeBERTa-NLI) above a fixed threshold; record entailment-graph degree k. (2) Unlearning baselines exactly as published: GA, NPO, and WHP, using their released hyperparameters, applied to the seed facts only. (3) Primary metric CA-AUC: train a logistic probe on layer-wise hidden states (and separately query a local LLM judge) to distinguish the unlearned model from a never-trained reference model on closure probes only; report AUC with 95% bootstrap CIs. Secondary: seed-fact recall, closure recall, and control-set retention on entity-frequency-matched facts not in the forget set. (4) Scaling test: regress CA-AUC on entailment degree k; prediction is a positive slope. (5) Failure-mode/ablation diagnostic: replace entailment closures with random distractor facts; CA-AUC should fall to chance (~0.5). Additional ablation: vary closure size and probe type to localize the leak. Falsification criterion: if CA-AUC <= 0.55 for all three methods while seed recall is low, the entailment-shadow hypothesis is rejected and seed-level metrics are adequate.
draft.limitations: (a) Closure construction depends on NLI/generator quality; noisy entailment labels could inflate or deflate CA-AUC. Mitigated by human spot-checks on 50 facts and the random-distractor ablation. (b) The auditor may exploit stylistic artifacts of unlearning rather than genuine fact leakage; mitigated by comparing a hidden-state probe against a prompt-only LLM judge and by the never-trained reference. (c) Results on 7B open models may not transfer to larger or proprietary models, though the qualitative claim is about metric validity. (d) ToFU facts are fictitious, so 'never saw the fact' reference models are easy to construct but real-world memorization may behave differently; the real-fact subset partially addresses this. (e) The proposal could be seen as an incremental extension of CIN2VRxPKU; the novelty claim rests on the auditor-indistinguishability fusion and the degree-scaling prediction, which we pre-register as the falsifiable core. (f) WHP/GA/NPO training stability and compute limits may force smaller forget sets, reducing statistical power.

draft.method[3]: Core definitions: a target fact is a TOFU forget-set QA record whose subject entity and relation are the object of unlearning. A direct probe asks for that target fact. An entity-sharing related fact is a distinct TOFU QA record in the same author profile that shares the target entity verbatim and is not the target fact. Direct suppression means no pre-specified direct probe template elicits the target answer under the normalized evaluator. Related-fact recovery means an entity-sharing related-fact cue causes the model to produce the target answer. Unrelated utility is performance on TOFU retain-split items whose author entities are not target entities. MIA auditor distinguishability is the auditor's cross-validated ability to separate the unlearned state from retrain_reference under declared knowledge.
draft.method[4]: Population and design scope: eligible target facts have at least one entity-sharing related fact in the same author profile; records without such a related fact are excluded and counted. The planned minimal validation uses 40 eligible target facts selected before execution by sorting eligible facts by a recorded hash of TOFU record ID and taking the first 40 after deduplicating by author entity; this is design scope, not a power claim. Direct probes and related probes use disjoint pre-specified prompt templates. Only entity-sharing related facts are used as the related-knowledge probe; the broader logical-deduction / indirect-inference recoverability part of rq-1 is excluded from this design's evidence basis and remains unresolved. Covering that disjunct requires either an accountable scope decision restricting rq-1 or an upstream Method revision adding a pre-specified indirect-inference probe; this Proposal does neither and does not claim coverage. Use three seeds per model_state and auditor_knowledge combination.
draft.method[5]: Factor levels: model_state is unlearned_whp_style_approx; retrain_reference; diagnostic_underforget, a controlled manipulation that suppresses direct target answers by direct-answer loss on target facts while retaining at least one entity-sharing related fact; and diagnostic_overforget, a controlled manipulation that degrades related or unrelated utility by additional retain-loss corruption. auditor_knowledge is limited, with public data distribution, model family, query access and the unlearning claim but not the target-fact list, membership labels, unlearning internals or retrain reference; or full, adding the target-fact list and a disjoint calibration set with membership labels but not held-out evaluation labels or model internals. Auditor architecture, training budget and query access are fixed across knowledge levels; calibration and evaluation data are disjoint; no target labels are leaked into the model. No condition is labeled a faithful supplied-paper baseline.
draft.method[6]: Measurement block A, direct suppression: apply pre-specified direct target-fact queries to each model state and seed. A target fact is directly suppressed only if the normalized exact-match evaluator returns no target-answer match across all direct templates. Evaluator, templates, decoding settings and reference answers are frozen before execution; prompt-order and paraphrase sensitivity are reported as diagnostics, not used post hoc to choose the primary outcome.
draft.method[7]: Measurement block B, entity-sharing related-fact recovery and related-fact retention: apply pre-specified cues that state or ask the entity-sharing related fact and then ask for the target fact. Recovery is recorded if the normalized evaluator returns the target answer. Related-fact accuracy is measured separately with direct queries about the related fact so that suppression of the related fact itself is not misread as recovery failure. The decisive RQ1 contrast is the conditional related-fact recovery rate among cases where direct suppression passes; this addresses only the entity-sharing related-knowledge disjunct of rq-1.
draft.method[8]: Measurement block C, unrelated utility: use TOFU retain-split items with target entities excluded and a pre-specified primary utility metric of normalized exact-match accuracy. The non-inferiority margin delta_util is fixed by a design formula before execution: one retrain_reference standard deviation of the utility metric across the three pre-specified seeds, with a floor of 1 absolute percentage point. This is a planned computation, not an obtained estimate. Sensitivity to delta_util is reported as a diagnostic, not used to select the primary conclusion.
draft.method[9]: Measurement block D, MIA auditor distinguishability: train auditor-lr-loss-min-k-v1 to distinguish unlearned_whp_style_approx from retrain_reference outputs under each declared knowledge level with matched query budgets. The primary auditor metric is cross-validated distinguishability with a pre-specified chance band and permutation test; indistinguishability requires failure to reject chance under that pre-specified test. A positive-control split known to differ is used only as a manipulation check that the auditor can detect a signal; failure of that check makes the MIA block uninformative rather than support for genuine removal.
draft.method[10]: Condition crossing and fairness: run the four model_state levels against the two auditor_knowledge levels where applicable with the same base checkpoint, TOFU splits, query templates, evaluator, seed count and computational budget unless a condition definition requires otherwise. unlearned_whp_style_approx and retrain_reference receive the same target-fact access and public training data; any extra information, different hyperparameter budget or selection rule is recorded as a fairness difference and limits the attribution claim. retrain_reference is the primary comparator under the supplied system-aware unlearning framing, but it is a newly specified reference, not a faithful supplied-paper baseline. unlearned_whp_style_approx is a newly specified unlearned condition, not a faithful baseline.
draft.method[11]: Primary analysis rule, applied per target fact and seed before aggregation: if direct suppression fails, classify not_directly_suppressed. If direct suppression passes and entity-sharing related-fact recovery succeeds, classify surface_suppression. If direct suppression passes but the related fact itself is suppressed outside the related-fact margin, classify over_forgetting_or_related_fact_suppression. If direct suppression passes, related-fact recovery fails, and unrelated utility falls outside delta_util, classify utility_degradation_or_over_forgetting. If direct suppression passes, related-fact recovery fails, unrelated utility is within delta_util, and the MIA auditor distinguishes unlearned from retrain_reference under declared knowledge, classify auditor_artifact. If direct suppression passes, related-fact recovery fails, unrelated utility is within delta_util, and the MIA auditor is indistinguishable, classify genuine_removal_candidate. Aggregate counts and seed variability are reported; no single aggregate score replaces the four-block conjunction. RQ1 is addressed prospectively only by the conditional entity-sharing related-fact recovery contrast; RQ2 is addressed prospectively by the utility and MIA blocks conditional on direct suppression.
draft.method[12]: Diagnostic validity and disconfirming outcomes: diagnostic_underforget is valid only if it produces direct suppression with retained entity-sharing related facts and subsequent target recovery; otherwise the classification pipeline is declared uninformative for surface suppression. diagnostic_overforget is valid only if its intended utility or related-fact degradation is detected by the corresponding block; otherwise the margin or measurement is declared insensitive. The attribution method is disconfirmed as uninformative if the conjoint rule cannot separate conditions across the four blocks, if a constant all-pass or all-fail classifier reproduces the classification pattern, if the unlearned state is not distinguished from retrain_reference or the WHP-style approximation on any block, or if direct suppression fails throughout. Genuine-removal attribution is not supported if entity-sharing related-fact probes recover the target whenever direct suppression passes, if utility degradation or related-fact suppression fully explains outcomes, or if auditor distinguishability alone changes across knowledge conditions without target-specific recovery. These are prospective disconfirming outcomes, not obtained results.
draft.method[13]: Provenance and resource accounting: record TOFU v1.0 release identity, recorded file hashes, Qwen/Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct checkpoint identity and recorded commit hash, selection script, 40-fact eligible list, target and related definitions, prompt templates, decoding parameters, evaluator version, seed values, condition assignment, auditor code and splits, MIA query budgets, and raw per-fact/per-seed outputs. Exact supplied-paper baseline implementation and hyperparameters are absent from the admitted evidence; if an authorized upstream revision supplies them, they must be bound as a distinct faithful baseline condition outside this artifact.

prior_work.title: Exploring Zero-Shot Cross-Lingual Biomedical Concept Normalization via Large Language Models
prior_work.abstract: Abstract Over the past few years, discriminative and generative large language models (LLMs) have emerged as the predominant approaches in natural language processing. However, despite significant advancements, there remains a gap in comparing the performance of discriminative and generative LLMs in cross-lingual biomedical concept normalization. In this paper, we perform a comparative study across several LLMs on the challenging task of cross-lingual biomedical concept normalization via dense retrieval. We utilize the XL-BEL dataset covering 10 languages to evaluate the model’s capacity to generalize across various linguistic contexts without further adaptation. The experimental findings demonstrate that e5, a discriminative model, exhibited superior performance, whereas BioMistral emerged as the top-performing generative LLM. The code for reproducing the experiments is available at: https://github.com/hrouhizadeh/zsh_cl_bcn .

Seb8c5b90cfb7.title: Enhancing Cross-lingual Biomedical Concept Normalization Using Deep Neural Network Pretrained Language Models
attribution_passages: Abstract In this study, we propose a new approach for cross-lingual biomedical concept normalization, the process of mapping text in non-English documents to English concepts of a knowledge base. The resulting mappings, named as semantic annotations, enhance data integration and interoperability of documents in different languages. The US FDA (Food and Drug Administration), therefore, requires all submitted medical forms to be semantically annotated. These standardized medical forms are used in health care practice and biomedical research and are translated/adapted into various languages. Mapping them to the same concepts (normally in English) facilitates the comparison of multiple medical studies even cross-lingually. However, the translation and adaptation of these forms can cause them to deviate from its original text syntactically and in wording. This leads the conventional string matching methods to produce low-quality annotation results. Therefore, our new approach incorporates semantics into the cross-lingual concept normalization process. This is done using sentence embeddings generated by BERT-based pretrained language models. We evaluate the new approach by annotating entire questions of German medical forms with concepts in English, as required by the FDA. The new approach achieves an improvement of 136% in recall, 52% in precision and 66% in F-measure compared to the conventional string matching methods.

Sb642629d4dfa.title: Adapter Based Fine-Tuning of Pre-Trained Multilingual Language Models for Code-Mixed and Code-Switched Text Classification
attribution_passages: Abstract Code-mixing and code-switching (CMCS) are frequent features in online conversations. Classification of such text is challenging if one of the languages is low-resourced. Fine-tuning pre-trained multilingual language models (PMLMs) is a promising avenue for code-mixed text classification. In this paper, we explore adapter-based fine-tuning of PMLMs for CMCS text classification. We introduce sequential and parallel stacking of adapters, continuous fine-tuning of adapters, and training adapters without freezing the original model as novel techniques with respect to single-task CMCS text classification. We also present a newly annotated dataset for the classification of Sinhala-English code-mixed and code-switched text data, where Sinhala is a low-resourced language. Our dataset of 10000 user comments has been manually annotated for five classification tasks: sentiment analysis, humor detection, hate speech detection, language identification, and aspects identification, thus making it the first publicly available Sinhala-English CMCS dataset with the largest number of annotation types. In addition to this dataset, we also carried out experiments on our proposed techniques with Kannada-English and Hindi-English datasets. These experiments confirm that our adapter-based PMLM fine-tuning techniques outperform, or are on par with the basic fine-tuning of PMLM models.

Sb78de3d42605.title: Zero-Shot Transfer Learning using Affix and Correlated Cross-Lingual Embeddings.
attribution_passages: Learning morphologically supplemented embedding spaces using cross-lingual models has become an active area of research and facilitated many research breakthroughs in various applications such as machine translation, named entity recognition, document classification, and natural language inference. However, the field has not become customary for Southern African low-resourced languages. In this paper, we present, evaluate and benchmark a cohort of cross-lingual embeddings for the English-Southern African languages on two classification tasks: News Headlines Classification (NHC) and Named Entity Recognition (NER). Our methodology considers four agglutinative languages from the eleven official South African languages: Isixhosa, Sepedi, Sesotho, and Setswana. Canonical correlation analyses and VecMap are the two cross-lingual alignment strategies adopted for this study. Monolingual embeddings used in this work are Glove (source), and FastText (source and target) embeddings. Our results indicate that with enough comparable corpora, we can develop strong inter-joined representations between English and the considered Southern African languages. More specifically, the best zero-shot transfer results on the available Setswana NHC dataset were achieved using canonically correlated embeddings with Multi-layered perceptron as the training model (54.5% accuracy). Furthermore, our NER best performance was achieved using canonically correlated cross-lingual embeddings with Conditional Random Fields as the training model (96.4% F1 score). Collectively, this study’s results were competitive with the benchmarks of the explored NHC and NER datasets, on both zero-short NHC and NER tasks with our advantage being the use of very minimal resources.

Scdd1fc15d67d.title: Improving biomedical entity linking for complex entity mentions with LLM-based text simplification
attribution_passages: Abstract Large amounts of important medical information are captured in free-text documents in biomedical research and within healthcare systems, which can be made accessible through natural language processing (NLP). A key component in most biomedical NLP pipelines is entity linking, i.e. grounding textual mentions of named entities to a reference of medical concepts, usually derived from a terminology system, such as the Systematized Nomenclature of Medicine Clinical Terms. However, complex entity mentions, spanning multiple tokens, are notoriously hard to normalize due to the difficulty of finding appropriate candidate concepts. In this work, we propose an approach to preprocess such mentions for candidate generation, building upon recent advances in text simplification with generative large language models. We evaluate the feasibility of our method in the context of the entity linking track of the BioCreative VIII SympTEMIST shared task. We find that instructing the latest Generative Pre-trained Transformer model with a few-shot prompt for text simplification results in mention spans that are easier to normalize. Thus, we can improve recall during candidate generation by 2.9 percentage points compared to our baseline system, which achieved the best score in the original shared task evaluation. Furthermore, we show that this improvement in recall can be fully translated into top-1 accuracy through careful initialization of a subsequent reranking model. Our best system achieves an accuracy of 63.6% on the SympTEMIST test set. The proposed approach has been integrated into the open-source xMEN toolkit, which is available online via https://github.com/hpi-dhc/xmen.

Se57a628d8c5a.title: Mining Fine-Grained Image-Text Alignment for Zero-Shot Captioning via Text-Only Training
attribution_passages: Image captioning aims at generating descriptive and meaningful textual descriptions of images, enabling a broad range of vision-language applications. Prior works have demonstrated that harnessing the power of Contrastive Image Language Pre-training (CLIP) offers a promising approach to achieving zero-shot captioning, eliminating the need for expensive caption annotations. However, the widely observed modality gap in the latent space of CLIP harms the performance of zero-shot captioning by breaking the alignment between paired image-text features. To address this issue, we conduct an analysis on the CLIP latent space which leads to two findings. Firstly, we observe that the CLIP's visual feature of image subregions can achieve closer proximity to the paired caption due to the inherent information loss in text descriptions. In addition, we show that the modality gap between a paired image-text can be empirically modeled as a zero-mean Gaussian distribution. Motivated by the findings, we propose a novel zero-shot image captioning framework with text-only training to reduce the modality gap. In particular, we introduce a subregion feature aggregation to leverage local region information, which produces a compact visual representation for matching text representation. Moreover, we incorporate a noise injection and CLIP reranking strategy to boost captioning performance. We also extend our framework to build a zero-shot VQA pipeline, demonstrating its generality. Through extensive experiments on common captioning and VQA datasets such as MSCOCO, Flickr30k and VQAV2, we show that our method achieves remarkable performance improvements. Code is available at https://github.com/Artanic30/MacCap.

S480314cd9553.title: Discover and Cure: Concept-aware Mitigation of Spurious Correlation
attribution_passages: With human-interpretable concepts, DISC iteratively 1) discovers unstable concepts across different environments as spurious attributes, then 2) intervenes on the training data using the discovered concepts to reduce spurious correlation.

Deep neural networks often rely on spurious correlations to make predictions, which hinders generalization beyond training environments. For instance, models that associate cats with bed backgrounds can fail to predict the existence of cats in other environments without beds. Mitigating spurious correlations is crucial in building trustworthy models. However, the existing works lack transparency to offer insights into the mitigation process. In this work, we propose an interpretable framework, Discover and Cure (DISC), to tackle the issue. With human-interpretable concepts, DISC iteratively 1) discovers unstable concepts across different environments as spurious attributes, then 2) intervenes on the training data using the discovered concepts to reduce spurious correlation. Across systematic experiments, DISC provides superior generalization ability and interpretability than the existing approaches. Specifically, it outperforms the state-of-the-art methods on an object recognition task and a skin-lesion classification task by 7.5% and 9.6%, respectively. Additionally, we offer theoretical analysis and guarantees to understand the benefits of models trained by DISC. Code and data are available at https://github.com/Wuyxin/DISC.
Specifically, it outperforms the state-of-the-art methods on an object recognition task and a skin-lesion classification task by 7.5% and 9.6%, respectively.
A potential explanation is that the images in the concept bank do not exactly cover the spurious attributes, which hinders the strength of mitigation.

Overall, DISC outperforms most of the baselines in terms of the worst group accuracy. In particular, we obtain large performance gains over the best baselines in MetaShift and ISIC datasets by 7.5% and 9.6%, respectively.

S903b3bc9b469.title: Exploring Zero-Shot Cross-Lingual Biomedical Concept Normalization via Large Language Models
S903b3bc9b469.fulltext_snippet: Abstract Over the past few years, discriminative and generative large language models (LLMs) have emerged as the predominant approaches in natural language processing. However, despite significant advancements, there remains a gap in comparing the performance of discriminative and generative LLMs in cross-lingual biomedical concept normalization. In this paper, we perform a comparative study across several LLMs on the challenging task of cross-lingual biomedical concept normalization via dense retrieval. We utilize the XL-BEL dataset covering 10 languages to evaluate the model’s capacity to generalize across various linguistic contexts without further adaptation. The experimental findings demonstrate that e5, a discriminative model, exhibited superior performance, whereas BioMistral emerged as the top-performing generative LLM. The code for reproducing the experiments is available at: https://github.com/hrouhizadeh/zsh_cl_bcn .

Seb8c5b90cfb7.title: Enhancing Cross-lingual Biomedical Concept Normalization Using Deep Neural Network Pretrained Language Models
Seb8c5b90cfb7.fulltext_snippet: Abstract In this study, we propose a new approach for cross-lingual biomedical concept normalization, the process of mapping text in non-English documents to English concepts of a knowledge base. The resulting mappings, named as semantic annotations, enhance data integration and interoperability of documents in different languages. The US FDA (Food and Drug Administration), therefore, requires all submitted medical forms to be semantically annotated. These standardized medical forms are used in health care practice and biomedical research and are translated/adapted into various languages. Mapping them to the same concepts (normally in English) facilitates the comparison of multiple medical studies even cross-lingually. However, the translation and adaptation of these forms can cause them to deviate from its original text syntactically and in wording. This leads the conventional string matching methods to produce low-quality annotation results. Therefore, our new approach incorporates semantics into the cross-lingual concept normalization process. This is done using sentence embeddings generated by BERT-based pretrained language models. We evaluate the new approach by annotating entire questions of German medical forms with concepts in English, as required by the FDA. The new approach achieves an improvement of 136% in recall, 52% in precision and 66% in F-measure compared to the conventional string matching methods.

Sb642629d4dfa.title: Adapter Based Fine-Tuning of Pre-Trained Multilingual Language Models for Code-Mixed and Code-Switched Text Classification
Sb642629d4dfa.fulltext_snippet: Abstract Code-mixing and code-switching (CMCS) are frequent features in online conversations. Classification of such text is challenging if one of the languages is low-resourced. Fine-tuning pre-trained multilingual language models (PMLMs) is a promising avenue for code-mixed text classification. In this paper, we explore adapter-based fine-tuning of PMLMs for CMCS text classification. We introduce sequential and parallel stacking of adapters, continuous fine-tuning of adapters, and training adapters without freezing the original model as novel techniques with respect to single-task CMCS text classification. We also present a newly annotated dataset for the classification of Sinhala-English code-mixed and code-switched text data, where Sinhala is a low-resourced language. Our dataset of 10000 user comments has been manually annotated for five classification tasks: sentiment analysis, humor detection, hate speech detection, language identification, and aspects identification, thus making it the first publicly available Sinhala-English CMCS dataset with the largest number of annotation types. In addition to this dataset, we also carried out experiments on our proposed techniques with Kannada-English and Hindi-English datasets. These experiments confirm that our adapter-based PMLM fine-tuning techniques outperform, or are on par with the basic fine-tuning of PMLM models.

Sb78de3d42605.title: Zero-Shot Transfer Learning using Affix and Correlated Cross-Lingual Embeddings.
Sb78de3d42605.fulltext_snippet: Learning morphologically supplemented embedding spaces using cross-lingual models has become an active area of research and facilitated many research breakthroughs in various applications such as machine translation, named entity recognition, document classification, and natural language inference. However, the field has not become customary for Southern African low-resourced languages. In this paper, we present, evaluate and benchmark a cohort of cross-lingual embeddings for the English-Southern African languages on two classification tasks: News Headlines Classification (NHC) and Named Entity Recognition (NER). Our methodology considers four agglutinative languages from the eleven official South African languages: Isixhosa, Sepedi, Sesotho, and Setswana. Canonical correlation analyses and VecMap are the two cross-lingual alignment strategies adopted for this study. Monolingual embeddings used in this work are Glove (source), and FastText (source and target) embeddings. Our results indicate that with enough comparable corpora, we can develop strong inter-joined representations between English and the considered Southern African languages. More specifically, the best zero-shot transfer results on the available Setswana NHC dataset were achieved using canonically correlated embeddings with Multi-layered perceptron as the training model (54.5% accuracy). Furthermore, our NER best performance was achieved using canonically correlated cross-lingual embeddings with Conditional Random Fields as the training model (96.4% F1 score). Collectively, this study’s results were competitive with the benchmarks of the explored NHC and NER datasets, on both zero-short NHC and NER tasks with our advantage being the use of very minimal resources.

Scdd1fc15d67d.title: Improving biomedical entity linking for complex entity mentions with LLM-based text simplification
Scdd1fc15d67d.fulltext_snippet: Abstract Large amounts of important medical information are captured in free-text documents in biomedical research and within healthcare systems, which can be made accessible through natural language processing (NLP). A key component in most biomedical NLP pipelines is entity linking, i.e. grounding textual mentions of named entities to a reference of medical concepts, usually derived from a terminology system, such as the Systematized Nomenclature of Medicine Clinical Terms. However, complex entity mentions, spanning multiple tokens, are notoriously hard to normalize due to the difficulty of finding appropriate candidate concepts. In this work, we propose an approach to preprocess such mentions for candidate generation, building upon recent advances in text simplification with generative large language models. We evaluate the feasibility of our method in the context of the entity linking track of the BioCreative VIII SympTEMIST shared task. We find that instructing the latest Generative Pre-trained Transformer model with a few-shot prompt for text simplification results in mention spans that are easier to normalize. Thus, we can improve recall during candidate generation by 2.9 percentage points compared to our baseline system, which achieved the best score in the original shared task evaluation. Furthermore, we show that this improvement in recall can be fully translated into top-1 accuracy through careful initialization of a subsequent reranking model. Our best system achieves an accuracy of 63.6% on the SympTEMIST test set. The proposed approach has been integrated into the open-source xMEN toolkit, which is available online via https://github.com/hpi-dhc/xmen.

draft.title: Concept-Information-Bottleneck Adapter for Faithful Zero-Shot Cross-Lingual Biomedical Concept Normalization
draft.literature_gap: The supplied paper benchmarks discriminative e5 against generative BioMistral for zero-shot cross-lingual biomedical concept normalization on XL-BEL, but treats normalization as a black-box retrieval/generation problem. It does not test whether an explicit concept bottleneck can preserve zero-shot cross-lingual accuracy or whether concept-level intermediate variables are causally faithful. This leaves an evaluation gap: no concept-intervention diagnostic and no ablation separating a real concept bottleneck from a generic adapter.
draft.hypothesis: A frozen multilingual e5 encoder plus a sparse concept-information-bottleneck adapter trained only on English XL-BEL will match or improve zero-shot non-English Acc@1 over vanilla e5, and its top concept activations will be causally faithful: deleting top activated concepts will reduce normalization accuracy substantially more than deleting random concepts.
draft.method: Use XL-BEL across its 10 languages. Train on English only and evaluate zero-shot on the other languages. Baseline: intfloat/multilingual-e5 dense retrieval, the top discriminative model reported in the supplied paper. Proposed model: freeze e5, add a concept-information-bottleneck adapter that maps mention/query embeddings to K sparse concept logits using a Gaussian information-bottleneck KL penalty plus sparsity; normalize by scoring candidate concepts through the learned concept embedding table and reranking e5 candidates. Diagnostic ablations: (1) random/shuffled concept labels; (2) same adapter without concept supervision; (3) concept interventions that zero or swap top-k concept activations and measure accuracy change versus random-concept deletion. Use public XL-BEL data and open-weight e5/BioMistral only.
draft.minimal_test: One English-only CIB training run, zero-shot evaluation on all non-English XL-BEL languages, and a concept-deletion intervention on 500 examples per language comparing top-concept deletion, random-concept deletion, and a shuffled-label CIB control.
draft.decisive_metric: Primary: zero-shot Acc@1 averaged over non-English XL-BEL languages, ΔAcc@1 = CIB − e5. Faithfulness: top-concept deletion accuracy drop minus random-concept deletion accuracy drop.
draft.supporting_result: CIB is within 1 Acc@1 point of e5 on average, improves Acc@1 by at least 2 points in at least 3 non-English languages, and shows a faithfulness gap of at least 10 points over random deletion; the shuffled-label control does not show this gap.
draft.falsifying_result: CIB drops more than 2 Acc@1 points on average versus e5, or shows no language-level gain, or top-concept deletion is not at least 5 points more damaging than random deletion, or the shuffled-label control matches the true CIB intervention gap.
draft.related_work[1]: Supplied paper: Rouhizadeh et al. 2025, 'Exploring Zero-Shot Cross-Lingual Biomedical Concept Normalization via Large Language Models', which compares e5 and BioMistral on XL-BEL but does not test concept bottlenecks or concept-level faithfulness.
draft.limitations: Only XL-BEL concept coverage and languages are tested; English-only bottleneck training may underrepresent low-resource concept morphology. The intervention tests causal relevance under the adapter, not full model causality. UMLS-derived assets may require licensing, so the run should use only released XL-BEL concept IDs or open vocabulary mappings. The <=8 A100-day budget excludes large-scale BioMistral fine-tuning and multi-seed hyperparameter sweeps.
draft.resource_plan: Public XL-BEL dataset; open-weight intfloat/multilingual-e5 and optional BioMistral-7B for a small generative reference only. Budget: 0.5 A100-day data/split preparation; 1.5 A100-days CIB training; 2 A100-days zero-shot evaluation across 9 non-English languages; 2 A100-days concept-intervention and shuffled-label ablations; 1 A100-day analysis/error inspection. Total 7 A100-days, within the 8 A100-day cap.

draft.title: The Ceiling-Gap Audit: Proving CBM Leakage with a Null-Concept Benchmark and Separating Encoder Leakage from Head Expressiveness
draft.hypothesis: Recent CBM variants (soft/hard, IB, SupCBM, zero-shot sparse-regression) claim gains that reviewers repeatedly find unexplained ('marginal', 'reason for improvement unclear') because the field measures leakage only with model-internal proxies (ICC, NEC, tree-path divergence, variational IB bounds) that can be satisfied without actually removing label information from the concept channel. Hypothesis: on synthetic data with known generative factors one can construct a concept set that is *statistically independent of the label*, making any above-chance accuracy a *provable* leakage certificate rather than an inferred proxy; on that ground truth, (a) existing leakage metrics will correlate with accuracy rather than with provable leakage, and (b) a large part of the 'bottleneck' accuracy attributed to better concepts is actually head expressiveness (nonlinear vs linear concept-to-label decoder), which is a distinct, harmless-in-principle effect that current metrics confound with leakage. A simple Nuisance-Consistency Regularizer (paired images with identical ground-truth concept vectors, penalizing label-logit divergence) should drive provable leakage to zero, and its known failure mode (accuracy collapse when the label truly depends on a held-out factor) yields an explicit leakage/accuracy tradeoff curve as a function of concept-set completeness.
draft.related_work: The supplied neighborhood all attacks concept leakage but measures it by proxy: Concepts' Information Bottleneck Models (2xRTdzmQ6C) add an IB variational penalty; SupCBM (Q9Z0c1Rb5i) adds label supervision plus an intervention matrix and quantifies leakage with auxiliary classifiers; Graph CBMs (qPH7lAyQgV) restructure concept dependencies; Z-CBM (5Aem9XFZ0t) removes training entirely via sparse regression on retrieved concepts. External work: Schon et al.'s ICC measures irrelevant concept contribution by concept ablation; VLG-CBM's NEC counts effective concepts needed for accuracy; Ragkousis & Parbhoo compare hard vs soft decision paths with trees; MCBM (Almudévar et al.) imposes an IB objective. All of these answer 'is this model's concept layer informative?' but none provides a *ground-truth leakage oracle*: a setting where leakage is provable by construction and where the metric can be wrong. Our key differentiation is (i) the null-concept construction (concept set independent of label ⇒ chance-level accuracy is the correct bottleneck answer, so accuracy minus chance IS leakage), (ii) the two-tier ceiling decomposition (linear vs nonlinear optimal decoder on ground-truth concepts) which separates leakage from head-expressiveness, and (iii) a paired-counterfactual consistency regularizer whose failure mode is characterized rather than hidden. This is a falsification test of the metrics, not another CBM architecture.
draft.approach: Concept Bottleneck Models promise transparency because the label is computed only from human concepts, yet reviewers of recent CBM papers repeatedly ask where the accuracy gain comes from and doubt that small margins reflect genuinely better concepts. The reason is methodological: every available leakage measure (ICC, NEC, tree-path divergence, IB variational bounds) is a model-internal proxy that has never been validated against a known ground truth. We propose the Ceiling-Gap Audit, one minimal falsifiable test. Using synthetic generators (3dShapes, MPI3D, dSprites) where all factors are known, we construct a concept set that is statistically independent of the label, so a true bottleneck must be at chance and any above-chance accuracy is a provable leakage certificate. We sweep concept-set completeness to obtain a continuous ground-truth leakage curve and compare five model families (hard CBM, SupCBM, IB-CBM, soft CBM, and a zero-shot sparse-regression Z-CBM head on frozen open-weight CLIP features). We then fit an optimal linear and an optimal nonlinear decoder on ground-truth concepts to decompose any accuracy advantage into encoder leakage versus head expressiveness, and we test whether existing leakage metrics rank-order models by provable leakage or merely by accuracy. Finally we test a Nuisance-Consistency Regularizer over pairs with identical ground-truth concepts, and quantify its accuracy cost when the label really depends on a missing factor. Prediction: current metrics will fail to track provable leakage, and a substantial share of reported CBM gains will be head expressiveness misread as better concepts.
draft.validation: Setup. dSprites (737k 64x64, factors: shape/scale/orientation/x/y), 3dShapes (480k, six factors), MPI3D. Labels are chosen as one or a boolean function of factors. Three regime families: (A) NULL-CONCEPT: label factor excluded from the concept set and independent of all included factors => provable leakage = accuracy - 1/|Y|; (B) PARTIAL: concept set includes k of the factors determining the label, k swept 0..all, giving a ground-truth curve of the optimal concept-only accuracy (computed by fitting logistic regression and gradient-boosted trees on true concept vectors on 100k held-out images); (C) COMPLETE: concept set determines the label, ceiling = 1.0, leakage observable only as 'correct label despite incorrect predicted concepts'. Models (3 seeds each): (1) standard joint hard CBM, (2) SupCBM (supplied-paper baseline; their label-supervised concept prediction + intervention matrix), (3) Concepts' Information Bottleneck model (supplied-paper baseline; IB penalty on concept activations), (4) soft/leaky CBM with continuous concept embeddings, (5) Z-CBM-style sparse-regression head on frozen open-weight CLIP ViT-B/32 features, (6) black-box CNN and (7) concept-only decoder as bounds. Measurements: accuracy; provable leakage gap (regimes A/B); CEAG = accuracy minus optimal-decoder accuracy on the model's own predicted concept vectors; collision disagreement rate = fraction of exact ground-truth concept-collision groups (identical true concept vector, different label) that receive different predicted labels; intervention correctness = fraction of concept edits that flip the label in the causally correct direction. Metric validation: Spearman correlation of ICC, NEC, tree-path leakage and an auxiliary-classifier leakage score against provable leakage across the model x regime grid; falsifiable prediction is high correlation with accuracy and low correlation with provable leakage (|rho| < 0.4). Fix test: Nuisance-Consistency Regularizer, L = L_task + lambda * mean ||logit(x) - logit(x')||^2 over pairs (x,x') generated to share the exact ground-truth concept vector while differing in every other factor (trivially constructible synthetically). Sweep lambda, report provable leakage vs accuracy. Ablations/diagnostics: (i) NCR off vs on; (ii) linear vs MLP concept-to-label head to quantify head expressiveness; (iii) partial-completeness failure mode: when the label depends on a held-out factor, measure NCR's accuracy cost versus leakage reduction (expected tradeoff curve); (iv) NCR with approximate pairs via augmentation on CUB to test practicality; (v) CUB transfer check with exact-duplicate 312-d attribute vectors, reported with an annotation-noise caveat. All training uses small 64x64 CNNs; estimated total <= 3 A100-days.
draft.limitations: Synthetic-to-real gap: the null-concept construction needs known generative factors, so conclusions about which real CBM gains are leakage are indirect; CUB's 312-d attributes are noisy and near-duplicate rather than exact, weakening the collision test there. The optimal-decoder ceiling is estimated, not analytic, so a weak decoder under-estimates the ceiling and over-estimates leakage (mitigated by strong GBM baselines plus the linear/nonlinear pair, but not eliminated). NCR requires counterfactual pairs sharing exact concepts, which are only approximable on real data. The 'head expressiveness' decomposition assumes the decoder class is the only confound; nonlinear heads can also encode leakage-like shortcuts, so the split is approximate. Provable leakage in regime A may be small in absolute magnitude for well-regularized models, and architecture choices (e.g., concept embedding dimension, binarization schedule) may dominate model differences. No human evaluation of interpretability is performed, and the proposal deliberately tests measurement rather than proposing a new CBM that wins on accuracy.

draft.claims[1].text: Source-specific evidence reports that DISC uses human-interpretable concepts to discover unstable concepts across environments as spurious attributes and then intervenes on training data with those concepts.
draft.claims[2].text: Source-specific reports state gains on object-recognition and skin-lesion tasks and worst-group accuracy gains on MetaShift and ISIC; these are admitted observations from the supplied source, not results of this proposal.
draft.claims[3].text: A supplied source discussion offers only a potential explanation that concept-bank images not exactly covering spurious attributes hinders mitigation; this motivates the coverage audit but is not established here.
draft.claims[4].text: This proposal tests attribution for the specified DISC baseline under fixed public-resource conditions; it does not generalize to all concept-bottleneck variants and does not claim faithful replication unless the exact public implementation and concept bank are obtained.
draft.claims[5].text: The decisive measurements are worst-group accuracy for C1-C0 and C1-C2, the residual-information probe on non-concept features, and correct-versus-randomized intervention faithfulness; a null or inconclusive coverage audit is reported as inconclusive.
draft.claims[6].text: The bound Idea and Method are elaborated without adding a new population or dataset; resource identity, licenses, split checksums, thresholds and coverage images remain Preparation checks, and execution remains a separate future stage.
draft.gap: The supplied materials provide source-specific reports and a potential coverage-related limitation, but they do not provide a matched public-data design that fixes splits, backbone class, preprocessing, compute envelope and evaluation protocol while manipulating concept-bank coverage and disabling concept intervention. They also do not resolve whether coverage audit, intervention-protocol sensitivity, or compute-matched baselines most affect falsifiability. This proposal's intended knowledge increment is a falsifiable attribution design with an explicit inconclusive outcome; positive, negative, and inconclusive findings would each be informative.
draft.idea: Use DISC as the supplied baseline in a prospective coverage-controlled attribution test. Compare C0 original DISC concept bank with intervention enabled, C1 coverage-controlled bank with intervention enabled, and C2 coverage-controlled bank with intervention disabled/residual-only under matched public MetaShift/ISIC evaluation and a fixed open-weight backbone, preprocessing, schedule and evaluation protocol. The primary outcome is worst-group accuracy with pre-specified contrasts C1-C0 and C1-C2; joint diagnostics are a residual-information linear probe on non-concept features and correct-versus-randomized intervention faithfulness. If the coverage audit cannot support every discovered spurious attribute, report the coverage manipulation as inconclusive. A disconfirming pattern is that C2 retains the original worst-group advantage within a declared equivalence margin, or C1 does not improve over C0 while the residual probe remains comparably high and faithfulness fails to separate correct from randomized interventions. This is a prospective design, not an executed result.
draft.method[1]: Scientific definitions and scope (prospective design only; no experiment has been executed). The target claim is that DISC's reported worst-group accuracy advantage on MetaShift and ISIC is attributable to concept-level mitigation rather than residual shortcut information under the specified matched public-resource protocol. This is a method-comparison/boundary test for the supplied DISC baseline, not a broad causal claim about all concept-bottleneck variants. The design elaborates the bound Idea and Method without adding a new population or dataset; applicability is limited to public MetaShift/ISIC, optional Waterbirds diagnostic, one open-weight backbone family/version, and <=8 A100 GPU-days with at least two seed repetitions.
draft.method[2]: Resource and implementation envelope: Use only public MetaShift and ISIC benchmark data and open-weight backbone models; no proprietary weights and no future-paper answer keys. Waterbirds is an optional coverage diagnostic only if public and license-compatible. Fix one open-weight backbone family/version, preprocessing pool, training schedule, evaluation protocol and public dataset split/version across all conditions. Total minimal-validation budget is <=8 A100 GPU-days for three conditions with at least two seed repetitions plus probes. Exact backbone, preprocessing constants, split checksums, licenses, thresholds and coverage images are Preparation checks and are not claimed as acquired here.
draft.method[3]: Conditions and controls: C0 = original DISC concept bank with concept intervention enabled; C1 = coverage-controlled concept bank with concept intervention enabled; C2 = coverage-controlled concept bank with concept intervention disabled/residual-only. Include DISC as the supplied-paper baseline and C2 as the failure-mode/ablation diagnostic. Hold public splits, open-weight backbone class, preprocessing pool, total compute envelope and evaluation protocol fixed across conditions. If the coverage audit cannot establish coverage, C1 is reported as inconclusive and is not treated as a successful coverage-controlled condition.
draft.method[4]: Coverage-controlled concept-bank construction and pre-training audit: From DISC's discovery stage, list the unstable concepts designated as candidate spurious attributes. Build the controlled bank only from public concept images/labels mapped to those attributes, using a declared inclusion rule of 10 distinct bank images per discovered attribute plus an independent label mapping for this prospective method, and record every exclusion. Before any condition is trained, run a coverage audit checking whether every discovered attribute has required bank support. If any discovered attribute lacks support, mark the coverage manipulation inconclusive and do not treat C1 as a successful coverage-controlled condition; report the audit gap. Thresholds are declared design decisions, and their sensitivity remains a limitation.
draft.method[5]: Residual-information probe on non-concept features: Freeze the trained representation and define the non-concept residual feature as the representation remaining after removing the concept-bottleneck path, or the pre-bottleneck feature with concept outputs held fixed.
