prior_work.title: Studying the Interplay Between the Actor and Critic Representations in Reinforcement Learning
prior_work.abstract: Extracting relevant information from a stream of high-dimensional observations is a central challenge for deep reinforcement learning agents. Actor-critic algorithms add further complexity to this challenge, as it is often unclear whether the same information will be relevant to both the actor and the critic. To this end, we here explore the principles that underlie effective representations for the actor and for the critic in on-policy algorithms. We focus our study on understanding whether the actor and critic will benefit from separate, rather than shared, representations. Our primary finding is that when separated, the representations for the actor and critic systematically specialise in extracting different types of information from the environment -- the actor's representation tends to focus on action-relevant information, while the critic's representation specialises in encoding value and dynamics information. We conduct a rigourous empirical study to understand how different representation learning approaches affect the actor and critic's specialisations and their downstream performance, in terms of sample efficiency and generation capabilities. Finally, we discover that a separated critic plays an important role in exploration and data collection during training. Our code, trained models and data are accessible at https://github.com/francelico/deac-rep.

prior_work.title: Langevin Soft Actor-Critic: Efficient Exploration through Uncertainty-Driven Critic Learning
prior_work.abstract: Existing actor-critic algorithms, which are popular for continuous control reinforcement learning (RL) tasks, suffer from poor sample efficiency due to lack of principled exploration mechanism within them. Motivated by the success of Thompson sampling for efficient exploration in RL, we propose a novel model-free RL algorithm, Langevin Soft Actor Critic (LSAC), which prioritizes enhancing critic learning through uncertainty estimation over policy optimization. LSAC employs three key innovations: approximate Thompson sampling through distributional Langevin Monte Carlo (LMC) based $Q$ updates, parallel tempering for exploring multiple modes of the posterior of the $Q$ function, and diffusion synthesized state-action samples regularized with $Q$ action gradients. Our extensive experiments demonstrate that LSAC outperforms or matches the performance of mainstream model-free RL algorithms for continuous control tasks. Notably, LSAC marks the first successful application of an LMC based Thompson sampling in continuous control tasks with continuous action spaces.

S66e68df6956c.title: Wasserstein Actor-Critic: Directed Exploration via Optimism for Continuous-Actions Control
attribution_passages: Uncertainty quantification has been extensively used as a means to achieve efficient directed exploration in Reinforcement Learning (RL). However, state-of-the-art methods for continuous actions still suffer from high sample complexity requirements. Indeed, they either completely lack strategies for propagating the epistemic uncertainty throughout the updates, or they mix it with aleatoric uncertainty while learning the full return distribution (e.g., distributional RL). In this paper, we propose Wasserstein Actor-Critic (WAC), an actor-critic architecture inspired by the recent Wasserstein Q-Learning (WQL), that employs approximate Q-posteriors to represent the epistemic uncertainty and Wasserstein barycenters for uncertainty propagation across the state-action space. WAC enforces exploration in a principled way by guiding the policy learning process with the optimization of an upper bound of the Q-value estimates. Furthermore, we study some peculiar issues that arise when using function approximation, coupled with the uncertainty estimation, and propose a regularized loss for the uncertainty estimation. Finally, we evaluate our algorithm on standard MujoCo tasks as well as suite of continuous-actions domains, where exploration is crucial, in comparison with state-of-the-art baselines. Additional details and results can be found in the supplementary material with our Arxiv preprint.

S068be06c43f0.title: Uncertainty-Driven Exploration During Planning
attribution_passages: In complex environments, the space of possible plans is vast. Generating a good plan therefore requires judicious selection of which parts of the plan space to mentally explore. Drawing on past studies of human exploration, we propose that mental exploration might invoke similar mechanisms. In particular, we test the hypothesis that mental exploration during planning is uncertainty-driven, such that people will exhibit a tendency to explore parts of the plan space that have high epistemic uncertainty. We developed a route-planning task, displayed as a binary tree, where participants were instructed to collect as many treats (rewards) as possible by traversing the tree. By separating the planning and execution phases, we encouraged participants to externalize their planning process. We manipulated uncertainty by varying the number of potential future states available from each current state. Across two studies, the data suggest that people preferred to explore options with more successor states after controlling for value differences, supporting the uncertainty-driven planning hypothesis. We also found that uncertainty played a larger role during the planning phase than during the execution phase, consistent with the hypothesis that the uncertainty effect primarily reflects a property of human planning algorithms rather than an intrinsic preference for uncertainty.

draft.title: Separated Actor/Critic Encoders for Uncertainty-Driven Critic Exploration in Continuous Control: A Minimal Falsifiable Test
draft.literature_gap: The supplied DEAC paper shows that separated actor and critic representations specialize and that a separated critic can aid exploration/data collection, while the supplied LSAC paper shows that uncertainty-driven critic learning via Langevin Monte Carlo and parallel tempering improves exploration in continuous actor-critic RL. The visible gap is that neither abstract tests whether representation separation between actor and critic interacts with uncertainty-based critic exploration: LSAC uses a critic-centric exploration mechanism but does not isolate actor-vs-critic representation sharing, and DEAC studies separation but not whether its exploration benefit depends on calibrated critic uncertainty. This leaves an evaluation gap: no minimal comparison measures both sample efficiency and critic-uncertainty calibration when actor/critic representations are separated under an uncertainty-driven critic.
draft.hypothesis: In continuous-control actor-critic RL, adding DEAC-style separate actor and critic encoders to an LSAC-style uncertainty-driven critic will improve early sample efficiency and critic-uncertainty calibration relative to a shared-encoder LSAC baseline, because critic-specific dynamics/value features reduce contamination of epistemic uncertainty estimates. The gain will disappear in a parameter-matched shared-trunk ablation and will be accompanied by measurable changes in exploration diagnostics; if no calibrated-uncertainty gain or sample-efficiency gain appears, the hypothesis is falsified.
draft.method: Use public MuJoCo/Gymnasium continuous-control tasks (HalfCheetah, Walker2d, Hopper) with small open-weight MLP policies. Implement three agents: (A) LSAC baseline from the supplied paper with a shared actor/critic encoder and distributional Langevin Monte Carlo Q updates plus parallel tempering; (B) LSAC + DEAC-inspired separate actor and critic encoders, with the critic encoder feeding the LMC Q posterior and the actor encoder receiving no critic-uncertainty gradients; (C) parameter-matched shared-trunk ablation where total encoder parameters match B but actor and critic share one trunk with stop-gradient on the actor path to mimic separation without architectural duplication. Diagnostic: uncertainty-off/shared-uncertainty probe where B's critic uncertainty is replaced by deterministic Q variance or a shuffled uncertainty signal, to test whether any gain is due to calibrated critic uncertainty rather than extra parameters. Train all agents for 1M environment steps with 4 seeds per task, logging return, action entropy, state-visitation entropy, and held-out absolute TD error versus LMC posterior variance.
draft.minimal_test: Run 3 tasks x 4 seeds x 3 agents plus one diagnostic condition on the best-performing task = 48 short runs at 1M steps each. Use small MLPs, public MuJoCo, and no proprietary weights. Primary comparison: B vs A on area under the return curve over the first 1M steps. Secondary gate: Spearman rank correlation between LMC critic uncertainty and absolute TD error on a fixed held-out replay buffer. Ablation/failure-mode diagnostic: B should beat C and the shuffled-uncertainty probe only if separation improves calibrated critic exploration; if B's gain persists under shuffled uncertainty or vanishes versus C, the proposed mechanism is not supported.
draft.decisive_metric: Sample-efficiency AUC of episodic return over the first 1M environment steps, normalized per task, with a pre-registered success threshold of at least 10% AUC improvement of B over A across tasks and seeds; this must be accompanied by a higher Spearman correlation between critic uncertainty and absolute TD error for B than A. If AUC improvement is absent or calibration does not improve, the hypothesis is rejected.
draft.supporting_result: B achieves at least 10% higher normalized return AUC than A on at least two of three tasks, with non-overlapping bootstrap confidence intervals, and B shows higher uncertainty-TD-error rank correlation than A. The parameter-matched shared-trunk ablation C and shuffled-uncertainty probe fail to reproduce the gain, while action entropy and state-visitation entropy indicate sustained exploration rather than premature collapse.
draft.falsifying_result: B shows no significant AUC improvement over A, or B improves return without improving critic-uncertainty calibration, or the parameter-matched shared-trunk ablation C matches B, or the shuffled-uncertainty probe preserves B's gain. Any of these outcomes falsifies the claim that separated actor/critic encoders specifically improve LSAC-style uncertainty-driven exploration.

draft.title: Test-Time Critic Repair: A Minimal Audit for Actor-Critic Failure Attribution
draft.hypothesis: At fixed checkpoints in continuous-control actor-critic RL, replacing the actor's action with a local critic maximizer at test time will improve true return when actor optimization failure dominates; if it raises Q-values but degrades true return, critic misestimation dominates. This provides a minimal falsifiable test that separates actor failure from critic error.
draft.related_work: QqqkskOFO9 argues actors often fail to maximize the critic and proposes successive actors, but reviewers note the claim lacks direct support and that gains may come from ensembles or exploration. tErHYBGlWc shows actor and critic representations specialize, but only studies on-policy algorithms. FvQsk3la17 proposes uncertainty-driven critic learning (LSAC) for exploration, with reviewer concerns about novelty and clarity. XO944P8prc decouples dynamics learning from action utility via afterstate RL, but its relation to model-based RL is questioned. Our proposal is not another actor-critic algorithm; it is a diagnostic intervention that directly tests whether higher critic values correspond to higher true return. prior_work.title: Active Test-Time Adaptation: Theoretical Analyses and An Algorithm
prior_work.abstract: Test-time adaptation (TTA) addresses distribution shifts for streaming test data in unsupervised settings. Currently, most TTA methods can only deal with minor shifts and rely heavily on heuristic and empirical studies. To advance TTA under domain shifts, we propose the novel problem setting of active test-time adaptation (ATTA) that integrates active learning within the fully TTA setting. We provide a learning theory analysis, demonstrating that incorporating limited labeled test instances enhances overall performances across test domains with a theoretical guarantee. We also present a sample entropy balancing for implementing ATTA while avoiding catastrophic forgetting (CF). We introduce a simple yet effective ATTA algorithm, known as SimATTA, using real-time sample selection techniques. Extensive experimental results confirm consistency with our theoretical analyses and show that the proposed ATTA method yields substantial performance improvements over TTA methods while maintaining efficiency and shares similar effectiveness to the more demanding active domain adaptation (ADA) methods. Our code is available at https://github.com/divelab/ATTA

prior_work.title: Neighborhood characteristics around schools and around students’ homes: Which one affects academic performance the most?
prior_work.abstract: Abstract Access to high-quality education is essential for achieving social and economic development, yet academic performance remains a challenge in many low- and middle-income countries, such as Brazil. The neighborhood environment is increasingly recognized as an important factor that can influence academic performance. The existing literature on this topic is limited. Most studies have focused either on the exposure surrounding a student's school or their home. To address this gap, this study aimed to evaluate the association between neighborhood characteristics around both the student's school and home in the Federal District (FD), Brazil, focusing on green spaces (NDVI and quantity of green spaces), roads (length of roads), and wildfires as potential predictors of academic performance. We analyzed 344,175 students who were enrolled in the public schools (256 schools) of the FD from 2017 to 2020. We employed a mixed-effects regression model to investigate the relationship between individual-level academic performance and the neighborhood characteristics, while controlling for temporal, socioeconomic, and school-specific variables. Our results suggest that neighborhood characteristics represented by green spaces, roads, and wildfires, can have a significant impact on academic performance. We found that some neighborhood characteristics had a stronger association with academic performance when they were located around schools, compared to when they were located around students' homes. For example, the coefficient for NDVI within the buffer of 250m and 500m surrounding schools was estimated to be 2.48 (95%CI: 2.33; 2.63) and 0.59 (95%CI: 0.47; 0.71), respectively, while for NDVI surrounding homes, it was 0.23 (95%CI: 0.15; 0.30) and 0.25 (95%CI: 0.17; 0.33) for the buffer of 250m and 500m, respectively. Our study provides valuable insights into the potential role of neighborhood characteristics in promoting academic performance, which could inform urban planning and public policy aimed at improving educational outcomes.

prior_work.title: Robust Online Test-Time Adaptation via a Multilayer Generative-Integrative Framework
prior_work.abstract: Test-time adaptation (TTA) has become an essential strategy for preserving model performance when confronted with distribution shifts in real-world environments. Existing approaches typically rely on rapid, single-timescale updates̶such as entropy minimization or batch-normalization adjustment̶which offer practical advantages but are prone to instability, short-horizon corrections, and, in severe cases, collapse of predictive behavior. These limitations point to a structural issue: adaptation occurring solely on a fast timescale lacks the stabilizing influence of slower, memory-like processes. In this work, we introduce Evolutionary Test-Time Adaptation (E-TTA), a multilayer algorithm designed to couple rapid exploratory adjustments with slower, stabilizing dynamics. E-TTA integrates three components into a unified adaptive cycle: (i) bounded hypothesis exploration via controlled input perturbations, (ii) Jensen-Shannon-based consistency integration across multiple hypotheses, and (iii) gradual structural stabilization through an exponential-moving anchor. Together, these mechanisms form a generativeintegrative-stabilizing loop that yields monotonic entropy reduction, bounded parameter trajectories, and an interpretable connection to two-timescale adaptive functionals. Empirical evaluations on CIFAR-10-C demonstrate that E-TTA consistently improves robustness over a non-adaptive baseline while remaining lightweight, introducing less than 20% additional computational cost. Ablation studies further show that both the consistency mechanism and the slow anchoring process are essential for long-horizon stability. These findings indicate that explicitly modeling multi-timescale dynamics provides a principled and practical route toward stable online adaptation.

S1b6d96ff7db9.title: Multimodal GIP-TTA: A Somatic-Psychic-Noetic Framework for Cross-Modal Test-Time Adaptation
attribution_passages: Multimodal systems (vision-language-audio) excel in-distribution but often fail under domain shift, missing modalities, or adversarial perturbation. We propose Multimodal GIP-TTA, a principled framework for test-time adaptation (TTA) grounded in the Genesis-Integration-Optimization (GIP) triad. Each modality is modeled across three strata: SOMA (signal reliability), PSYCHE (representation agreement), and NOUS (goal alignment). Our contributions are threefold: (i) a tri-layer functional map linking multimodal processing to SOMA/PSYCHE/NOUS; (ii) the Systemic Coherence Score (SCS-mm), a metric integrating intra-modal stability, cross-modal agreement, and goal fidelity; and (iii) a lightweight TTA procedure combining entropy minimization, agreement maximization, and goal-prior regularization. Preliminary benchmarks on CLIP, BLIP-2/LLaVA, and Whisper/AudioSet demonstrate improved robustness under synthetic and natural shifts. This work reframes test-time adaptation from a narrow technical fix into a core capacity for adaptive intelligence, establishing a foundation for more resilient multimodal AI.

Sf221a4923af8.title: A Multi-Timescale Operational Strategy for Active Distribution Networks with Load Forecasting Integration
attribution_passages: To enhance the operational stability of distribution networks during peak periods, this paper proposes a multi-timescale operational method considering load forecasting impacts. Firstly, the Crested Porcupine Optimizer (CPO) is employed to optimize the hyperparameters of long short-term memory (LSTM) networks for an accurate prediction of the next-day load curves. Building on this foundation, a multi-timescale optimization strategy is developed: During the day-ahead operation phase, a conservation voltage reduction (CVR)-based regulation plan is formulated to coordinate the control of on-load tap changers (OLTCs) and distributed resources, alleviating peak-shaving pressure on the upstream grid. In the intraday optimization phase, real-time adjustments of OLTC tap positions are implemented to address potential voltage violations, accompanied by an electrical distance-based control strategy for flexible adjustable resources, enabling rapid voltage recovery and enhancing system stability and robustness. Finally, a modified IEEE-33 node system is adopted to verify the effectiveness of the proposed multi-timescale operational method. The method demonstrates a load forecasting accuracy of 93.22%, achieves a reduction of 1.906% in load power demand, and enables timely voltage regulation during intraday limit violations, effectively maintaining grid operational stability.

S3585265a1342.title: A Multi-Objective Multi-Label Feature Selection Algorithm Based on Shapley Value
attribution_passages: Multi-label learning is dedicated to learning functions so that each sample is labeled with a true label set. With the increase of data knowledge, the feature dimensionality is increasing. However, high-dimensional information may contain noisy data, making the process of multi-label learning difficult. Feature selection is a technical approach that can effectively reduce the data dimension. In the study of feature selection, the multi-objective optimization algorithm has shown an excellent global optimization performance. The Pareto relationship can handle contradictory objectives in the multi-objective problem well. Therefore, a Shapley value-fused feature selection algorithm for multi-label learning (SHAPFS-ML) is proposed. The method takes multi-label criteria as the optimization objectives and the proposed crossover and mutation operators based on Shapley value are conducive to identifying relevant, redundant and irrelevant features. The comparison of experimental results on real-world datasets reveals that SHAPFS-ML is an effective feature selection method for multi-label classification, which can reduce the classification algorithm’s computational complexity and improve the classification accuracy.

Sfd0797093bb7.title: Beyond ResNet: A Custom CNN Architecture for High-Performance CIFAR-10 Classification
attribution_passages: Abstract This paper introduces a custom Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) architecture that achieves superior performance on the CIFAR-10 dataset compared to a standard ResNet-18 baseline. Through a methodical, step-by-step enhancement process, we demonstrate that a carefully designed and optimized classical CNN can outperform a more complex, modern architecture. My baseline model achieved a strong accuracy of 88.36%. I then systematically integrated and evaluated two key enhancements: channel attention mechanisms and stochastic depth regularization. The incorporation of stochastic depth proved particularly effective, yielding our best model which attained 89.90% accuracy; a significant improvement over the 80.55% accuracy achieved by a comparably tuned ResNet-18. This research challenges the automatic preference for very deep architectures with residual connections for standard benchmarks and underscores the potential of methodically refined custom designs.

S66398089eb96.title: OMAL: A Multi-Label Active Learning Approach from Data Streams
attribution_passages: With the rapid growth of digital computing, communication, and storage devices applied in various real-world scenarios, more and more data have been collected and stored to drive the development of machine learning techniques. It is also noted that the data that emerge in real-world applications tend to become more complex. In this study, we regard a complex data type, i.e., multi-label data, acquired with a time constraint in a dynamic online scenario. Under such conditions, constructing a learning model has to face two challenges: it requires dynamically adapting the variances in label correlations and imbalanced data distributions and it requires more labeling consumptions. To solve these two issues, we propose a novel online multi-label active learning (OMAL) algorithm that considers simultaneously adopting uncertainty (using the average entropy of prediction probabilities) and diversity (using the average cosine distance between feature vectors) as an active query strategy. Specifically, to focus on label correlations, we use a classifier chain (CC) as the multi-label learning model and design a label co-occurrence ranking strategy to arrange label sequence in CC. To adapt the naturally imbalanced distribution of the multi-label data, we select weight extreme learning machine (WELM) as the basic binary-class classifier in CC. The experimental results on ten benchmark multi-label datasets that were transformed into streams show that our proposed method is superior to several popular static multi-label active learning algorithms in terms of both the Macro-F1 and Micro-F1 metrics, indicating its specifical adaptions in the dynamic data stream environment.

S3fbd1f8fb6d3.title: Active Test-Time Adaptation: Theoretical Analyses and An Algorithm
S3fbd1f8fb6d3.fulltext_snippet: Test-time adaptation (TTA) addresses distribution shifts for streaming test data in unsupervised settings. Currently, most TTA methods can only deal with minor shifts and rely heavily on heuristic and empirical studies. To advance TTA under domain shifts, we propose the novel problem setting of active test-time adaptation (ATTA) that integrates active learning within the fully TTA setting. We provide a learning theory analysis, demonstrating that incorporating limited labeled test instances enhances overall performances across test domains with a theoretical guarantee. We also present a sample entropy balancing for implementing ATTA while avoiding catastrophic forgetting (CF). We introduce a simple yet effective ATTA algorithm, known as SimATTA, using real-time sample selection techniques. Extensive experimental results confirm consistency with our theoretical analyses and show that the proposed ATTA method yields substantial performance improvements over TTA methods while maintaining efficiency and shares similar effectiveness to the more demanding active domain adaptation (ADA) methods. Our code is available at https://github.com/divelab/ATTA

S8e15231214be.title: Neighborhood characteristics around schools and around students’ homes: Which one affects academic performance the most?
S8e15231214be.fulltext_snippet: Abstract Access to high-quality education is essential for achieving social and economic development, yet academic performance remains a challenge in many low- and middle-income countries, such as Brazil. The neighborhood environment is increasingly recognized as an important factor that can influence academic performance. The existing literature on this topic is limited. Most studies have focused either on the exposure surrounding a student's school or their home. To address this gap, this study aimed to evaluate the association between neighborhood characteristics around both the student's school and home in the Federal District (FD), Brazil, focusing on green spaces (NDVI and quantity of green spaces), roads (length of roads), and wildfires as potential predictors of academic performance. We analyzed 344,175 students who were enrolled in the public schools (256 schools) of the FD from 2017 to 2020. We employed a mixed-effects regression model to investigate the relationship between individual-level academic performance and the neighborhood characteristics, while controlling for temporal, socioeconomic, and school-specific variables. Our results suggest that neighborhood characteristics represented by green spaces, roads, and wildfires, can have a significant impact on academic performance. We found that some neighborhood characteristics had a stronger association with academic performance when they were located around schools, compared to when they were located around students' homes. For example, the coefficient for NDVI within the buffer of 250m and 500m surrounding schools was estimated to be 2.48 (95%CI: 2.33; 2.63) and 0.59 (95%CI: 0.47; 0.71), respectively, while for NDVI surrounding homes, it was 0.23 (95%CI: 0.15; 0.30) and 0.25 (95%CI: 0.17; 0.33) for the buffer of 250m and 500m, respectively. Our study provides valuable insights into the potential role of neighborhood characteristics in promoting academic performance, which could inform urban planning and public policy aimed at improving educational outcomes.

S3983dbfc8c32.title: Robust Online Test-Time Adaptation via a Multilayer Generative-Integrative Framework
S3983dbfc8c32.fulltext_snippet: Test-time adaptation (TTA) has become an essential strategy for preserving model performance when confronted with distribution shifts in real-world environments. Existing approaches typically rely on rapid, single-timescale updates̶such as entropy minimization or batch-normalization adjustment̶which offer practical advantages but are prone to instability, short-horizon corrections, and, in severe cases, collapse of predictive behavior. These limitations point to a structural issue: adaptation occurring solely on a fast timescale lacks the stabilizing influence of slower, memory-like processes. In this work, we introduce Evolutionary Test-Time Adaptation (E-TTA), a multilayer algorithm designed to couple rapid exploratory adjustments with slower, stabilizing dynamics. E-TTA integrates three components into a unified adaptive cycle: (i) bounded hypothesis exploration via controlled input perturbations, (ii) Jensen-Shannon-based consistency integration across multiple hypotheses, and (iii) gradual structural stabilization through an exponential-moving anchor. Together, these mechanisms form a generativeintegrative-stabilizing loop that yields monotonic entropy reduction, bounded parameter trajectories, and an interpretable connection to two-timescale adaptive functionals. Empirical evaluations on CIFAR-10-C demonstrate that E-TTA consistently improves robustness over a non-adaptive baseline while remaining lightweight, introducing less than 20% additional computational cost. Ablation studies further show that both the consistency mechanism and the slow anchoring process are essential for long-horizon stability. These findings indicate that explicitly modeling multi-timescale dynamics provides a principled and practical route toward stable online adaptation.

S1b6d96ff7db9.title: Multimodal GIP-TTA: A Somatic-Psychic-Noetic Framework for Cross-Modal Test-Time Adaptation
S1b6d96ff7db9.fulltext_snippet: Multimodal systems (vision-language-audio) excel in-distribution but often fail under domain shift, missing modalities, or adversarial perturbation. We propose Multimodal GIP-TTA, a principled framework for test-time adaptation (TTA) grounded in the Genesis-Integration-Optimization (GIP) triad. Each modality is modeled across three strata: SOMA (signal reliability), PSYCHE (representation agreement), and NOUS (goal alignment). Our contributions are threefold: (i) a tri-layer functional map linking multimodal processing to SOMA/PSYCHE/NOUS; (ii) the Systemic Coherence Score (SCS-mm), a metric integrating intra-modal stability, cross-modal agreement, and goal fidelity; and (iii) a lightweight TTA procedure combining entropy minimization, agreement maximization, and goal-prior regularization. Preliminary benchmarks on CLIP, BLIP-2/LLaVA, and Whisper/AudioSet demonstrate improved robustness under synthetic and natural shifts. This work reframes test-time adaptation from a narrow technical fix into a core capacity for adaptive intelligence, establishing a foundation for more resilient multimodal AI.

Sf221a4923af8.title: A Multi-Timescale Operational Strategy for Active Distribution Networks with Load Forecasting Integration
Sf221a4923af8.fulltext_snippet: To enhance the operational stability of distribution networks during peak periods, this paper proposes a multi-timescale operational method considering load forecasting impacts. Firstly, the Crested Porcupine Optimizer (CPO) is employed to optimize the hyperparameters of long short-term memory (LSTM) networks for an accurate prediction of the next-day load curves. Building on this foundation, a multi-timescale optimization strategy is developed: During the day-ahead operation phase, a conservation voltage reduction (CVR)-based regulation plan is formulated to coordinate the control of on-load tap changers (OLTCs) and distributed resources, alleviating peak-shaving pressure on the upstream grid. In the intraday optimization phase, real-time adjustments of OLTC tap positions are implemented to address potential voltage violations, accompanied by an electrical distance-based control strategy for flexible adjustable resources, enabling rapid voltage recovery and enhancing system stability and robustness. Finally, a modified IEEE-33 node system is adopted to verify the effectiveness of the proposed multi-timescale operational method. The method demonstrates a load forecasting accuracy of 93.22%, achieves a reduction of 1.906% in load power demand, and enables timely voltage regulation during intraday limit violations, effectively maintaining grid operational stability.

S3585265a1342.title: A Multi-Objective Multi-Label Feature Selection Algorithm Based on Shapley Value
S3585265a1342.fulltext_snippet: Multi-label learning is dedicated to learning functions so that each sample is labeled with a true label set. With the increase of data knowledge, the feature dimensionality is increasing. However, high-dimensional information may contain noisy data, making the process of multi-label learning difficult. Feature selection is a technical approach that can effectively reduce the data dimension. In the study of feature selection, the multi-objective optimization algorithm has shown an excellent global optimization performance. The Pareto relationship can handle contradictory objectives in the multi-objective problem well. Therefore, a Shapley value-fused feature selection algorithm for multi-label learning (SHAPFS-ML) is proposed. The method takes multi-label criteria as the optimization objectives and the proposed crossover and mutation operators based on Shapley value are conducive to identifying relevant, redundant and irrelevant features. The comparison of experimental results on real-world datasets reveals that SHAPFS-ML is an effective feature selection method for multi-label classification, which can reduce the classification algorithm’s computational complexity and improve the classification accuracy.

Sfd0797093bb7.title: Beyond ResNet: A Custom CNN Architecture for High-Performance CIFAR-10 Classification
Sfd0797093bb7.fulltext_snippet: Abstract This paper introduces a custom Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) architecture that achieves superior performance on the CIFAR-10 dataset compared to a standard ResNet-18 baseline. Through a methodical, step-by-step enhancement process, we demonstrate that a carefully designed and optimized classical CNN can outperform a more complex, modern architecture. My baseline model achieved a strong accuracy of 88.36%. I then systematically integrated and evaluated two key enhancements: channel attention mechanisms and stochastic depth regularization. The incorporation of stochastic depth proved particularly effective, yielding our best model which attained 89.90% accuracy; a significant improvement over the 80.55% accuracy achieved by a comparably tuned ResNet-18. This research challenges the automatic preference for very deep architectures with residual connections for standard benchmarks and underscores the potential of methodically refined custom designs.

draft.title: Active Multi-Timescale Test-Time Adaptation for Severe Distribution Shifts
draft.literature_gap: The ATTA paper (2404.05094) introduces active test-time adaptation with theoretical guarantees but relies on single-timescale updates and does not address long-horizon stability under severe shifts. The E-TTA paper (2025-12-19) introduces multi-timescale dynamics for stable unsupervised TTA but does not leverage limited labels. No work combines active learning with multi-timescale stability for TTA, leaving open whether active querying can enhance both accuracy and stability under severe distribution shifts.
draft.hypothesis: Incorporating active sample selection (via sample entropy balancing from SimATTA) into E-TTA's multi-timescale framework will improve average accuracy on severe distribution shifts (CIFAR-10-C severity 5) compared to E-TTA alone, without increasing instability (measured by batch-wise accuracy variance).
draft.method: We will implement E-TTA as the baseline and an active variant: during streaming test-time adaptation on CIFAR-10-C, after each E-TTA unsupervised update, we use a small label budget (1% of test samples per batch) selected by sample entropy balancing (from SimATTA) to perform an additional supervised update on the slow anchor. We will evaluate on all 15 corruption types at severity 5 using a ResNet-18 pretrained on CIFAR-10 (public weights). We will run 5 random seeds and compare average accuracy and stability (standard deviation of batch-wise accuracy).
draft.minimal_test: Train ResNet-18 on CIFAR-10, then stream CIFAR-10-C severity 5 test data in batches of 64. For each batch, E-TTA performs unsupervised adaptation; the active variant queries labels for the top 1% most uncertain samples (by entropy) and uses them to update the slow anchor via cross-entropy. Compare both methods across 15 corruption types. Runtime: ~3-4 A100 GPU-days.
draft.decisive_metric: Average accuracy over the entire test stream on CIFAR-10-C severity 5 corruptions. Improvement threshold: active variant must exceed E-TTA by at least 3% absolute accuracy, with no significant increase in batch-wise accuracy variance (non-inferiority margin of 20% relative increase).
draft.supporting_result: The active multi-timescale TTA achieves at least 3% higher average accuracy than E-TTA on severity 5 corruptions, with consistent gains across at least 12 of 15 corruption types, and batch-wise accuracy variance not significantly higher than E-TTA's (p > 0.05).
draft.falsifying_result: No significant accuracy improvement over E-TTA (difference < 3% or p > 0.05), or improvement accompanied by significantly higher accuracy variance (p < 0.05), or active selection does not outperform random selection of the same label budget.
draft.related_work: ATTA (10.48550/arxiv.2404.05094) introduces active test-time adaptation with theoretical guarantees and SimATTA using sample entropy balancing. E-TTA (10.36227/techrxiv.176611667.71137127/v1) introduces multi-timescale dynamics for stable unsupervised TTA. No prior work combines these two lines.
draft.limitations: Evaluation limited to CIFAR-10-C and ResNet-18; may not generalize to other datasets or architectures. The label budget (1%) and entropy-based selection may not reflect practical annotation constraints. Stability metric is heuristic and does not guarantee long-horizon robustness. Hyperparameter tuning for active query frequency and update strength may affect results.
draft.resource_plan: Use 2 A100 GPUs for 2 days (4 GPU-days) for main experiments across 15 corruptions × 5 seeds, plus 1 A100 GPU for 1 day (1 GPU-day) for ablation (random vs entropy selection) and hyperparameter search. Total: 5 A100 GPU-days, within the 8 GPU-day limit. Public datasets (CIFAR-10, CIFAR-10-C) and open-weight ResNet-18 pretrained on CIFAR-10 are used; no proprietary models or future-paper answer keys.

draft.title: When to Ask? Agreement-on-the-Line Gating for Label-Efficient Active Test-Time Adaptation
draft.hypothesis: Under severe but label-balanced distribution shift, Agreement-on-the-Line (AGL) provides a label-free online reliability estimate that can gate binary-feedback active test-time adaptation, matching BiTTA accuracy with 2-5x fewer binary labels and fewer harmful updates; however, the gate should predictably fail under label shift where the agreement-accuracy line is misspecified.
draft.related_work: ATTA (YHUGlwTzFB) introduces active TTA with full-class labels; BiTTA (6ZdXp2Tbb6) reduces annotation to binary correctness feedback using RL and agreement-based self-adaptation; AGL (iEFMwP5wng) predicts TTA accuracy from pairwise model agreement but is used passively for evaluation. This proposal closes the loop by using AGL to decide when to query binary feedback, when to trust self-training, and when to reset. It is not a trivial combination because the central claim—that AGL remains a valid online controller under active feedback and continual non-i.i.d. shifts—is falsifiable, and we explicitly characterize failure under label shift, batch size 1, and severe corruption. The segmentation critique (RAB5gmMBPS) motivates evaluating calibration and failure modes rather than only average accuracy.
draft.approach: Test-time adaptation (TTA) can recover accuracy under distribution shift, but severe shifts can cause catastrophic adaptation. Active TTA adds labels; full-class labels are costly, and binary correctness feedback is cheaper but can be wasted or misleading when the model is already correct or miscalibrated. Agreement-on-the-Line (AGL) shows that TTAed-model accuracy can be predicted from pairwise model agreement without labels, yet existing work uses AGL passively for evaluation. We propose a minimal falsifiable next-step test: use AGL as a label-free controller for binary-feedback active TTA. At each test batch we maintain a small ensemble of TTA variants, compute pairwise agreement, and map it to a predicted accuracy using an AGL line fitted on source validation. Only when predicted reliability is low, or observed agreement deviates from the line, do we spend a binary query; queried samples are selected by maximal pairwise disagreement and used in a BiTTA-style dual-path update. High-confidence batches use self-adaptation, and persistent low reliability triggers a reset. We compare against BiTTA, ATTA with full labels, AGL-only, and entropy/margin/random binary querying on CIFAR-10-C/100-C, PACS, and an ImageNet-C subset. Metrics include accuracy, ECE, selective risk, query count, accuracy-per-query, harmful-query rate, and continual forgetting. The hypothesis is that AGL gating matches BiTTA accuracy with 2-5x fewer binary labels and improves calibration, but fails under label shift where the agreement-accuracy line is misspecified. The test is feasible within 8 A100-days using public checkpoints and datasets.
draft.validation: 1) Main label-efficiency experiment: CIFAR-10-C and CIFAR-100-C (15 corruptions x 5 severities), PACS (4 domains), and ImageNet-C subset (5 corruptions at severity 5). Models: 3-seed ResNet-26/50 for CIFAR/PACS; public ResNet-50 checkpoints for ImageNet subset. Streams: i.i.d. and continual non-i.i.d. (random domain/corruption order). Compare AGL-gated binary feedback to BiTTA with the same binary budget, ATTA with an equal number of full labels, AGL-only with no labels, random/entropy/margin binary querying, and no adaptation. Fixed budgets: 1%, 5%, 10% of test samples; report accuracy, ECE, NLL, and area under accuracy-vs-query curve. 2) Query diagnostic: for every queried batch, measure query regret (accuracy change after feedback), fraction of queries on already-correct samples, and AGL prediction error against actual batch accuracy; correlate gate decisions with harmful updates. 3) Failure-mode ablation: synthetic label shift (90% one class), severe severity-5 corruption, batch size 1, and class-imbalanced PACS; perturb AGL by shuffling agreements or using a random gate with the same budget; report slope/intercept drift and performance collapse. 4) Continual TTA test: stream 15 corruptions or 4 PACS domains; AGL gate triggers reset when predicted reliability stays below threshold for K batches; measure average accuracy, forgetting, backward transfer, and reset count vs BiTTA. 5) Component ablation: model-pair choice (seeds vs learning rates vs EMA), number of ensemble members (2/3/5), threshold sensitivity, and query selection (disagreement vs entropy) with 3 seeds; use paired bootstrap for significance.
draft.limitations: AGL may not hold online under active updates; multiple models increase compute and memory; threshold tuning without test labels is tricky and may require source-side synthetic shifts; binary feedback simulation uses ground-truth correctness and may overestimate real annotator reliability; ImageNet-C subset may be compute-heavy; public code for BiTTA/ATTA may require reimplementation; label shift may break AGL, so negative results are expected and should be reported as a failure-mode map; small ensembles may make AGL noisy; the study covers classification and only a limited segmentation extension; 8 A100-days limits ImageNet and segmentation scale; human feedback latency and annotation noise are not fully modeled.

Research Background & Open Challenges:
# Towards Agentic AI for Science: Hypothesis Generation, Comprehension, Quantification, and Validation

**Conference Context**: ICLR 2025 Workshop Call for Papers & Research Context

# Towards Agentic AI for Science: Hypothesis Generation, Comprehension, Quantification, and Validation

## About the Workshop
Our mission is to foster interdisciplinary collaboration to develop fully autonomous AI systems, addressing challenges like benchmark datasets, human-AI collaboration, robust tools and methods for validating AI outputs, and trustworthiness. By tackling these issues, we can unlock AI's transformative potential in research. In this workshop, themed Agentic AI for Science, we will explore these critical topics and welcome diverse perspectives. We will focus on integrating agentic AI systems to enhance scientific discovery while upholding rigorous standards. For AI to contribute effectively, it must generate novel hypotheses, comprehend their applications, quantify testing resources, and validate feasibility through well-designed experiments. This workshop serves as a vital forum for collaboration and knowledge-sharing aimed at redefining the landscape of scientific discovery. This workshop aims to address four main research thrusts to propel future research, including (non-exclusively):

**Thrust 1. Design and development of agentic AI systems for scientific discovery**. The emergence of agentic AI, powered by foundation models—particularly generative models—opens up unprecedented opportunities for scientific discovery. These systems can potentially revolutionize various aspects of the scientific process, including hypothesis generation, comprehension of complex scientific phenomena, quantification, and validation. Designing and developing effective agentic AI systems for scientific discovery is both exciting and non-trivial. Pioneering work in this field has already demonstrated the promise of leveraging scientific tools, agents, and knowledge graphs. Notable examples include ChemCrow, which showcases the potential of AI in chemistry; Crispr-GPT, which applies AI to genetic engineering; and SciAgents , which illustrates the power of multi-agent systems in scientific discovery. These groundbreaking studies highlight the transformative potential of agentic AI in accelerating scientific progress and opening new avenues for research. Key research topics in this thrust include (but not limited to):

- Developing scientific foundation models: Tailoring general foundation models specifically for various scientific fields to enhance relevance and accuracy.
- Effective scientific tool augmentation: Enhancing existing scientific tools and methodologies with agentic AI capabilities.
- Multi-agent decomposition design: Developing frameworks for scientific hypothesis generation using multiple specialized AI agents.
- Human-in-the-loop agentic systems: Improving reliability and interpretability of AI-driven scientific discoveries through strategic human intervention.

**Thrust 2. Theoretical foundation for scientific agentic AI**. Developing agentic scientific AI requires methods to quantify the predictions and performance of these systems, as well as to validate the scientific hypotheses they generate. A thorough investigation of agentic scientific AI systems also demands solid theoretical foundations and tools to ensure guarantees on their behavior. To analyze and evaluate such systems, we will incorporate theoretical tools in modeling, logical reasoning, model validation and diagnosis, interpretable AI, and other general methods that can provide guarantees on agentic systems. Key topics in this area include, but are not limited to, the following:

- Theoretical foundation: Statistical models and theories of agentic scientific AI, such as theoretical studies on in-context learning, multi-agent communications, game theory, physics-informed hard and soft optimization constraints, and neural operators.
- Logic reasoning: Inductive, deductive, and abductive reasoning; Bayesian reasoning and probabilistic programming; neural-symbolic approaches.
- Model quantification, validation, diagnosis: Theory-driven metrics for quantifying AI system performance; self-evaluation of LLMs; data valuation and data-centric AI; diagnostics for data, architecture, and training processes; creation of standardized benchmarks for evaluating the validity of scientific hypothesis generation; scientific facts and hallucination.
- Interpretable AI: Approach

S97baa12cee79.title: Count With Confidence: Calibrated Confidence Interval Prediction for Crowd Counting
attribution_passages: Deep neural networks (DNNs) have emerged as powerful predictors, demonstrating impressive performance across a spectrum of applications. They efficiently map high-dimensional input data to an output. However, a notable drawback is the lack of transparency and interpretability in DNN outputs. In critical domains such as healthcare, finance, public safety, and autonomous systems, transparency in DNN output is paramount for informed decision-making and trustworthiness. Recognizing and quantifying uncertainty in outputs can significantly improve decision-making capabilities. In crowd counting, where deep learning models are prevalent, uncertainty estimation is vital for robust decision-making in resource allocation, event planning, and public safety. However, existing work often overlooks the associated uncertainty in crowd count predictions, focusing solely on estimation. In this work, we propose a method to not only estimate the count but also the uncertainty in these estimated counts, considering both data uncertainty and model uncertainty. Furthermore, to enhance the calibration of model uncertainty, we utilize adaptive dropout rates within a Monte Carlo dropoutbased Bayesian framework. By utilizing isotonic regression, we calibrate overall predictive uncertainty, covering both data and model uncertainties. This leads to well-calibrated confidence intervals for the model predictions. Through extensive simulations on widely used datasets, our method sets a new benchmark.

Saacb67111403.title: Prompt-to-Pill: Multi-Agent Drug Discovery and Clinical Simulation Pipeline
attribution_passages: Abstract This study presents a comprehensive, modular framework for AI-driven drug discovery (DD) and clinical trial simulation, spanning from target identification to virtual patient recruitment. Synthesized from a systematic analysis of 51 LLM-based systems, the proposed Prompt-to-Pill * architecture and corresponding implementation leverages a multi-agent system (MAS) divided into DD, preclinical and clinical phases, coordinated by a central Orchestrator . Each phase comprises specialized large language model (LLM) for molecular generation, toxicity screening, docking, trial design, and patient matching. To demonstrate the full pipeline in practice, the well-characterized target Dipeptidyl Peptidase 4 (DPP4) was selected as a representative use case. The process begins with generative molecule creation and proceeds through ADMET evaluation, structure-based docking, and lead optimization. Clinical-phase agents then simulate trial generation, patient eligibility screening using EHRs, and predict trial outcomes. By tightly integrating generative, predictive, and retrieval-based LLM components, this architecture bridges drug discovery and preclinical phase with virtual clinical development, offering a demonstration of how LLM-based agents can operationalize the drug development workflow in silico.

S10093afcaef2.title: AI for Scientific Discovery: Automating Hypothesis Generation
attribution_passages: The accelerating pace of scientific advancement has underscored the need for innovative tools to assist researchers in navigating the ever-growing volumes of data and literature. Artificial Intelligence (AI) has emerged as a transformative force in this domain, particularly in automating the process of hypothesis generation-a core component of scientific discovery. This paper explores the current capabilities and methodologies of AI systems designed to formulate plausible, testable scientific hypotheses by synthesizing patterns, identifying anomalies, and integrating multi-domain knowledge. Emphasis is placed on machine learning algorithms, knowledge graphs, and natural language processing tools that mimic cognitive reasoning. Through case studies in biomedical and material science fields, we demonstrate the potential of these systems to accelerate discovery and enhance research efficiency. The study concludes by addressing the epistemological and ethical implications of delegating aspects of scientific reasoning to machines and offers a roadmap for future advancements in hybrid human-AI discovery systems.

Sa3916f0a633a.title: FATA: A Framework-Agnostic, Task-Agnostic Agentic AI Platform for Serverless Multi-Agent Orchestration
attribution_passages: Contemporary agentic AI systems face critical challenges in tool orchestration, dynamic coordination, and framework interoperability. I present FATA (Framework Agnostic and Task Agnostic Agentic AI), a novel control plane design pattern that enables scalable, distributed multi-agent orchestration through serverless architecture. FATA introduces a unified tool management layer that dynamically routes, validates, and governs tool interactions while maintaining framework independence. My approach distinguishes between specialized AI agents for targeted automation and collaborative agentic ecosystems with emergent collective intelligence. Through systematic evaluation across cybersecurity, compliance, and document processing domains, FATA demonstrates the capability to reduce developer complexity, enable runtime adaptability, and provide robust governance mechanisms for enterprise-scale agentic deployments.

S7c4cc4888158.title: LLM-SRBench: A New Benchmark for Scientific Equation Discovery with Large Language Models
attribution_passages: Each discovery task takes as input the problem description, variables, the corresponding dataset, and an instruction specifying the task.

Scientific equation discovery is a fundamental task in the history of scientific progress, enabling the derivation of laws governing natural phenomena. Recently, Large Language Models (LLMs) have gained interest for this task due to their potential to leverage embedded scientific knowledge for hypothesis generation. However, evaluating the true discovery capabilities of these methods remains challenging, as existing benchmarks often rely on common equations that are susceptible to memorization by LLMs, leading to inflated performance metrics that do not reflect discovery. In this paper, we introduce LLM-SRBench, a comprehensive benchmark with 239 challenging problems across four scientific domains specifically designed to evaluate LLM-based scientific equation discovery methods while preventing trivial memorization. Our benchmark comprises two main categories: LSR-Transform, which transforms common physical models into less common mathematical representations to test reasoning beyond memorized forms, and LSR-Synth, which introduces synthetic, discovery-driven problems requiring data-driven reasoning. Through extensive evaluation of several state-of-the-art methods, using both open and closed LLMs, we find that the best-performing system so far achieves only 31.5% symbolic accuracy. These findings highlight the challenges of scientific equation discovery, positioning LLM-SRBench as a valuable resource for future research.

We have only changed some hyperparameters in different baselines that affect the number of LLM calls in the search framework. This is to make sure we have a fair comparison across baseline discovery frameworks with same access budget to LLMs. In our experiments, all baseline frameworks have 1k calls to LLMs (per problem) through the discovery process.

S97baa12cee79.title: Count With Confidence: Calibrated Confidence Interval Prediction for Crowd Counting
S97baa12cee79.fulltext_snippet: Deep neural networks (DNNs) have emerged as powerful predictors, demonstrating impressive performance across a spectrum of applications. They efficiently map high-dimensional input data to an output. However, a notable drawback is the lack of transparency and interpretability in DNN outputs. In critical domains such as healthcare, finance, public safety, and autonomous systems, transparency in DNN output is paramount for informed decision-making and trustworthiness. Recognizing and quantifying uncertainty in outputs can significantly improve decision-making capabilities. In crowd counting, where deep learning models are prevalent, uncertainty estimation is vital for robust decision-making in resource allocation, event planning, and public safety. However, existing work often overlooks the associated uncertainty in crowd count predictions, focusing solely on estimation. In this work, we propose a method to not only estimate the count but also the uncertainty in these estimated counts, considering both data uncertainty and model uncertainty. Furthermore, to enhance the calibration of model uncertainty, we utilize adaptive dropout rates within a Monte Carlo dropoutbased Bayesian framework. By utilizing isotonic regression, we calibrate overall predictive uncertainty, covering both data and model uncertainties. This leads to well-calibrated confidence intervals for the model predictions. Through extensive simulations on widely used datasets, our method sets a new benchmark.

Saacb67111403.title: Prompt-to-Pill: Multi-Agent Drug Discovery and Clinical Simulation Pipeline
Saacb67111403.fulltext_snippet: Abstract This study presents a comprehensive, modular framework for AI-driven drug discovery (DD) and clinical trial simulation, spanning from target identification to virtual patient recruitment. Synthesized from a systematic analysis of 51 LLM-based systems, the proposed Prompt-to-Pill * architecture and corresponding implementation leverages a multi-agent system (MAS) divided into DD, preclinical and clinical phases, coordinated by a central Orchestrator . Each phase comprises specialized large language model (LLM) for molecular generation, toxicity screening, docking, trial design, and patient matching. To demonstrate the full pipeline in practice, the well-characterized target Dipeptidyl Peptidase 4 (DPP4) was selected as a representative use case. The process begins with generative molecule creation and proceeds through ADMET evaluation, structure-based docking, and lead optimization. Clinical-phase agents then simulate trial generation, patient eligibility screening using EHRs, and predict trial outcomes. By tightly integrating generative, predictive, and retrieval-based LLM components, this architecture bridges drug discovery and preclinical phase with virtual clinical development, offering a demonstration of how LLM-based agents can operationalize the drug development workflow in silico.

S10093afcaef2.title: AI for Scientific Discovery: Automating Hypothesis Generation
S10093afcaef2.fulltext_snippet: The accelerating pace of scientific advancement has underscored the need for innovative tools to assist researchers in navigating the ever-growing volumes of data and literature. Artificial Intelligence (AI) has emerged as a transformative force in this domain, particularly in automating the process of hypothesis generation-a core component of scientific discovery. This paper explores the current capabilities and methodologies of AI systems designed to formulate plausible, testable scientific hypotheses by synthesizing patterns, identifying anomalies, and integrating multi-domain knowledge. Emphasis is placed on machine learning algorithms, knowledge graphs, and natural language processing tools that mimic cognitive reasoning. Through case studies in biomedical and material science fields, we demonstrate the potential of these systems to accelerate discovery and enhance research efficiency. The study concludes by addressing the epistemological and ethical implications of delegating aspects of scientific reasoning to machines and offers a roadmap for future advancements in hybrid human-AI discovery systems.

draft.title: CHG-Agent: Calibrated Multi-Agent Hypothesis Generation with Tool-Grounded Comprehension, Resource Quantification, and Validation
draft.literature_gap: Existing agentic-for-science systems such as ChemCrow, Coscientist, CRISPR-GPT, SciAgents, and AI Scientist demonstrate tool use and multi-agent scientific workflows, but they are rarely evaluated in a controlled masked-discovery setting that jointly measures (i) hypothesis validity, (ii) comprehension of mechanism and assumptions, (iii) resource-estimate realism, and (iv) calibrated feasibility confidence. Current evaluations tend to be end-to-end, domain-specific, or dependent on expensive wet-lab follow-up, making it difficult to attribute gains to generation versus validation. There is a gap for a budget-feasible, reproducible benchmark and agent design that explicitly separates generation, comprehension, quantification, and tool-grounded validation, and that tests whether this separation improves expert-judged feasibility and calibration over strong single-agent and unvalidated multi-agent baselines.
draft.hypothesis: A multi-agent system that separates scientific hypothesis generation from explicit comprehension probes, resource quantification, and tool-grounded validation, and that reports calibrated feasibility confidence, will produce hypotheses with higher expert-judged scientific feasibility and lower calibration error than single-LLM, chain-of-thought, and unvalidated multi-agent baselines on masked-discovery tasks, under a fixed academic compute and annotation budget.
draft.method.benchmark: Build a 48-item masked-discovery benchmark: 16 chemistry, 16 molecular/cell biology, and 16 climate/earth-science items from open-access papers published 2020-2024. For each paper, provide title-free context through methods and partial results; mask the final discovery/conclusion sentence. Expert annotators use the held-out conclusion only for post hoc scoring, not for generation. Each item includes a short context, available data/tools, and a requested hypothesis with a testable prediction.
draft.method.systems: Compare six systems under identical prompts and budgets: (S0) single open-weight LLM; (S1) single LLM with chain-of-thought; (S2) multi-agent generator+critic without validation; (S3) full CHG-Agent: generator, comprehender, resource quantifier, tool-grounded validator, calibrator; (S4) CHG-Agent without validator; (S5) CHG-Agent without quantifier. A commercial API model is used only as an external baseline for S0/S3 on a subset if budget permits.
draft.method.agent_design: Generator proposes 5 candidate hypotheses. Comprehender answers structured probes: mechanism, independent/dependent variables, assumptions, falsifiable prediction, and closest known work. Quantifier estimates time, cost, key instruments/datasets, failure modes, and a 0-100 feasibility confidence. Validator invokes lightweight tools: RDKit for chemical validity/property sanity, PubMed/arXiv retrieval for evidence overlap, gene/protein name checks, and unit/dataset-availability checks for climate items. Calibrator maps evidence and tool-check outcomes to a final confidence using a small LoRA head or isotonic regression fit on a disjoint 12-item development set.
draft.method.annotation: Three domain-trained annotators score each final hypothesis on 1-5 Likert scales for novelty, mechanistic plausibility, testability, resource realism, and evidence grounding; they also provide a binary feasible/unfeasible judgment and a 1-5 overall feasibility score. Annotation load: 48 items x 3 annotators x 15 min = 36 h, plus 4 h adjudication = 40 h. Report inter-annotator ICC and adjudicate disagreements.
draft.method.statistics: Run 5 seeds per system. Primary analysis uses paired bootstrap over the 48 items with 10,000 resamples and mixed-effects models with item and domain random effects. Report 95% CIs and per-domain breakdowns. Secondary metrics: expected calibration error (ECE) between stated confidence and expert feasible/unfeasible labels, resource-estimate error, tool-check pass rate, and comprehension-probe accuracy.
draft.method.ablations: Remove validator, remove quantifier, remove comprehension probes, disable calibration, and replace tool-grounded validation with self-critique. Control for output length and retrieval-token count. Include a random/retrieval-only hypothesis baseline to estimate lower bounds.
draft.minimal_test: On 48 masked-discovery items across 3 domains, compare S0-S5 with 5 seeds each using a local 7-8B open-weight model served by vLLM on 4xA100 40GB. Use 40 annotator-hours for 3 annotators to score all final hypotheses. The minimal test is complete when the full CHG-Agent and the strongest baseline have been evaluated on all 48 items with expert scores and calibration labels, and paired bootstrap CIs are computed. Estimated compute: 60 GPU-hours inference/evaluation, 40 GPU-hours LoRA calibration training, 20 GPU-hours retrieval embedding/indexing, 80 GPU-hours reruns/ablation/error-bar replication. API budget is reserved for a commercial-model sanity baseline and retrieval fallback.
draft.decisive_metric: Primary decisive metric: expert-judged overall feasibility score (1-5, mean of 3 annotators) for the full CHG-Agent minus the strongest baseline, with success requiring a paired-bootstrap 95% CI lower bound > 0 and a mean improvement of at least 0.5 points, together with ECE <= 0.10 or at least 20% lower ECE than the strongest baseline.
draft.supporting_result: The full CHG-Agent achieves mean expert feasibility >= 4.0/5, exceeds the strongest baseline by >= 0.5 points with a 95% bootstrap CI excluding zero, reduces ECE by >= 20%, and shows ablation drops of >= 0.4 points when the validator or quantifier is removed. Tool-check pass rate and comprehension-probe accuracy are positively associated with expert feasibility, and gains persist after controlling for output length and retrieval-token count.
draft.falsifying_result: The full CHG-Agent fails to exceed the strongest baseline by 0.5 feasibility points with a 95% CI excluding zero, or its ECE is not improved by at least 20%, or any observed gain disappears after controlling for output length/retrieval tokens, or inter-annotator ICC is below 0.5 so the expert signal is unreliable. The hypothesis is also falsified if removing the validator and quantifier does not reduce performance, indicating that the proposed decomposition is not the source of any gain.

draft.limitations[1]: No wet-lab or real experimental validation; expert rubric scores are proxy outcomes.
draft.limitations[2]: Small benchmark size (48 items) limits domain-specific claims; report per-domain CIs.
draft.limitations[3]: Annotation subjectivity; mitigate with 3 annotators, ICC reporting, and adjudication.
draft.limitations[4]: Potential temporal leakage if local models know masked papers; use title removal, 2024 papers, and leakage checks.
draft.limitations[5]: Single open-weight model family for main experiments; commercial API only as sanity baseline.
draft.limitations[6]: Resource quantification is judged by experts, not by executing experiments.
draft.limitations[7]: Tool coverage is uneven across domains; climate validation relies on unit/data checks rather than causal tools.
draft.limitations[8]: API model/version drift may affect reproducibility; pin versions and cache outputs.
draft.resource_plan.annotator_plan: 3 annotators x 48 items x 15 min = 36 h; 4 h adjudication and training.
draft.resource_plan.milestones.week_1_2: Curate 48 masked-discovery items; define rubric; pilot 6 items; freeze prompts.
draft.resource_plan.milestones.week_3_4: Implement S0-S5 and tools; run development-set calibration fitting.
draft.resource_plan.milestones.week_5: Run main generations with 5 seeds; begin expert annotation.
