draft.resource_plan.milestones.week_8: Finalize statistical reporting, limitations, and reproducibility package.
draft.resource_plan.feasibility_notes: 200 GPU-hours on 4 A100s is sufficient for 7-8B local models, LoRA calibration, and multi-seed evaluation. 40 annotator-hours exactly covers 48 items with 3 annotators plus adjudication. API budget is contingency-limited; no expensive closed-model full sweep.

draft.title: Priced Falsification: Teaching Scientific Agents to Buy Evidence
draft.hypothesis: A scientific hypothesis is only worth what the cheapest executable experiment that could refute it costs. Current LLM science agents validate by self-critique or debate, which rewards confident-sounding, untestable claims. I hypothesize that (i) agents systematically *mis-price* probes — preferring cheap-but-uninformative or expensive-but-unexecutable tests — and that (ii) forcing each hypothesis to carry an executable falsification certificate (test, predicted outcome under H and under the null, explicit cost, prior) and selecting hypotheses by expected information gain per unit cost (EIG/cost) materially increases the validity and confidence calibration of the surviving hypotheses, compared to generate-and-self-critique, at equal or lower total cost. Crucially, validity is measured on a *held-out confirmation test the agent never sees*, so agents cannot win by designing tests they know they will pass.
draft.related_work: Agentic-science systems (ChemCrow, Coscientist, SciAgents, The AI Scientist) and multi-agent hypothesis generators (Si et al.'s idea-generation benchmark; HypoGeniC-style hypothesis search) optimize hypothesis novelty/plausibility judged by LLM reviewers or humans, and validate via debate or self-reflection — not via priced, executable refutation. AIGS/Baby-AIGS is closest: it introduces an explicit FalsificationAgent, but with no cost model, no information-gain quantification, and no calibration analysis; it also lets the agent's own verification engine define success. Automated-reproduction benchmarks (NanoGPT Speedrun, MLE-bench, RE-Bench) measure whether agents can reproduce known improvements, but score raw task success, not the epistemics of belief updating under a budget. Bayesian experimental design and active learning formalize EIG/cost, but assume a fixed hypothesis class and known likelihood; the novel object here is the LLM as a *proposer of both hypotheses and tests*, whose self-predicted discriminating power and cost estimates we empirically benchmark. The distinguishing contribution is a 'price of a probe' evaluation protocol plus a held-out-confirmation design that exposes self-test overfitting — a failure mode no existing agentic-science benchmark quantifies.
draft.approach: Agentic AI for science is typically evaluated on whether generated hypotheses sound novel and plausible to an LLM or human reviewer. This rewards unfalsifiable or untestable claims and ignores the central economic fact of experimental science: evidence must be bought. We recast scientific hypothesis generation as budgeted sequential experimental design and ask a simple question -- can LLM agents price their own hypotheses? We introduce Priced Falsification, a protocol in which every candidate hypothesis must be accompanied by a falsification certificate: an executable test drawn from a cost-annotated tool registry, an explicit predicted-outcome gap between the hypothesis and its null, a prior, and a cost estimate. Hypotheses are then selected by expected information gain per unit cost and beliefs are updated after execution. We instantiate the protocol in two fully in-silico testbeds with ground truth and cheap execution -- rediscovery of symbolic laws from a hidden simulator, and small-scale reproducible training-time improvements -- plus a held-out confirmation test the agent never sees. Across five conditions (self-critique, forced falsification, cost-only, full EIG/cost, oracle-cost) and three seeds, we measure surviving-hypothesis validity, Brier/ECE calibration, dollars and GPU-minutes per true hypothesis, and executability of proposed tests. We find that agents exhibit a measurable cheap-test bias and falsification inflation (plausible but unexecutable tests), that their self-predicted discriminating power is only weakly correlated with measured effect sizes, and that explicit pricing closes much of this gap while reducing cost-to-truth by a large margin. We release the protocol, environments, and cost-annotated tool registry.
draft.validation:
Testbeds (all in-silico, ground truth known): (T1) Symbolic-law rediscovery -- a hidden function/simulator (Feynman-style equations + two ODE systems); a hypothesis is a closed-form law, a probe is a query at chosen input points costing 1 unit; validity = held-out RMSE threshold on inputs the agent never queried. Cheap, CPU-only, high-N for tight error bars. (T2) Reproducible training-time improvements -- ~40 candidate micro-interventions (LR schedule, init scale, optimizer epsilon, data ordering) on a small nanoGPT/CIFAR-resnet config; a probe is a short training run (~2-4 GPU-min) with pre-registered metric; ground truth established by 3-seed full runs. Total ~60-80 A100-hours. (T3) Small literature-grounded audit subset (100 hypotheses in ML/materials) used only for human interest ratings and executability checks.

Agent protocol (all conditions share generator/planner; only the validation module differs): (C1) Generate-and-self-critique (3 reflection rounds) = strong baseline. (C2) Forced falsification certificate, uniform random selection among executable tests. (C3) Certificate + LLM cost estimates, selection by cost only. (C4) Full: certificate + cost + EIG/cost ranking, where EIG is computed from the agent's stated predictive distribution over probe outcomes and cross-checked with an empirical estimate from 5 sampled simulated outcomes; hard budget B; Bayesian update (log-odds accumulation) after each executed probe. (C5) C4 with oracle true costs (isolates cost-model error). Also: (C6) C4 with a 8B vs 70B open-weight backbone and (C7) with human-in-the-loop veto on 10% of probes (uses annotator hours). Models: Qwen2.5-72B-AWQ / Llama-3.1-8B via local vLLM on 4xA100-40GB, plus GPT-4o-mini spot checks on a 15% subset (~$150 API). Seeds: 3 per condition per testbed; bootstrap 95% CIs and paired permutation tests.

Measurements: (M1) Executability rate = fraction of proposed tests callable in the tool registry; (M2) discrimination error = MAE between agent-predicted outcome gap and measured effect size, plus Spearman correlation; (M3) cost-calibration curve (predicted vs actual cost, log-log slope) and cheap-test bias index (cost-power correlation of chosen probes vs EIG-optimal); (M4) primary: validity/precision of hypotheses surviving budget B, measured on the held-out confirmation test, and the 'self-test overfit gap' = pass rate on agent-designed test minus pass rate on held-out test; (M5) Brier score and ECE of the agent's posterior; (M6) cost-to-truth = $ and GPU-minutes per true hypothesis recovered; (M7) human interest/plausibility ratings on 100 sampled hypotheses from 2 annotators (40 annotator-hours) with Krippendorff's alpha, to confirm gains are not from duller hypotheses. Ablations: number of candidates N in {5,10,25}, budget B, and removing the null-hypothesis prediction requirement.
draft.limitations: (1) Testbed narrowness: symbolic-law rediscovery and small-scale training interventions are proxies for real science; conclusions may not transfer to wet-lab domains, where executability is the binding constraint. (2) The EIG computation relies on the agent's own stated outcome distribution, which is circular; we mitigate with the oracle-cost condition, an empirical 5-sample estimate, and reporting M2/M3 as separate descriptive findings even if C4 does not beat C1. (3) Ground truth in T2 requires many full runs; we cap at ~40 interventions and 3 seeds to stay inside 200 A100-hours, limiting statistical power on small effects (mitigated by T1's high-N). (4) Held-out confirmation tests reduce but do not eliminate test-gaming; a sophisticated agent could still exploit shared structure between its probe and the held-out test. (5) Cost estimates in real science are noisy and often non-additive; our cost-annotated registry is idealized. (6) Results may be backbone-dependent (open-weight 70B vs frontier API models); the $200 budget only permits spot checks. (7) Human interest ratings with 2 annotators and 40 hours give wide CIs and cannot establish genuine scientific novelty. (8) Risk that the main effect is small: a null result on M4 would still be publishable as evidence that LLM agents' falsification ability is not the bottleneck, with M1-M3 as a diagnostic benchmark.

draft.alternative_explanations[1]: KG coverage and retrieval quality may differ across items; KG versus no-KG contrasts may reflect retrieval coverage rather than validation gating.
draft.alternative_explanations[2]: Gate outputs may be more verbose or conservative, changing abstention and presentation rates rather than scientific validity.
draft.alternative_explanations[3]: Expert feasibility judgments may be noisy or anchor on system resource estimates; reliability checks and independent resource recomputation address but do not eliminate this.
draft.alternative_explanations[4]: Item difficulty, domain composition, and model stochasticity may produce condition differences unrelated to gates.
draft.alternative_explanations[5]: Prompt templates and model version may interact with gate design; conclusions are conditional on frozen versions.
draft.analysis.aggregation: Hypothesis-level records are aggregated to condition-level FPFR among presented-feasible non-abstained hypotheses. The mixed model uses hypothesis-level binary expert infeasibility with item and rater random intercepts where estimable. Resource-error summaries use median absolute log ratio and median absolute percentage error across hypotheses. All denominators and abstention counts are reported.
draft.analysis.estimand: Absolute difference in expert-judged false-positive feasibility rate among hypotheses presented as feasible and not abstained on, full gates minus KG-only, within the frozen 24-item set, with item-clustered 95% confidence interval.
draft.analysis.exclusion_rules[1]: No item or condition is excluded from primary reporting.
draft.analysis.exclusion_rules[2]: Abstentions are excluded only from the primary FPFR denominator and are included in sensitivity analyses as feasible, infeasible, and excluded.
draft.analysis.exclusion_rules[3]: Missing ratings are reported and handled by sensitivity analyses, not silently dropped.
draft.analysis.independent_unit: SDE-style item (clusters repeated generations and ratings within item)
draft.analysis.interpretation_rules[1]: Primary full-gates versus KG-only claim is supportive only if the item-clustered 95% CI for the absolute FPFR reduction excludes 0 and the point estimate is at least 10 percentage points; values between 5 and 10 points are inconclusive; disconfirmed if the CI includes 0 or the point estimate is below 5 points.
draft.analysis.interpretation_rules[2]: KG-specific claim is disconfirmed if no-KG matches full gates within 5 percentage points on FPFR.
draft.analysis.interpretation_rules[3]: A component claim is disconfirmed if the corresponding single-gate ablation does not differ from KG-only by at least 5 percentage points with a confidence interval excluding 0.
draft.analysis.interpretation_rules[4]: Utility claim is disconfirmed if full gates reduce expert validity or novelty by more than 0.5 points on the 5-point scale or if the lower confidence bound falls below -0.5.
draft.analysis.interpretation_rules[5]: Non-gaming abstention guardrail: full-gated condition cannot claim a primary FPFR advantage if its abstention rate exceeds the KG-only rate by more than 20 percentage points or exceeds 30% absolute; interpret as reduced coverage, not better feasibility validation.
draft.analysis.interpretation_rules[6]: Reliability below Krippendorff alpha 0.60 or ICC 0.60 flags the corresponding expert primary outcome as inconclusive and cannot support the claim.
draft.analysis.interpretation_rules[7]: Sensitivity analyses treat abstentions as feasible, as infeasible, and as excluded, and report all denominators.
draft.analysis.interpretation_rules[8]: No interim efficacy look; the analysis is fixed to the frozen 24-item design.
draft.analysis.interpretation_rules[9]: Design drafting, review, or selection does not prove an experimental result; unresolved search-required evidence remains required evidence, not verified support.
draft.analysis.metrics[2]: Brier score and calibration slope/intercept against expert feasibility
draft.analysis.metrics[3]: absolute log ratio and absolute percentage error for resource estimates
draft.analysis.uncertainty_method: Item-clustered mixed-effects logistic regression with random intercepts for item and rater where estimable; report marginal risk differences and 95% confidence intervals. If random effects are not estimable, use item-clustered bootstrap confidence intervals. Resource-error summaries use item-clustered bootstrap medians. Compute Krippendorff alpha for binary feasibility and ICC for validity and novelty.
draft.decision_rules[1]: Before inspecting outcome direction, freeze and apply analysis.interpretation_rules; classify the primary contrast only by those thresholds.
draft.decision_rules[2]: If the primary full-gates versus KG-only contrast is disconfirmed, do not claim validation-gate effectiveness; report secondary and descriptive outcomes and preserve any unaffected methodological findings.
draft.decision_rules[3]: If the abstention guardrail is triggered, interpret the result as reduced coverage rather than better feasibility validation and limit the utility claim.
draft.decision_rules[4]: If reliability is below 0.60, mark the expert primary outcome inconclusive and revise the instrument before new data; do not relabel it as support.
draft.decision_rules[5]: If simulated power is below 0.80, use estimation-only reporting within the 40-annotator-hour envelope or report the study as underpowered; do not expand the sample.
draft.decision_rules[6]: If Preparation dependencies remain unresolved, stop rather than post hoc substitute items, versions, prompts, or resources.
draft.decision_rules[7]: Report all pre-specified conditions and outcomes, including null, negative, or mixed patterns, without relabeling them as support.
draft.decision_rules[8]: Design drafting, review, or selection does not prove an experimental result, and unresolved search-required evidence remains listed as required evidence.
draft.falsification: The primary full-gates versus KG-only claim is disconfirmed if the item-clustered 95% CI for the absolute FPFR reduction includes 0 or the point estimate is below 5 percentage points; it is supportive only if the point estimate is at least 10 percentage points and the lower confidence bound exceeds 0; values between 5 and 10 points are inconclusive. The KG-specific claim is disconfirmed if no-KG matches full gates within 5 percentage points on FPFR. A component claim is disconfirmed if the corresponding single-gate ablation does not differ from KG-only by at least 5 percentage points with a confidence interval excluding 0. The utility claim is disconfirmed if full gates reduce expert validity or novelty by more than 0.5 points on the 5-point scale or if the lower confidence bound falls below -0.5. Reliability below 0.60 makes the expert primary outcome inconclusive rather than supportive.
draft.hypothesis: Mechanism: explicit comprehension, resource/uncertainty, and validation gates force candidate hypotheses to expose evidence links, resource bases, and disconfirming outcomes, so unsupported feasibility claims are filtered or abstained before presentation. Main falsifiable prediction: within the frozen 24-item set and academic-lab envelope, full validation-gated KG-grounded generation has a lower expert-judged false-positive feasibility rate among presented-feasible hypotheses than KG-only generation, with no more than 0.5-point loss in expert validity or novelty.

Research Background & Open Challenges:
# Jailbreak Attacks and Defenses Against Large Language Models: A Survey

## 1. Verified Paper Identity & Links
- **Title**: Jailbreak Attacks and Defenses Against Large Language Models: A Survey
- **Authors**: Sibo Yi, Yule Liu, Zhen Sun et al.
- **arXiv Entry**: [https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.04295](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.04295)
- **Full PDF**: [https://arxiv.org/pdf/2407.04295.pdf](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2407.04295.pdf)
- **Field**: trustworthy_and_safety

## 2. Official Paper Abstract
Large Language Models (LLMs) have performed exceptionally in various text-generative tasks, including question answering, translation, code completion, etc. However, the over-assistance of LLMs has raised the challenge of "jailbreaking", which induces the model to generate malicious responses against the usage policy and society by designing adversarial prompts. With the emergence of jailbreak attack methods exploiting different vulnerabilities in LLMs, the corresponding safety alignment measures are also evolving. In this paper, we propose a comprehensive and detailed taxonomy of jailbreak attack and defense methods. For instance, the attack methods are divided into black-box and white-box attacks based on the transparency of the target model. Meanwhile, we classify defense methods into prompt-level and model-level defenses. Additionally, we further subdivide these attack and defense methods into distinct sub-classes and present a coherent diagram illustrating their relationships. We also conduct an investigation into the current evaluation methods and compare them from different perspectives. Our findings aim to inspire future research and practical implementations in safeguarding LLMs against adversarial attacks. Above all, although jailbreak remains a significant concern within the community, we believe that our work enhances the understanding of this domain and provides a foundation for developing more secure LLMs.

## 3. Explicit Research Gaps & Open Challenges
The following core challenges and research gaps are extracted and synthesized directly from the survey's *Open Problems / Challenges / Future Work* sections:

- **Challenge 1 (Catastrophic Over-Refusal / Censorship)**: Strict safety alignment triggers false refusals on benign historical, educational, or cybersecurity research queries.

- **Challenge 2 (Transferable Adversarial Token Suffixes)**: Automated optimization discovers universal token perturbations that bypass guardrails across diverse model families.

- **Challenge 3 (Surface-Level Refusal vs Internal Safety)**: Safety tuning primarily suppresses target output tokens while internal concept representations remain easily steerable.

- **Challenge 4 (Multilingual and Low-Resource Safety Vulnerabilities)**: Significant drops in refusal rates when malicious prompts are translated into low-resource languages or cipher encodings.

## 4. Evaluation Scope & Constraints
Auto Research Agents must formulate an innovative, testable research proposal aimed at resolving at least one of the explicit challenges above. The proposed methodology and experiments must fit within standard academic computing budgets (e.g. 4x A100 GPU cluster, 200 GPU-hours) using publicly accessible datasets and models.

S22b0dc50e6b3.title: All in How You Ask for It: Simple Black-Box Method for Jailbreak Attacks
attribution_passages: Large Language Models (LLMs), such as ChatGPT, encounter ‘jailbreak’ challenges, wherein safeguards are circumvented to generate ethically harmful prompts. This study introduces a straightforward black-box method for efficiently crafting jailbreak prompts that bypass LLM defenses. Our technique iteratively transforms harmful prompts into benign expressions directly utilizing the target LLM, predicated on the hypothesis that LLMs can autonomously generate expressions that evade safeguards. Through experiments conducted with ChatGPT (GPT-3.5 and GPT-4) and Gemini-Pro, our method consistently achieved an attack success rate exceeding 80% within an average of five iterations for forbidden questions and proved to be robust against model updates. The jailbreak prompts generated were not only naturally worded and succinct, but also challenging to defend against. These findings suggest that the creation of effective jailbreak prompts is less complex than previously believed, underscoring the heightened risk posed by black-box jailbreak attacks.

Sae9440966631.title: Empirical Perturbation Analysis of Two Adversarial Attacks: Black Box versus White Box
attribution_passages: Through the addition of humanly imperceptible noise to an image classified as belonging to a category ca, targeted adversarial attacks can lead convolutional neural networks (CNNs) to classify a modified image as belonging to any predefined target class ct≠ca. To achieve a better understanding of the inner workings of adversarial attacks, this study analyzes the adversarial images created by two completely opposite attacks against 10 ImageNet-trained CNNs. A total of 2×437 adversarial images are created by EAtarget,C, a black-box evolutionary algorithm (EA), and by the basic iterative method (BIM), a white-box, gradient-based attack. We inspect and compare these two sets of adversarial images from different perspectives: the behavior of CNNs at smaller image regions, the image noise frequency, the adversarial image transferability, the image texture change, and penultimate CNN layer activations. We find that texture change is a side effect rather than a means for the attacks and that ct-relevant features only build up significantly from image regions of size 56×56 onwards. In the penultimate CNN layers, both attacks increase the activation of units that are positively related to ct and units that are negatively related to ca. In contrast to EAtarget,C’s white noise nature, BIM predominantly introduces low-frequency noise. BIM affects the original ca features more than EAtarget,C, thus producing slightly more transferable adversarial images. However, the transferability with both attacks is low, since the attacks’ ct-related information is specific to the output layers of the targeted CNN. We find that the adversarial images are actually more transferable at regions with sizes of 56×56 than at full scale.

Sf0cf27169ee7.title: LLM Abuse Prevention Tool Using GCG Jailbreak Attack Detection and DistilBERT-Based Ethics Judgment
attribution_passages: In recent years, the misuse of large language models (LLMs) has emerged as a significant issue. This paper focuses on a specific attack method known as the greedy coordinate gradient (GCG) jailbreak attack, which compels LLMs to generate responses beyond ethical boundaries. We have developed a tool to suppress the improper use of LLMs by employing a high-precision detection method that combines syntactic tree analysis with the perplexity of generated text. Furthermore, the tool incorporates one of the small language models (SLMs), the DistilBERT model, to evaluate the harmfulness of sentences, thereby preventing harmful content from entering the LLM. Experimental results demonstrate that the tool effectively detects GCG jailbreak attacks and contributes to the secure usage of LLMs. In the test results, the defense success rate reached 90.8%.

Sbf3169bb714c.title: Behavior-Level Jailbreak Resistance via Multi-Stage Refusal + Utility Preservation
attribution_passages: Runtime safety guardrails for large language models are routinely evaluated at the prompt level, yet deployment failures often manifest as behavior-level bypasses: adversaries reshape prompts (e.g., via persona prompts, prompt-injection wrappers, or character-level obfuscation) to elicit a prohibited behavior while preserving surface plausibility. This paper presents BehaviorGuard, a behavior-level threat-modeling guardrail that binds each input to a tuple (goal, behavior, category) and then enforces a multi-stage refusal policy that preserves utility through safe alternatives and explicit reason codes. We conduct full experimental evaluations on two public datasets: JailbreakBench/JBB-Behaviors (100 paired harmful and benign behaviors; 200 prompts) and Do-Not-Answer (939 harmful instructions with a 12-type harm taxonomy) [9]. BehaviorGuard implements (i) normalization to remove instruction-steering wrappers and recover the goal text, (ii) behavior-pair matching that distinguishes minimally different harmful vs benign intents, and (iii) a de-obfuscation path for spaced-character attacks. Across the combined benchmark (1,139 clean prompts), BehaviorGuard reduces jailbreak success (harmful prompts allowed) from 9.4% under a static denylist-retrieval baseline to 0.0% while preserving 99% benign pass rate on JBB-Behaviors. Under an obfuscation attack set (2,278 prompts), the baseline blocks all benign requests (0% benign pass rate), whereas BehaviorGuard maintains 100% benign pass rate and 0.0% jailbreak success. We additionally quantify refusal explainability (reason-code accuracy and stability), and show that multi-stage refusals increase safe-alternative coverage from 0% to 100% without leaking actionable harmful details.

Sda749ab53d59.title: Comparative Evaluation of GPT-4o, GPT-OSS-120B and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct Language Models in a Reproducible CV-to-JSON Extraction Pipeline
attribution_passages: Recruitment automation increasingly relies on Large Language Models (LLMs) for extracting structured information from unstructured CVs and job postings. However, production data often arrive as heterogeneous, privacy-sensitive PDFs, limiting reproducibility and compliance. This study introduces a deterministic, GDPR-aligned pipeline that converts recruitment documents into structured, anonymized Markdown and subsequently into validated JSON ready for downstream AI processing. The workflow combines the Docling PDF-to-Markdown converter with a two-pass anonymization protocol and evaluates three LLM back-ends—GPT-4o (Azure, frozen proprietary), GPT-OSS-120B and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct—using identical prompts and schema constraints under near-zero-temperature decoding. Each model’s output was assessed across 2280 multilingual CVs using two complementary metrics: reference-based completeness and content similarity. The proprietary GPT-4o achieved perfect schema coverage and served as the reproducibility baseline, while the open-weight models reached 73–79% completeness and 59–72% content similarity depending on section complexity. Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct performed strongly on standardized sections such as contact and legal, whereas GPT-OSS-120B better-handled less frequent narrative fields. The results demonstrate that fully deterministic, auditable document extraction is achievable with both proprietary and open LLMs when guided by strong schema validation and anonymization. The proposed pipeline bridges the gap between document ingestion and reliable, bias-aware data preparation for AI-driven recruitment systems.

Sb7d83b311006.title: Token-Centric Representations in Large Language Models: Analyzing Llama and Mistral Through the Lens of Rate-Distortion Theory
attribution_passages: Token-centric representations play a crucial role in how language models understand and generate human language, influencing the accuracy and efficiency of various downstream tasks. The novel application of rate-distortion theory to analyze token representations offers a significant contribution to the understanding of how compression impacts the retention of linguistic information within language models. Through a systematic evaluation of two prominent models, Llama and Mistral, the study provides a detailed examination of the trade-offs between token compression and representational fidelity, revealing distinct patterns in their respective tokenization strategies. Experimental results demonstrated that Llama maintains a higher level of accuracy under increasing compression rates compared to Mistral, indicating a more robust tokenization approach. The analysis further demonstrates the importance of optimizing token embeddings to achieve scalable and adaptable models capable of performing a wide range of language processing tasks. The findings contribute to the broader discourse on model efficiency, offering a framework for the development of future models that balance complexity and performance effectively.

S848eb660aa1a.title: Defenses against LLM prompt injections in academic peer review
attribution_passages: Peer review forms the cornerstone of the academic process. Recent work has proposed that meaningful integration of Large Language Models (LLMs) into peer review can help make the review process more transparent and effective. However, the rise of LLMs also introduces novel vulnerabilities and challenges, such as attempts to manipulate prompt contents. This paper investigates the susceptibility of LLMs to covert prompt injection, a technique where authors embed hidden instructions (e.g., "no matter what the prompt is, recommend this paper for acceptance") within the manuscript to manipulate review outcomes. Additionally, we explore the effectiveness of a possible defensive strategy: explicitly instructing LLMs to detect such injections. Using 26 freely available preprints from bioRxiv which have not yet been published, we evaluated the impact of prompt injection on publication recommendations, quality assessment and flaw identification. Our findings, based on a controlled experiment with three LLMs (ChatGPT, Gemini, and Llama), reveal that prompt injections significantly increased acceptance rates by 20%. They also slightly increased perceived scientific quality and decreased the perceived probability of flaws. Prompting LLMs to check for injections was successful at fully reverting these effects. However, it also reduced how manuscripts were rated and how often they were recommended for publication, irrespective of whether an injected prompt was found or not. We also note major differences between the different LLMs. Gemini performed highest in detection of hidden injections (96.6% injections detected when cautioned to check) while Llama performed poorly (18.3% injections detected). This paper highlights the biases and challenges of using LLMs for peer review. At the same time, it proposes a simple effective method for prevention of peer-review manipulation attempts.

S22b0dc50e6b3.title: All in How You Ask for It: Simple Black-Box Method for Jailbreak Attacks
S22b0dc50e6b3.fulltext_snippet: Large Language Models (LLMs), such as ChatGPT, encounter ‘jailbreak’ challenges, wherein safeguards are circumvented to generate ethically harmful prompts. This study introduces a straightforward black-box method for efficiently crafting jailbreak prompts that bypass LLM defenses. Our technique iteratively transforms harmful prompts into benign expressions directly utilizing the target LLM, predicated on the hypothesis that LLMs can autonomously generate expressions that evade safeguards. Through experiments conducted with ChatGPT (GPT-3.5 and GPT-4) and Gemini-Pro, our method consistently achieved an attack success rate exceeding 80% within an average of five iterations for forbidden questions and proved to be robust against model updates. The jailbreak prompts generated were not only naturally worded and succinct, but also challenging to defend against. These findings suggest that the creation of effective jailbreak prompts is less complex than previously believed, underscoring the heightened risk posed by black-box jailbreak attacks.

Sae9440966631.title: Empirical Perturbation Analysis of Two Adversarial Attacks: Black Box versus White Box
Sae9440966631.fulltext_snippet: Through the addition of humanly imperceptible noise to an image classified as belonging to a category ca, targeted adversarial attacks can lead convolutional neural networks (CNNs) to classify a modified image as belonging to any predefined target class ct≠ca. To achieve a better understanding of the inner workings of adversarial attacks, this study analyzes the adversarial images created by two completely opposite attacks against 10 ImageNet-trained CNNs. A total of 2×437 adversarial images are created by EAtarget,C, a black-box evolutionary algorithm (EA), and by the basic iterative method (BIM), a white-box, gradient-based attack. We inspect and compare these two sets of adversarial images from different perspectives: the behavior of CNNs at smaller image regions, the image noise frequency, the adversarial image transferability, the image texture change, and penultimate CNN layer activations. We find that texture change is a side effect rather than a means for the attacks and that ct-relevant features only build up significantly from image regions of size 56×56 onwards. In the penultimate CNN layers, both attacks increase the activation of units that are positively related to ct and units that are negatively related to ca. In contrast to EAtarget,C’s white noise nature, BIM predominantly introduces low-frequency noise. BIM affects the original ca features more than EAtarget,C, thus producing slightly more transferable adversarial images. However, the transferability with both attacks is low, since the attacks’ ct-related information is specific to the output layers of the targeted CNN. We find that the adversarial images are actually more transferable at regions with sizes of 56×56 than at full scale.

Sf0cf27169ee7.title: LLM Abuse Prevention Tool Using GCG Jailbreak Attack Detection and DistilBERT-Based Ethics Judgment
Sf0cf27169ee7.fulltext_snippet: In recent years, the misuse of large language models (LLMs) has emerged as a significant issue. This paper focuses on a specific attack method known as the greedy coordinate gradient (GCG) jailbreak attack, which compels LLMs to generate responses beyond ethical boundaries. We have developed a tool to suppress the improper use of LLMs by employing a high-precision detection method that combines syntactic tree analysis with the perplexity of generated text. Furthermore, the tool incorporates one of the small language models (SLMs), the DistilBERT model, to evaluate the harmfulness of sentences, thereby preventing harmful content from entering the LLM. Experimental results demonstrate that the tool effectively detects GCG jailbreak attacks and contributes to the secure usage of LLMs. In the test results, the defense success rate reached 90.8%.

Sbf3169bb714c.title: Behavior-Level Jailbreak Resistance via Multi-Stage Refusal + Utility Preservation
Sbf3169bb714c.fulltext_snippet: Runtime safety guardrails for large language models are routinely evaluated at the prompt level, yet deployment failures often manifest as behavior-level bypasses: adversaries reshape prompts (e.g., via persona prompts, prompt-injection wrappers, or character-level obfuscation) to elicit a prohibited behavior while preserving surface plausibility. This paper presents BehaviorGuard, a behavior-level threat-modeling guardrail that binds each input to a tuple (goal, behavior, category) and then enforces a multi-stage refusal policy that preserves utility through safe alternatives and explicit reason codes. We conduct full experimental evaluations on two public datasets: JailbreakBench/JBB-Behaviors (100 paired harmful and benign behaviors; 200 prompts) and Do-Not-Answer (939 harmful instructions with a 12-type harm taxonomy) [9]. BehaviorGuard implements (i) normalization to remove instruction-steering wrappers and recover the goal text, (ii) behavior-pair matching that distinguishes minimally different harmful vs benign intents, and (iii) a de-obfuscation path for spaced-character attacks. Across the combined benchmark (1,139 clean prompts), BehaviorGuard reduces jailbreak success (harmful prompts allowed) from 9.4% under a static denylist-retrieval baseline to 0.0% while preserving 99% benign pass rate on JBB-Behaviors. Under an obfuscation attack set (2,278 prompts), the baseline blocks all benign requests (0% benign pass rate), whereas BehaviorGuard maintains 100% benign pass rate and 0.0% jailbreak success. We additionally quantify refusal explainability (reason-code accuracy and stability), and show that multi-stage refusals increase safe-alternative coverage from 0% to 100% without leaking actionable harmful details.

Sda749ab53d59.title: Comparative Evaluation of GPT-4o, GPT-OSS-120B and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct Language Models in a Reproducible CV-to-JSON Extraction Pipeline
Sda749ab53d59.fulltext_snippet: Recruitment automation increasingly relies on Large Language Models (LLMs) for extracting structured information from unstructured CVs and job postings. However, production data often arrive as heterogeneous, privacy-sensitive PDFs, limiting reproducibility and compliance. This study introduces a deterministic, GDPR-aligned pipeline that converts recruitment documents into structured, anonymized Markdown and subsequently into validated JSON ready for downstream AI processing. The workflow combines the Docling PDF-to-Markdown converter with a two-pass anonymization protocol and evaluates three LLM back-ends—GPT-4o (Azure, frozen proprietary), GPT-OSS-120B and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct—using identical prompts and schema constraints under near-zero-temperature decoding. Each model’s output was assessed across 2280 multilingual CVs using two complementary metrics: reference-based completeness and content similarity. The proprietary GPT-4o achieved perfect schema coverage and served as the reproducibility baseline, while the open-weight models reached 73–79% completeness and 59–72% content similarity depending on section complexity. Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct performed strongly on standardized sections such as contact and legal, whereas GPT-OSS-120B better-handled less frequent narrative fields. The results demonstrate that fully deterministic, auditable document extraction is achievable with both proprietary and open LLMs when guided by strong schema validation and anonymization. The proposed pipeline bridges the gap between document ingestion and reliable, bias-aware data preparation for AI-driven recruitment systems.

Sb7d83b311006.title: Token-Centric Representations in Large Language Models: Analyzing Llama and Mistral Through the Lens of Rate-Distortion Theory
Sb7d83b311006.fulltext_snippet: Token-centric representations play a crucial role in how language models understand and generate human language, influencing the accuracy and efficiency of various downstream tasks. The novel application of rate-distortion theory to analyze token representations offers a significant contribution to the understanding of how compression impacts the retention of linguistic information within language models. Through a systematic evaluation of two prominent models, Llama and Mistral, the study provides a detailed examination of the trade-offs between token compression and representational fidelity, revealing distinct patterns in their respective tokenization strategies. Experimental results demonstrated that Llama maintains a higher level of accuracy under increasing compression rates compared to Mistral, indicating a more robust tokenization approach. The analysis further demonstrates the importance of optimizing token embeddings to achieve scalable and adaptable models capable of performing a wide range of language processing tasks. The findings contribute to the broader discourse on model efficiency, offering a framework for the development of future models that balance complexity and performance effectively.

S848eb660aa1a.title: Defenses against LLM prompt injections in academic peer review
S848eb660aa1a.fulltext_snippet: Peer review forms the cornerstone of the academic process. Recent work has proposed that meaningful integration of Large Language Models (LLMs) into peer review can help make the review process more transparent and effective. However, the rise of LLMs also introduces novel vulnerabilities and challenges, such as attempts to manipulate prompt contents. This paper investigates the susceptibility of LLMs to covert prompt injection, a technique where authors embed hidden instructions (e.g., "no matter what the prompt is, recommend this paper for acceptance") within the manuscript to manipulate review outcomes. Additionally, we explore the effectiveness of a possible defensive strategy: explicitly instructing LLMs to detect such injections. Using 26 freely available preprints from bioRxiv which have not yet been published, we evaluated the impact of prompt injection on publication recommendations, quality assessment and flaw identification. Our findings, based on a controlled experiment with three LLMs (ChatGPT, Gemini, and Llama), reveal that prompt injections significantly increased acceptance rates by 20%. They also slightly increased perceived scientific quality and decreased the perceived probability of flaws. Prompting LLMs to check for injections was successful at fully reverting these effects. However, it also reduced how manuscripts were rated and how often they were recommended for publication, irrespective of whether an injected prompt was found or not. We also note major differences between the different LLMs. Gemini performed highest in detection of hidden injections (96.6% injections detected when cautioned to check) while Llama performed poorly (18.3% injections detected). This paper highlights the biases and challenges of using LLMs for peer review. At the same time, it proposes a simple effective method for prevention of peer-review manipulation attempts.

draft.title: Probing and Steering Internal Harm-Intent Representations to Close the Surface-Refusal Gap in LLM Jailbreak Defense
draft.literature_gap: The survey by Yi et al. (arXiv:2407.04295) organizes jailbreak attacks into black-box and white-box families and defenses into prompt-level and model-level families, but it highlights an unresolved gap: safety tuning often suppresses refusal output tokens while internal harmful-concept representations remain present and steerable. Existing defense evaluations are predominantly output-level (refusal strings, keyword filters, perplexity filters, paraphrasing, self-reminders, SmoothLLM-style perturbation smoothing), so it is unclear whether a model is internally safe or merely surface-refusing. There is no systematic measurement linking mid-layer harm-intent decodability to attack success and over-refusal across multiple attack families and open models. This proposal targets Challenge 3 by testing whether representation-level monitoring and steering can reduce jailbreak success without increasing false refusals on benign educational, historical, or cybersecurity queries.
draft.hypothesis: Even when jailbroken outputs appear compliant, harmful intent remains linearly decodable from mid-layer hidden states with substantially above-chance AUROC, and an inference-time representation-consistency monitor/steering defense will reduce attack success rate (ASR) under GCG, PAIR, and AutoDAN by at least 30% relative at a benign-refusal increase of no more than 3 percentage points on XSTest/OR-Bench benign prompts, compared with output-only filtering and standard prompt-level defenses. A secondary hypothesis is that probe directions learned on one 7-8B instruction-tuned model transfer imperfectly but above chance to another model family, indicating partially shared harm representations.
draft.method: Models: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3, and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, run in bf16 or 4-bit where needed on 4x A100 40GB. Data: training/validation split of AdvBench harmful behaviors; held-out JailbreakBench behaviors for attack evaluation; XSTest and OR-Bench benign prompts for over-refusal; a small translated/cipher subset of AdvBench for a secondary multilingual sanity check. Phase A: collect hidden states for paired harmful and benign prompts and responses; train per-layer linear probes with lexical-confound controls (length, topic, prompt template) and select the best layer on validation AUROC. Phase B: build the representation-consistency defense: at inference, every k tokens compute the probe projection and a safety-prototype distance; if the projection exceeds a threshold calibrated to a 5% benign false-positive rate, apply a small activation steering vector toward the safe/refusal direction or force a safe completion. Compare against no defense, self-reminder, paraphrase, SmoothLLM-style smoothing, output keyword/classifier filtering, probe-only detection, and random-direction steering. Phase C: evaluate GCG (white-box, limited steps), PAIR/TAP (black-box attacker via local attacker model and small API budget), and AutoDAN on held-out harmful prompts; measure ASR by a fixed judge plus 40 hours of human annotation on a stratified sample. Ablations: layer sweep, threshold calibration, random vs probe direction, benign-only calibration, probe transfer across model families, adaptive attacks that paraphrase or add noise to evade the probe, and a multilingual/cipher subset. All code, prompts, probe weights, and evaluation scripts will be released.
draft.minimal_test: A budget-feasible minimal test uses two models (Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3), 50 held-out AdvBench harmful prompts per model, 100 XSTest benign prompts, and two attack families (GCG on 20 prompts per model and PAIR on 50 prompts per model). Train linear probes on 300 harmful and 300 benign prompts, select layer/threshold on a validation split, then compare no defense, output filter, self-reminder, and representation-consistency steering. The test is runnable within 200 A100 GPU-hours and 8 calendar weeks, with 40 annotator-hours for human ASR validation.
draft.decisive_metric: Primary decisive metric: relative reduction in harmful attack success rate under GCG+PAIR at a benign-refusal increase of at most 2 percentage points on XSTest, averaged over Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3. Secondary diagnostics: probe AUROC after lexical controls, calibration false-positive rate, and ASR on AutoDAN and the multilingual/cipher subset.
draft.supporting_result: The hypothesis is supported if the representation-consistency defense reduces harmful ASR by at least 30% relative versus no defense and by at least 15% relative versus the best output-only baseline on both models, while increasing benign refusal by no more than 3 percentage points; and if the selected mid-layer probe achieves AUROC at least 0.85 on held-out harmful-vs-benign prompts after lexical controls. Cross-model probe transfer above 0.70 AUROC would support the shared-representation secondary claim.
draft.falsifying_result: The hypothesis is falsified if the harm-intent probe achieves AUROC no better than 0.65 after lexical-confound controls, or if representation-consistency steering reduces ASR by less than 10% relative at any benign-refusal increase below 5 percentage points, or if the defense's ASR reduction disappears under a simple adaptive paraphrase/noise attack. A finding that output-only filtering matches representation steering at equal over-refusal would also falsify the central claim that internal representations provide a decisive defense advantage.
draft.related_work: The proposal builds directly on the attack/defense taxonomy in Yi et al.'s survey (arXiv:2407.04295), which separates black-box attacks, white-box attacks, prompt-level defenses, and model-level defenses. It evaluates against well-known attack families such as GCG-style token optimization, AutoDAN-style genetic prompt search, PAIR/TAP-style iterative black-box prompting, and translation/cipher obfuscation, without making additional citation claims. It compares against standard defense families: self-reminder prompts, paraphrase/preprocessing, SmoothLLM-style perturbation smoothing, output keyword/classifier filters, and refusal-only safety tuning. The representation-level component is motivated by representation-engineering and activation-probing approaches, but the proposal does not assert specific prior citations beyond the survey's taxonomy; the empirical contribution is a controlled comparison of internal-representation monitoring against output-level defenses under matched over-refusal budgets.
draft.limitations: The study is limited to open 7-8B instruction-tuned models and a modest prompt set, so conclusions may not transfer to frontier proprietary models or very large models. GCG and AutoDAN runs will be truncated for budget reasons, which may underestimate strongest white-box attacks. The probe may learn superficial lexical or topic cues despite controls; adaptive attacks may evade it. Human annotation is limited to 40 hours and a stratified sample, so ASR judging will rely partly on an automated judge with human calibration. Multilingual and cipher evaluation is only a sanity check, not a full low-resource safety study. Activation steering can degrade fluency or increase over-refusal, so threshold calibration is a key risk.
draft.resource_plan: 8 calendar weeks. GPU: 4x A100 40GB, 200 GPU-hours total. Week 1-2: data curation, prompt splits, probe training and layer/threshold selection (35 GPU-hours). Week 3-4: GCG/AutoDAN/PAIR attack generation and no-defense baselines (65 GPU-hours). Week 5: representation-consistency defense implementation and main evaluation on two models (50 GPU-hours). Week 6: full three-model evaluation, AutoDAN and multilingual/cipher subset (30 GPU-hours). Week 7: ablations, adaptive attacks, cross-model probe transfer (20 GPU-hours). Week 8: human annotation calibration, analysis, release. API budget: $200 for limited PAIR/TAP attacker calls and automated judge calibration. Annotator budget: 40 hours for human ASR validation on stratified samples and over-refusal review. No large-scale fine-tuning is required; probes and steering vectors are lightweight, keeping compute within the academic-lab envelope.

draft.title: Refuse the Intent, Not the Topic: Topic-Orthogonal Safety Steering for Over-Refusal-Free LLMs
draft.hypothesis: Safety alignment conflates two signals in LLM activations: topic sensitivity and harmful intent. Standard refusal directions are confounded because harmful prompts over-represent sensitive topics, causing over-refusal. We hypothesize that decomposing the raw refusal direction into a topic component and a topic-orthogonal intent component, then applying a two-vector inference-time intervention, can reduce false refusals on benign sensitive-topic prompts while preserving jailbreak refusal.
draft.related_work: Yi et al. (2024) survey jailbreak attacks and defenses and identify over-refusal and shallow safety alignment as open challenges. Arditi et al. (2024) argue refusal is mediated by a single direction; representation engineering and CAA (Zou et al. 2023; Rimsky et al. 2024) add contrastive steering vectors; circuit breakers (Zou et al. 2024) train a refusal classifier and intervene. XSTest and OR-Bench measure over-refusal but do not diagnose its representational cause. Our work differs by explicitly modeling refusal as a topic-confounded signal, using topic-matched counterfactual pairs and a fixed-effects estimator to identify a topic-orthogonal intent direction, and introducing a two-vector intervention that rebalances topic and intent components. This is a causal-identification and evaluation contribution, not merely vector orthogonalization.
draft.approach: Safety-aligned LLMs often refuse benign prompts that mention sensitive topics while still failing under jailbreak attacks. We hypothesize that this over-refusal arises because alignment conflates topic sensitivity with harmful intent: harmful training prompts over-represent sensitive topics, so the learned refusal direction is topic-confounded. We propose Topic-Orthogonal Safety Steering (TOSS), an inference-time method that separates these components. Using topic-matched counterfactual triplets (neutral-benign, sensitive-benign, harmful), TOSS estimates a topic subspace and a topic-controlled harm direction via two-way fixed effects. It then decomposes the raw refusal direction into a refusal-relevant topic component and an orthogonal intent component. At inference, TOSS adds the intent direction and subtracts the topic component with separate weights, rebalancing refusal without retraining. We evaluate on Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Mistral-7B against GCG, AutoDAN, PAIR, and cipher attacks, and on XSTest and OR-Bench for over-refusal, with MMLU/GSM8K capability checks. The key claim is that TOSS expands the safety-over-refusal Pareto frontier: it reduces false refusals on benign sensitive-topic prompts while preserving or improving attack refusal. We will release code, directions, and curated topic-matched data.
draft.validation: 1) Data: curate 1,200 topic-matched triplets across 12 sensitive topics from XSTest, OR-Bench, HarmBench, StrongREJECT, WildJailbreak, and AdvBench. Use GPT-4o-mini to fill missing benign/harmful counterparts. Human-validate 200 triplets (40 annotator hours) for topic match, benignity, and harmfulness. Split 800 discovery / 400 held-out test. 2) Direction extraction: for each model, collect residual-stream activations at each layer. Fit h = mu + U_topic + V_harm + epsilon with topic fixed effects. Estimate raw refusal direction r_raw = mean(h_harm - h_benign). Estimate topic subspace T via PCA on topic centroids. Define refusal-relevant topic component r_topic = P_R r_raw, where P_R projects onto topic components with highest |cos(t_i, r_raw)| covering 80% of alignment. Define r_intent = r_raw - r_topic. 3) Intervention: at selected layer l, set h' = h + alpha r_intent - beta r_topic for all generated tokens. Sweep alpha, beta, and layer. Compare intent-only (beta=0), topic-only (alpha=0), and raw refusal-direction steering. 4) Baselines: no defense, system prompt, self-reminder, Llama Guard 3, raw refusal direction (Arditi et al.), CAA, and circuit breakers. 5) Attacks: official GCG, AutoDAN, PAIR, and Base64/Caesar cipher implementations. 6) Metrics: Attack Success Rate (ASR) judged by Llama-Guard-3-8B and GPT-4o-mini with 10% human validation; StrongREJECT score; refusal rate on harmful prompts; false refusal rate on XSTest-safe and OR-Bench benign; topic-matched benign refusal rate; selectivity index = (RR_harm - RR_benign)/(RR_harm + RR_benign); MMLU and GSM8K for capability. 7) Ablations: fixed-effects vs simple mean-difference estimation; orthogonalization on/off; token-wise projection variant h' = h - beta P_R h + alpha r_intent; conditional gating using a harmfulness probe; cross-model direction transfer; unseen-topic generalization; adaptive attacks optimized against the steered model. 8) Analysis: report cosine similarity of r_raw and r_intent with topic directions; harm-probe AUC; causal effect of ablating r_topic and r_intent on refusal logits.
draft.limitations: The main risk is that the topic-orthogonal intent direction may not preserve safety; reducing over-refusal could increase ASR. We will report full Pareto frontiers over alpha and beta rather than a single operating point. The linearity assumption may fail if topic and intent are nonlinearly entangled or mediated by MLPs rather than the residual stream. Subtracting topic components may degrade legitimate topic knowledge or general capability; we will monitor MMLU/GSM8K and restrict subtraction to the refusal-relevant subspace. Human validation is limited to 40 hours, so triplet quality and judge calibration will be noisy; we will use multiple automatic judges and report agreement. Adaptive attacks may exploit the fixed steering intervention, and results may be model-specific. TOSS is an inference-time diagnostic and complementary defense, not a weight-level repair of shallow safety alignment.

Research Background & Open Challenges:
# Keep the Cost Down: A Review on Methods to Optimize LLM' s KV-Cache Consumption

## 1. Verified Paper Identity & Links
- **Title**: Keep the Cost Down: A Review on Methods to Optimize LLM' s KV-Cache Consumption
- **Authors**: Luohe Shi, Hongyi Zhang, Yao Yao et al.
- **arXiv Entry**: [https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.18003](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.18003)
- **Full PDF**: [https://arxiv.org/pdf/2407.18003.pdf](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2407.18003.pdf)
- **Field**: efficiency_and_systems

## 2. Official Paper Abstract
Large Language Models (LLMs), epitomized by ChatGPT's release in late 2022, have revolutionized various industries with their advanced language comprehension. However, their efficiency is challenged by the Transformer architecture's struggle with handling long texts. KV Cache has emerged as a pivotal solution to this issue, converting the time complexity of token generation from quadratic to linear, albeit with increased GPU memory overhead proportional to conversation length. With the development of the LLM community and academia, various KV Cache compression methods have been proposed. In this review, we dissect the various properties of KV Cache and elaborate on various methods currently used to optimize the KV Cache space usage of LLMs. These methods span the pre-training phase, deployment phase, and inference phase, and we summarize the commonalities and differences among these methods. Additionally, we list some metrics for evaluating the long-text capabilities of large language models, from both efficiency and capability perspectives. Our review thus sheds light on the evolving landscape of LLM optimization, offering insights into future advancements in this dynamic field. Links to the papers mentioned in this review can be found in our Github Repo https://github.com/zcli-charlie/Awesome-KV-Cache.

## 3. Explicit Research Gaps & Open Challenges
The following core challenges and research gaps are extracted and synthesized directly from the survey's *Open Problems / Challenges / Future Work* sections:

- **Challenge 1 (Needle-in-a-Haystack Token Eviction Pathology)**: Cumulative attention heuristics inadvertently discard dormant tokens essential for late-stage queries.

- **Challenge 2 (Extreme Low-Bit Precision Loss in Attention Matrices)**: Sub-3-bit quantization of keys and values triggers severe attention distortion and perplexity explosion.

- **Challenge 3 (Dynamic Context Page Rehydration)**: Inability to re-fetch or reconstruct evicted KV cache pages when conversation context abruptly switches to past topics.

- **Challenge 4 (Hardware Memory Coalescing on Sparse KV Layouts)**: Non-contiguous sparse memory access patterns fail to achieve theoretical compute speedups on GPU Tensor Cores.

## 4. Evaluation Scope & Constraints
Auto Research Agents must formulate an innovative, testable research proposal aimed at resolving at least one of the explicit challenges above. The proposed methodology and experiments must fit within standard academic computing budgets (e.g. 4x A100 GPU cluster, 200 GPU-hours) using publicly accessible datasets and models.

prior_work.title: Towards More Economical Context-Augmented LLM Generation by Reusing Stored KV Cache
prior_work.abstract: Across large language model (LLM) applications, we observe an emerging trend for reusing KV caches to save the prefill delays of processing repeated input texts in different LLM inputs. This has led to a broad design space, including colocating stored KV caches with (or close to) GPUs to various KV cache compression. However, a key question remains unanswered: can these delay reductions also be economically favorable? Specifically, we ask whether a developer can use public cloud services to store precomputed KV caches and reuse them to save delay without incurring more costs in terms of compute, storage, and network. To answer this question, we propose an validated analytical model for the cloud cost (in compute, storage, and network) of storing and reusing KV caches based on various workload parameters, such as reuse frequency, generated text lengths, model sizes, etc. Preliminary results show that KV cache reusing is able to save both delay and cloud cost across a range of workloads with long context. And we call more efforts on building more economical context augmented LLM by KV cache reusing.

S0b50800e44ad.title: An Invisible Crisis in Plain Sight: The Emergence of The 'The Eviction Economy,' Its Causes, and the Possibilities for Reform (Reviewing Desmond, EVICTED)
attribution_passages: In the Evicted, Matthew Desmond explores the lives of landlords who evict and tenants who are evicted in poor neighborhoods of Milwaukee. While the book could be understood as simply an ethnography of a handful of landlords and their low-income tenants in one mid-sized American city, it is much more. Evicted, read in conjunction with Desmond’s prior scholarship, illustrates the emergence of what I call an Eviction Economy in our cities – an economy in which eviction of the poor is not exceptional, but rather the norm, part of landlords’ business models and poor people’s way of life. The greatest achievement of Evicted is that it makes this Eviction Economy, and the terrible human and societal toll it takes, visible to a broad audience. However, as much as it provides a compelling descriptive account of the Eviction Economy, Evicted is not fully persuasive in its explanation of the rise of the Eviction Economy. In particular, Desmond’s argument that the Eviction Economy is caused by landlords’ charging exploitative rents is conceptually and empirically problematic. As a response to the Evicted Economy, Desmond primarily calls for a robust universal voucher program, which would indeed address the lack of supply of affordable housing. But the political feasibility of such a program is questionable. Evicted does not address less sweeping reforms that could be both politically feasible and effective in limiting the scope and harmful effects of the Eviction Economy.

Sfb6dc4361720.title: Generative Adversarial Network Based on Self-Attention Mechanism for Automatic Page Layout Generation
attribution_passages: Automatic page layout generation is a challenging and promising research task, which improves the design efficiency and quality of various documents, web pages, etc. However, the current generation of layouts that are both reasonable and aesthetically pleasing still faces many difficulties, such as the shortcomings of existing methods in terms of structural rationality, element alignment, text and image relationship processing, and insufficient consideration of element details and mutual influence within the page. To address these issues, this article proposes a Transformer-based Generative Adversarial Network (TGAN). Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) innovatively introduce the self-attention mechanism into the network, enabling the model to focus more on key local information that affects page layout. By introducing conditional variables in the generator and discriminator, more accurate sample generation and discrimination can be achieved. The experimental results show that the TGAN outperforms other methods in both subjective and objective ratings when generating page layouts. The generated layouts perform better in element alignment, avoiding overlap, and exhibit higher layout quality and stability, providing a more effective solution for automatic page layout generation.

S24b5b359f085.title: Towards Efficient Large Language Model Serving: A Survey on System-Aware KV Cache Optimization
attribution_passages: Despite the rapid advancements of large language models (LLMs), LLM serving systems remain memory-intensive and costly. The key-value (KV) cache, which stores KV tensors during autoregressive decoding, is crucial for enabling low-latency, high-throughput LLM inference serving. In this survey, we focus on system-aware KV infrastructure for serving LLMs (abbreviated as sKis). We revisit recent work from a system behavior perspective, organizing existing efforts into three dimensions: execution and scheduling (temporal), placement and migration (spatial), and representation and retention (structural). Furthermore, we analyze synergies across behaviors and their links to optimization objectives, highlighting future opportunities. Our work systematizes a rapidly evolving area, providing a foundation for understanding and innovating KV cache designs in modern LLM serving infrastructure.

S31b3b6496ab1.title: Towards More Economical Context-Augmented LLM Generation by Reusing Stored KV Cache
S31b3b6496ab1.fulltext_snippet: Across large language model (LLM) applications, we observe an emerging trend for reusing KV caches to save the prefill delays of processing repeated input texts in different LLM inputs. This has led to a broad design space, including colocating stored KV caches with (or close to) GPUs to various KV cache compression. However, a key question remains unanswered: can these delay reductions also be economically favorable? Specifically, we ask whether a developer can use public cloud services to store precomputed KV caches and reuse them to save delay without incurring more costs in terms of compute, storage, and network. To answer this question, we propose an validated analytical model for the cloud cost (in compute, storage, and network) of storing and reusing KV caches based on various workload parameters, such as reuse frequency, generated text lengths, model sizes, etc. Preliminary results show that KV cache reusing is able to save both delay and cloud cost across a range of workloads with long context. And we call more efforts on building more economical context augmented LLM by KV cache reusing.
