draft.title: ReHydra-KV: Attention-Triggered Page Rehydration with Coalesced Sparse KV Layouts for Long-Context LLMs
draft.literature_gap: The survey identifies two coupled open problems: irreversible KV-cache eviction causes needle-in-a-haystack failures when a late query returns to an evicted topic (Challenge 3), and token-sparse KV layouts fail to realize Tensor-Core speedups because of non-coalesced memory access (Challenge 4). The supplied 2025 dated paper on reusing stored KV caches studies economic delay/cost tradeoffs for repeated context but does not address abrupt topic switches within a live conversation, attention-triggered reconstruction of evicted pages, or coalesced page-granular sparse attention. Existing survey-reviewed eviction and quantization methods can reduce memory but generally discard dormant tokens permanently; they do not provide a falsifiable mechanism for low-overhead rehydration under a fixed GPU budget.
draft.hypothesis: A page-granular KV cache that keeps compact per-page key signatures for evicted pages and asynchronously rehydrates pages when late-query attention probes those signatures will recover much of the accuracy lost by irreversible eviction on topic-switch long-context queries, while a page-contiguous sparse layout will keep decode throughput close to the eviction baseline. Specifically, at 50% KV-memory budget on 32K-token topic-switch NIAH, signature-triggered rehydration will improve exact-match accuracy by at least 10 points over irreversible eviction and remain within 5 points of full-cache accuracy, with no more than 15% decode-throughput overhead.
draft.method: Implement ReHydra-KV on a 7B long-context open model (e.g., Mistral-7B-v0.2 or LongChat-7B) using HuggingFace attention hooks. (1) Page store: split KV cache into 64-token pages; active pages stay on GPU under a fixed budget; evicted pages are copied to pinned host memory. For each evicted page and layer, store a 32-dimensional random-projection sketch of key centroids plus max key norm and page id; signature memory is <2 MB for 32K contexts. (2) Rehydration trigger: maintain a query sketch per decode step; score evicted pages by cosine similarity to the query sketch, normalized by active-page attention mass. Trigger rehydration when the top evicted-page score exceeds alpha times the current top active-page score and a query-drift detector fires, or every N decode steps. Rehydrate top-r pages asynchronously over PCIe using a separate CUDA stream; until ready, use signature-based approximate attention as fallback. (3) Coalesced sparse layout: store active and rehydrated KV in fixed 64-token contiguous pages with a valid-page bitmask; implement a block-sparse attention kernel that loads only valid pages and uses 16x16 MMA tiles, avoiding per-token gather. Ablations: no signatures/random trigger, synchronous vs asynchronous rehydration, page sizes 32/64/128, r in {1,2,4,8}, alpha thresholds, and signature dimension 16/32/64. Baselines use the survey's Awesome-KV-Cache official implementations where available: full cache, sliding-window/StreamingLLM-style eviction, heavy-hitter/H2O-style eviction, query-aware/SnapKV-style eviction, and 4-bit KIVI-style quantization; otherwise reimplement from the survey description and validate against full-cache outputs.
draft.minimal_test: Use one 7B long-context model, 200 topic-switch NIAH examples built from public text: an early target fact is separated from the final query by 24K-32K distractor tokens, with an explicit topic switch back to the early segment. Evaluate four conditions at 50% KV-memory budget: full cache (upper bound), irreversible eviction baseline, oracle rehydration (knows the target page), and ReHydra-KV. Also run standard NIAH and a small LongBench subset for sanity. Measure exact-match accuracy, peak GPU memory, decode tokens/s, rehydration bytes and stall time. Repeat with 3 seeds and report mean plus bootstrap 95% CI.
draft.decisive_metric: Primary: exact-match accuracy on the 32K topic-switch NIAH at 50% KV-memory budget. Guardrails: decode throughput relative to the irreversible eviction baseline and peak GPU memory not exceeding full-cache memory. Success requires at least +10 points accuracy over irreversible eviction, within 5 points of full cache, and throughput at least 0.90x the eviction baseline.
draft.supporting_result: ReHydra-KV reaches at least 60% exact-match accuracy versus at most 50% for irreversible eviction and at least 65% for full cache on 32K topic-switch NIAH, while decoding at at least 0.90x the eviction baseline tokens/s and using no more peak GPU memory than the 50% budget plus signature overhead. Ablations show asynchronous page-granular rehydration and the coalesced block-sparse kernel are each necessary for the accuracy-throughput combination.
draft.falsifying_result: The hypothesis is falsified if ReHydra-KV improves topic-switch accuracy by less than 5 points over irreversible eviction, or fails to exceed 53% exact match, or decodes below 0.80x the eviction baseline, or exceeds the 50% KV-memory budget after signature and page metadata overhead. It is also falsified if oracle rehydration shows no accuracy gap, indicating the benchmark or eviction baseline is not sensitive to Challenge 3.
draft.related_work: Shi et al., 2024, arXiv:2407.18003, 'Keep the Cost Down: A Review on Methods to Optimize LLM's KV-Cache Consumption', defines the open challenges on needle-in-a-haystack eviction, low-bit precision, dynamic context page rehydration, and hardware memory coalescing. The supplied 2025 dated paper 'Towards More Economical Context-Augmented LLM Generation by Reusing Stored KV Cache' (DOI 10.32388/xi1064) provides a cloud-cost model for storing and reusing precomputed KV caches but does not study within-conversation topic-switch rehydration or coalesced sparse-page attention. Baseline method families are taken from the survey and its Awesome-KV-Cache repository; no additional unverified citations are claimed.
draft.limitations: The study uses 7B open models and up to 32K context, not frontier models or multi-tenant serving. Topic-switch NIAH is synthetic and may overstate the benefit of rehydration; we include standard NIAH and a small LongBench subset but not a full production trace. PCIe rehydration latency varies by host and is modeled rather than tested across many machines. The signature router may miss needles whose keys are poorly represented by centroids. The method does not address sub-3-bit quantization or pretraining changes. Results are limited to one academic 4xA100 40GB cluster and 200 GPU-hours.
draft.resource_plan.api_plan: Use at most $150 for synthetic topic-switch data generation/validation prompts and $50 for a final LLM-judge consistency check; all primary metrics are local exact-match and throughput.
draft.resource_plan.annotator_plan: 40 hours for manually validating 200 topic-switch examples, auditing 50 model outputs for attribution errors, and checking rehydration-trigger traces.
draft.resource_plan.compute_notes: Use 4-bit or 8-bit model loading where needed to fit baselines; reserve full-precision runs for the primary 7B model. Log GPU memory, PCIe bytes, and kernel occupancy for every run. All datasets and models are public; code and prompts will be released.

draft.title: Ghost Cache: Making KV Eviction Reversible with Softmax-Mass-Correct Attention Pseudo-Tokens
draft.hypothesis: Hard KV eviction (H2O, SnapKV, StreamingLLM) is irreversible, so dormant tokens needed by late queries cause needle-in-a-haystack and context-switch failures. Hypothesis: the exact softmax contribution of any set of evicted tokens can be preserved by a small number of 'ghost' pseudo-tokens, where a ghost covering an evicted cluster contributes logit = log Z_g(q) and value = S_g(q)/Z_g(q), with S_g and Z_g the unnormalized attention numerator and denominator of that cluster. Using positive random features, S_g and Z_g collapse into an O(G*d) per-head sketch computed once per eviction, independent of how many tokens were evicted. Hence eviction becomes lossless-in-expectation compression rather than forgetting, and partitioning evicted tokens into G key-space clusters preserves distinct needles that a single aggregated ghost would dilute. Ghost Cache is training-free, composes with any eviction policy and base model as G extra attention columns, and improves NIAH and LongBench at a matched hot-cache budget with overhead independent of evicted-token count.
draft.related_work: Hard eviction (H2O heavy hitters, SnapKV observation-window selection, StreamingLLM attention sinks+recency, Scissorhands) drops tokens permanently and is documented to fail when a rare/dormant token is needed late (survey Challenges 1 & 3). Token merging (KVMerger, CaM, D2O) merges or reweights retained tokens per-step using similarity heuristics; it does not maintain a separate cold tier, does not reconstruct the softmax numerator/denominator, and offers no principled guarantee that an evicted needle survives. Linear/hybrid attention (Performer random features, Longformer/BigBird) and Native Sparse Attention (DeepSeek 2025) use compact branches but require TRAINING/architecture co-design and cannot be plugged into arbitrary pretrained checkpoints. Our proposal is the first training-free, eviction-agnostic soft-eviction layer that (a) reconstructs the softmax mass of evicted tokens exactly in expectation via the ghost pseudo-token identity, (b) uses a mixture of G key-space-clustered ghosts to prevent needle dilution, and (c) optionally promotes low-bit cold-stored pages when a ghost's attention gate spikes, realized as dynamic context rehydration (Challenge 3).
draft.approach: KV-cache eviction is the standard way to fit long contexts on a fixed GPU budget, yet all popular policies (H2O, SnapKV, StreamingLLM) are irreversible: once a token is dropped, any late query needing it fails, causing well-known needle-in-a-haystack and context-switch pathologies. We introduce Ghost Cache, a training-free deployment layer that turns eviction into soft, reversible compression. Our observation is exact: for any set of evicted tokens, their combined softmax contribution equals that of a single pseudo-token with logit log Z(q) and value S(q)/Z(q), where S and Z are the unnormalized attention numerator and denominator. We approximate S and Z with positive random features, collapsing them into a tiny O(G*d) per-head sketch computed once at eviction time and independent of the number of evicted tokens. To prevent a rare but decisive needle from being diluted, we partition evicted tokens into G key-space clusters, each contributing its own ghost. No token is ever forgotten: it is compressed into a ghost that participates in every subsequent attention computation as G extra columns, FlashAttention-compatible and plug-in to any eviction policy. We optionally keep an int8 cold store to promote a ghost's pages when its gate spikes (dynamic rehydration). Across Llama-2-7B, Mistral-7B and LongChat-7B, Ghost Cache improves NIAH accuracy and LongBench scores at matched hot-cache budgets while adding only tens of megabytes and sub-millisecond overhead; we verify the aggregation identity via direct attention-reconstruction error.
draft.validation:
Setup: inference-only on Llama-2-7B-chat, Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.2, LongChat-7B in fp16 (fit 4xA100-40GB). Baselines: full cache, StreamingLLM, H2O, SnapKV, KVMerger at matched hot-cache budgets (256/512/1024 slots). Ghost insertion: append G extra attention columns (logits log Z_g, values S_g/Z_g) before softmax, so FlashAttention compatibility is preserved.

E1 (Identity validation & estimator quality): For held-out prompts at 50% eviction, compare full-cache head outputs and attention distributions against ghost-augmented versions; report MSE of head outputs, MSE of attention distributions, and MAE of Z. Sweep feature dim d_phi in {32,64,128} and G in {1,4,8,16}; report estimator bias/variance and reconstruction error to surface random-feature limitations early.

E2 (NIAH): Single- and multi-needle (2-8), depths 0-100%, contexts 4K-32K. Exact-match accuracy vs hot-budget. Primary test of dormant-needle recovery and of the clustering hypothesis (G>1 vs single ghost dilution).

E3 (Context-switch recall): Synthetic multi-turn dialogue where the answer needs a fact stated K turns earlier, separated by unrelated topical turns; measure recall when the fact's tokens are evicted. Targets Challenge 3.

E4 (LongBench): narrativeqa, qasper, multifieldqa_en, hotpotqa, 2wikimqa, passage_retrieval_en at matched budgets; report LongBench score.

E5 (Language modeling): PG19 long-context perplexity at 8K/16K; PPL vs budget.

E6 (Extension & ablation): (a) int8 cold store with gate-triggered promotion of top-1 ghost's pages vs always-on ghosts — recall gain vs added memory/latency (Challenge 3, and int8 sketches touch Challenge 2). (b) Plugin compatibility: attach Ghost Cache to H2O, SnapKV, StreamingLLM to show orthogonal gains. (c) Ablations: clustering method (k-means on normalized keys vs random-projection LSH), sink-token protection (keep sinks exact), random-feature clipping vs a centroid+log-mass ghost estimator, ghost-sketch precision, and per-token latency/memory. All experiments inference-only, total <150 GPU-hours.
draft.limitations: 1) Positive random features can have high variance for large key norms, biasing S/Z; mitigated by key normalization/clipping, keeping attention-sink tokens exact, and reporting a centroid+log-mass estimator as a robust fallback. 2) A rare needle may still be diluted if clustering does not isolate it; E1/E2 explicitly test the clustering hypothesis and we map the dilution boundary vs budget. 3) Ghosts are built from post-RoPE keys, so they are position-correct by construction, but the sketch must be re-computed when the eviction set changes; we amortize this and report its cost. 4) Per-token compute grows with G (G extra dot products); we bound G and report latency. 5) Evaluation is limited to <=7B models and <=32K context by budget; transfer to frontier models/longer contexts is unverified. 6) Baseline reimplementation (H2O/SnapKV/KVMerger) may add fair-comparison noise; we use official implementations where released and control budgets. 7) If random-feature error dominates, gains over hard eviction may be marginal; E1 surfaces this early and the promotion/cold-store fallback preserves utility.

prior_work.title: A Doctor's Guide to Foundation Models
prior_work.abstract: The rapid advancement of artificial intelligence (AI) has led to the emergence of foundation models as powerful tools for various applications, including healthcare. These large-scale machine learning models, such as GPT and LLaMA have demonstrated potential for improving patient outcomes and transforming medical practice. However, healthcare professionals without a background in data science may find it challenging to understand and utilize these models effectively. This paper aims to provide an accessible introduction to foundation models for healthcare professionals, discussing their core concepts, relevant applications in healthcare, ethical considerations, challenges, and future directions. By offering a comprehensive overview of foundation models, I hope to foster a more informed and collaborative future between healthcare professionals and data scientists, ultimately driving better patient care and medical advancements.

S6a77eebd1109.title: Evaluation of Embedding Models for Hungarian Question-Answer Retrieval on Domain-Specific and Public Benchmarks
attribution_passages: Embedding models have become a fundamental component of modern natural language processing, yet their performance in morphologically rich, low-resource languages such as Hungarian remains underexplored. In this paper, we present a systematic evaluation of state-of-the-art embedding models for Hungarian question-answer retrieval. We construct two complementary evaluation datasets: (i) a domain-specific corpus collected from company documentation, preprocessed into topical chunks with human-verified question-answer pairs, and (ii) the publicly available HuRTE benchmark. Using FAISS as the vector database, we compare eight multilingual and crosslingual embedding models. Performance is measured using Mean Reciprocal Rank (MRR) and Recall@k. Results show substantial variation across models and datasets, with notable differences between domain-specific and general-purpose retrieval tasks. We complement the evaluation with error analysis, highlighting challenges posed by Hungarian morphology and compounding, and discuss trade-offs in efficiency. Our findings provide the first comparative study of embedding-based retrieval in Hungarian, offering practical guidance for downstream applications and setting a foundation for future research in Hungarian representation learning. The dataset and the corresponding evaluation code are publicly accessible at https://github.com/margitantal68/ hu-embeddings-hurte.

Sb6784d0ac1f6.title: Question Answering
attribution_passages: Textual Question Answering (QA) identifies the answer to a question in large collections of on-line documents. By providing a small set of exact answers to questions, QA takes a step closer to information retrieval rather than document retrieval. A QA system comprises three modules: a question-processing module, a document-processing module, and an answer extraction and formulation module. Questions may be asked about any topic, in contrast with Information Extraction (IE), which identifies textual information relevant only to a predefined set of events and entities. The natural language processing (NLP) techniques used in open-domain QA systems may range from simple lexical and semantic disambiguation of question stems to complex processing that combines syntactic and semantic features of the questions with pragmatic information derived from the context of candidate answers. This article reviews current research in integrating knowledge-based NLP methods with shallow processing techniques for QA.

S4e1798e4cc2c.title: Watermarking Fine-Tuning Datasets for Robust Provenance
attribution_passages: Large Language Models are often fine-tuned on proprietary corpora, motivating reliable provenance signals. A corpus-level watermark method is proposed for fine-tuning datasets that survives training and common text transformations. The method subtly biases synonym choices according to a secret key (PRF) and encodes a multi-bit payload with an error-correcting code, enabling keyed detection via a generalized likelihood ratio test with permutation-calibrated p-values. For short offline passages (~100 words), the channel is valid but statistically underpowered: the average density is ~0.0165, and the median p-value is close to 1.0. In generative tests with Mistral 7B across 12 configurations and 12,720 texts, 0.00% detection was observed at very high quality (~99.8%). As limited base cases, positive detection was reported for other setups: 8.9% (offline), 5.0% (Mistral 7B), and 3.0% (Llama2-13B). A permutation test (R = 5000), confidence intervals, and power analysis were added. Quality impact statements were refined, with “minimal impact” used instead of “imperceptible.” In this study, limitations and ethical use are discussed, and directions for stronger semantic channels and model-based detectors are outlined.

S087a91af5405.title: Revolutionizing Large Model Fine-Tuning: The Role of LoRA in Parameter-Efficient Adaptation
attribution_passages: Fine-tuning large-scale neural networks for specific tasks often requires significant computational power and memory, making it an expensive and resource-intensive process. To address this issue, Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) methods have been introduced, enabling adaptation with a reduced number of trainable parameters. Among these techniques, Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) has gained widespread recognition for its efficiency and ease of integration. This survey provides a thorough exploration of LoRA, covering its mathematical principles, implementation techniques, and real-world applications. By comparing LoRA to traditional full fine-tuning and other PEFT methods, we highlight its ability to maintain strong performance while significantly cutting down on computational overhead. Empirical evaluations across various NLP benchmarks further demonstrate its effectiveness in reducing memory consumption without sacrificing accuracy. Beyond its advantages, we also examine the challenges associated with LoRA, such as rank selection sensitivity, compatibility with different model architectures, and potential hardware optimizations. Additionally, we discuss promising future directions, including hybrid fine-tuning strategies, dynamic rank adjustment, and expansion into multi-modal learning. By enabling more efficient adaptation of complex models, LoRA represents a crucial advancement in scalable fine-tuning. This survey aims to serve as a valuable resource for researchers and practitioners looking to leverage LoRA for optimized model training across diverse applications.

Sa21497be345c.title: A Doctor's Guide to Foundation Models
Sa21497be345c.fulltext_snippet: The rapid advancement of artificial intelligence (AI) has led to the emergence of foundation models as powerful tools for various applications, including healthcare. These large-scale machine learning models, such as GPT and LLaMA have demonstrated potential for improving patient outcomes and transforming medical practice. However, healthcare professionals without a background in data science may find it challenging to understand and utilize these models effectively. This paper aims to provide an accessible introduction to foundation models for healthcare professionals, discussing their core concepts, relevant applications in healthcare, ethical considerations, challenges, and future directions. By offering a comprehensive overview of foundation models, I hope to foster a more informed and collaborative future between healthcare professionals and data scientists, ultimately driving better patient care and medical advancements.

draft.title: Open Curation Audit: Quantifying Data Provenance and Contamination Effects in Small Open Foundation Models for Scientific QA
draft.literature_gap: Open-science foundation-model efforts increasingly release weights and data, but controlled evidence is scarce on how open data-curation choices (deduplication, provenance filtering, synthetic augmentation) affect small open models in scientific question answering under academic compute budgets. The dated literature supplied here includes accessible overviews and open-science workshop context, but not empirical audits linking curation provenance to contamination-adjusted evaluation. This leaves a reproducibility gap: without contamination audits and data-provenance ablations, reported gains for open scientific FMs may reflect benchmark leakage or undocumented filtering rather than robust capability.
draft.hypothesis: At fixed small-model scale and compute, provenance-aware curation (deduplication plus source/provenance filtering) improves contamination-adjusted scientific QA accuracy of open foundation models more than raw or synthetic-only fine-tuning; apparent gains from uncurated data will shrink after n-gram and embedding-based contamination audits.
draft.method: Use three small open models (Pythia-410M, OLMo-1B, TinyLlama-1.1B) with LoRA fine-tuning on scientific instruction data under three conditions: (1) raw collected data, (2) deduplicated + provenance-filtered data, (3) synthetic-augmented data. Evaluate zero-shot and fine-tuned checkpoints on SciQ, PubMedQA, and a held-out 300-example expert-annotated scientific QA set. Run contamination audits using 13-gram overlap and embedding nearest-neighbor similarity against training data. Ablate deduplication alone, provenance filtering alone, and both. Use 3 random seeds per condition; report bootstrap 95% CIs over test items and seeds. Baselines: zero-shot open models and a limited proprietary API baseline on the same 300 held-out items.
draft.minimal_test: A 3 models x 3 data conditions x 3 seeds LoRA fine-tuning grid on ~10k scientific instruction examples, evaluated on 3 benchmarks plus contamination audits. Total training/eval within 200 A100-40GB GPU hours. Human annotation: 40 hours to validate 300 held-out items and audit 150 contamination-flagged pairs. Decisive comparison: curated-minus-raw accuracy difference before and after removing contaminated test items.
draft.decisive_metric: Contamination-adjusted accuracy difference (curated minus raw) with bootstrap 95% CI; secondary: contamination rate and F1. Success requires a positive curated-minus-raw difference whose CI excludes zero after contamination removal, and a reduction in apparent raw-data gains after audit.
draft.supporting_result: Curated models show a statistically significant contamination-adjusted accuracy gain of at least +2 points over raw-data models on the held-out set, with overlapping or smaller gains on public benchmarks; contamination audit removes at least 30% of the raw-data advantage, and provenance-only and dedup-only ablations show separable contributions.
draft.falsifying_result: No statistically significant curated-minus-raw difference after contamination adjustment (95% CI includes zero), or raw-data gains remain unchanged after removing contaminated items, or synthetic augmentation matches curated data without provenance benefits, indicating the hypothesis is false at this scale and budget.
draft.related_work[1]: Workshop on Open Science for Foundation Models (ICLR 2025 context): motivates open datasets, evaluation transparency, and replication.
draft.related_work[2]: 10.31219/osf.io/5zg3q: A Doctor's Guide to Foundation Models (2023) provides an accessible foundation-model overview but not a controlled curation audit.
draft.related_work[3]: 10.59350/jrhpp-kgz32: Open Bioinformatics Foundation event fellowship report (2022) illustrates open-science community practices but not FM evaluation.
draft.related_work[4]: 10.59350/6p8de-ant18: Open Knowledge Foundation visualization workshop note (2008) is historical open-science context, not technical evidence on FM curation.
draft.limitations: Small models and limited scientific domains may not transfer to larger FMs; the 300-example held-out set limits statistical power; contamination detection is imperfect; the proprietary API baseline is budget-limited; human annotation covers validation and audit but not full re-annotation; results are specific to LoRA fine-tuning and the selected open data sources.
draft.resource_plan: GPU: 4x A100 40GB, 200 GPU-hours over 8 weeks. Allocate ~120 h LoRA training (27 runs), ~50 h evaluation/contamination audits, ~30 h reruns and error bars. API: $200 for limited proprietary baseline on 300 held-out items and embedding-based similarity checks. Annotators: 40 h for 300-item validation and 150 flagged-pair audits. Calendar: weeks 1 data curation and provenance metadata; weeks 2-3 fine-tuning grid; week 4 public-benchmark evaluation; week 5 contamination audit and annotation; week 6 statistical analysis and ablations; weeks 7-8 write-up and release of code, prompts, audit scripts, and non-restricted artifacts. No pretraining from scratch; all experiments fit the academic budget.

draft.title: Free Error Bars: Calibrating Checkpoint-Based Variance Estimates Against Seed Variance for Open Foundation-Model Evaluation
draft.hypothesis: Almost every open foundation-model release publishes a long checkpoint trajectory, while almost no academic lab can afford the 5-10 full training runs needed to estimate seed variance of downstream benchmark scores. The central hypothesis is that late-to-mid training checkpoints, despite being highly correlated rather than independent, carry a *calibratable* amount of information about run-to-run variance: there exists a simple, stable mapping from variance measured across a checkpoint window (with essentially zero marginal training cost) to true seed-level variance. If such a mapping exists and its scaling behaviour is characterizable, every lab with one training run can attach honest error bars to its benchmark deltas, turning reproducibility from a budget problem into a calibration problem. The question is best answered in this setting because open checkpoint series (Pythia, OLMo, LLM360, and our own self-trained multi-seed grids) provide both the 'free' variation (checkpoints) and, in a few cases, the 'expensive' ground truth (multiple seeds) needed to fit and validate the calibration, and because small models at 30M-160M parameters can be trained at 8 seeds per grid inside a 200 GPU-hour budget.
draft.related_work: Bouthillier et al. (2021) model the benchmarking process and show that adding sources of variation improves estimator quality, but treat data sampling, initialization, and hyperparameters alike and assume multiple full runs are available; we instead ask whether a *free* and *structurally biased* source (checkpoints inside one run) can substitute for the expensive one after calibration. Henderson et al. (2018) and Agarwal et al. (2021) established that deep-RL comparisons need intervals and propose robust aggregates (IQM, performance profiles); that line assumes N independent runs and does not address the single-run academic regime we target. Madaan et al. (2024) measure seed variance in LLM evaluation benchmarks and recommend variance-aware reporting, but require 3-10 full pretraining runs per model, which is infeasible for open academic labs; crucially they do not test checkpoint-derived proxies and report that some variance-reduction tricks (IRT, item analysis) fail for smaller models, leaving the cost problem open. Melis et al. (2018) and Kaddour et al. (2023) show that conclusions flip under uncontrolled configuration changes and decayed-LR baselines, motivating our controlled multi-seed grids. Wang et al. (2025) show small *proxy models* mislead data-recipe decisions; we study a different axis (uncertainty of the score, not the ranking of recipes) and propose to correct rather than abandon cheap proxies. Polo et al. (2024, tinyBenchmarks) reduces cost by subsampling *items* via IRT; ours is orthogonal (variance across *runs*), and the two compose. Existing practice of reporting checkpoint-level standard deviations in open-model reports is, to our knowledge, never validated against seed variance - we show it is systematically anti-conservative by a measurable factor and provide the correction.
draft.approach: Foundation-model papers routinely draw conclusions from benchmark deltas obtained from a single training run, yet the variance induced by random seed, data order, and hardware non-determinism is rarely quantified, because replicating a pretraining run 5-10 times is beyond academic budgets. Meanwhile, open releases (Pythia, OLMo, LLM360) publish dozens of intermediate checkpoints per run, and authors informally use variation across these checkpoints as a stand-in for run-to-run variation - a practice that has never been validated and that is known to be anti-conservative, since nearby checkpoints are highly correlated. We propose to treat checkpoints as pseudo-seeds and to *calibrate* them. We train controlled multi-seed grids at two small scales (roughly 30M and 160M parameters, 8 seeds each) on a permissive corpus, saving dense checkpoint trajectories, and evaluate all runs and checkpoints on a battery of open benchmarks (LAMBADA, PIQA, ARC-easy, HellaSwag, WinoGrande, and a held-out MMLU subset). For every checkpoint window (last checkpoint, last 5 percent/10 percent/25 percent, decay phase only) we measure the variance inflation factor relative to true seed variance, the empirical coverage of nominal 95 percent confidence intervals for model means and for pairwise deltas, and how often checkpoint-based intervals correctly predict the sign of seed-level differences across 12 controlled interventions. We then fit a small predictor of the inflation factor from benchmark size, task format, and checkpoint window, and test whether the same factor transfers to publicly released checkpoint series. Finally we test a one-factor model in which most cross-benchmark noise is attributable to a scalar run-competence term, which would permit uncertainty propagation from a single cheap proxy. The output is an empirically calibrated, open-source recipe for honest error bars from one training run, directly serving the workshop's open-evaluation and reproducibility goals.
draft.validation:
Setup and budget. Two model scales (GPT-style decoder, ~30M and ~160M params) trained on a permissive small corpus (~1-2B tokens of SlimPajama/Dolma subset or TinyStories for the small scale), 8 seeds per scale, dense checkpoints (every ~2 percent of training) plus a fixed token budget; estimated 3 and 10 GPU-hours per run respectively, ~110 GPU-hours total including evaluation, well inside 200. Benchmark battery: LAMBADA, PIQA, ARC-easy, HellaSwag, WinoGrande, plus a fixed 1000-item MMLU subset, via lm-evaluation-harness; two scoring formats (log-likelihood MC and completion) to test task-format heterogeneity. Compute per-run bootstrap over items (1000 resamples) so item noise is separated from run noise.

E1 (Core calibration). For each (scale, task) compute (a) true seed variance of scores across 8 seeds using only final checkpoints, and (b) checkpoint pseudo-seed variance within each run for windows W in {final checkpoint only, last 2, last 5, last 10, last 25 percent, decay-phase-only}. Report the variance inflation factor VIF = Var_true / Var_checkpoint, with bootstrap CIs over tasks and seeds, and test the hypothesis VIF > 1 (anti-conservative checkpoint variance) via a sign test across task-scale pairs. Ablate: token-budget-matched vs step-matched checkpoint sampling; excluding the LR-decay phase.

E2 (CI coverage). Construct 95 percent CIs from checkpoint windows (bootstrap over checkpoints and items) for (i) the mean score of a model and (ii) the difference between two models; measure empirical coverage against the seed-level truth over all task-scale-window combinations and over the 12 intervention pairs. Compare to naive point estimates and to an equal-compute 2-3 seed baseline. Nominal 95 percent should be reached after applying the fitted VIF; report pre- and post-calibration coverage.

E3 (Decision fidelity). Build 12 cheap ablation arms on top of the grids (data mix A vs B, LR schedule, weight decay, dropout, tokenizer, sequence length), 4 seeds each, ~24 GPU-hours. For each arm pair, define ground truth as the sign and significance of the seed-level delta. Metrics: sign-agreement accuracy, false-positive rate of the uncalibrated checkpoint test, and Spearman rank correlation between checkpoint-based and seed-based effect sizes.

E4 (Predictor of VIF). Regress log VIF on log(number of benchmark items), task format (perplexity vs multiple-choice vs generation), checkpoint window width, model scale, and observed checkpoint-to-checkpoint score correlation; report cross-validated R^2 and whether a single task-agnostic default factor (e.g., a constant ~k) is within 25 percent of the fitted value. Ablate the number of checkpoints used to estimate the within-run variance to find the minimum practical window.

E5 (Transfer to public open families). Apply the calibrated recipe to publicly released checkpoint series with multiple seeds where available (Pythia suite, OLMo, LLM360 Amber/K2), evaluating a sparse checkpoint subset on the same battery with a fixed inference budget; measure whether the fitted VIF and the resulting interval widths are stable across families, and whether any family requires a scale-dependent correction. This is the key external-validity test.

E6 (One-factor analysis). Perform PCA/factor analysis on the runs x benchmarks matrix of final scores to measure how much variance a rank-1 'run competence' factor explains; if R^2 is high, test whether a single cheap proxy (perplexity on held-out in-distribution text at an early checkpoint) predicts the run's benchmark offset, enabling uncertainty propagation with one additional short run.

All experiments report mean +/- bootstrap CIs; paired tests (sign test / Wilcoxon) across task-scale pairs; ablations of checkpoint window, scoring format, and subset size; code, checkpoints, and per-item scores released openly.
draft.limitations: Scale: models of 30M-160M parameters may exhibit different variance structure than multi-billion models, so the calibrated factor may not extrapolate, and only two scales give a weak scaling trend; we mitigate by testing transfer on public larger checkpoint series (E5) and by reporting the factor as scale-conditional rather than universal. Checkpoint correlation: late checkpoints may be so similar, or their variation so dominated by LR-decay dynamics, that within-run variance is a poor proxy and VIF is unstable across seeds, in which case the central hypothesis fails - we treat that as an informative negative result but it reduces publishable impact. Public validation data: few open families release true multi-seed runs, so ground-truth calibration at large scale may rest on a small number of families. Small-corpus confound: training on a reduced corpus may not reproduce the benchmark-difficulty profile of large-scale pretraining, and several of our small benchmarks may be near floor for 30M models, compressing variance and distorting VIF; we screen tasks for dynamic range and report results per task. Statistical fragility: with 8 seeds and ~12 intervention pairs, effect-size estimates are noisy, so we rely on hierarchical/bootstrap CIs and pre-registered decision rules. Practicality gap: the recipe yields intervals correct in expectation but cannot detect a single unlucky run's outlier behaviour, and the inflation factor must be re-estimated as benchmarking practices change; we therefore also deliver a small open tool and a living calibration table rather than a single number. Finally, 200 GPU-hours leaves no room for failed runs; we fix seeds and configs up front and allocate a 20 percent contingency.

Research Background & Open Challenges:
# Workshop on World Models: Understanding, Modelling and Scaling

**Conference Context**: ICLR 2025 Workshop Call for Papers & Research Context

# Workshop on World Models: Understanding, Modelling and Scaling

## Workshop Scope

The concept of the "World Model" focuses on how intelligent agents can understand and model the external interactive worlds/environments to improve their decision-making and planning abilities. World models were initially focused on modelling low-level physical quantities and interactions by recurrent neural networks (RNNs). Over time, the "World Models" concept has expanded to real-world simulation (e.g. Sora and Genie) and the generation of complex, realistic, and high-dimensional environments.

This workshop explores classical World Modelling backbones for understanding and modelling the world, such as Transformers, RNNs, state-space models (SSMs), spatial-temporal modelling and causality analysis. Building from these foundational topics, the workshop will also discuss the broader and evolving concept of "World Models" for complex real-world prediction and simulation, like video/text generation and more specific applications like embodied AI, healthcare and sciences. This evolution highlights the growing complexity and capabilities of World Models. By bringing together leading researchers, the workshop will cover both classical and cutting-edge techniques, and discuss how World Models can be applied across a wide range of emerging applications.  Some of the fundamental questions and specific challenges that this workshop aims to address are:


- Understanding the World and Extracting Knowledge.

- World Model Training and Evaluation.

- Scaling World Models Predictions Across Language, Vision, and Control.

- World Models in General Domains: Embodied AI, Healthcare, Natural and Social Sciences, and Beyond.


The workshop covers the widest range of World Models topics, including understanding, modelling, as well as scaling with cutting-edge generative AI. We welcome submissions related to the construction, analysis and applications of world models, such as Model-Based Reinforcement Learning, Causality, Sequential Modelling, Simulation of the Environment, Diffusion Models, Video Generation, Foundation World Models, 2D to 3D, Robotics, and Embodied AI etc.


We also encourage submissions from the Natural Sciences (e.g., physics, chemistry, biology) and Social Sciences (e.g., pedagogy, virtual sociology simulation) related to world/environment construction in the science domain to offer attendees a more comprehensive perspective. In summary, topics of interest mainly include, but are not limited to:


- Understanding World Rules: Exploring how World Models capture environment dynamics, causal understanding, spatial-temporal patterns, model-based RL, and theoretical foundations for simulation and prediction. 

- World model training and evaluation: strengths, limitations, and challenges of current modelling architectures (e.g. Transformers, RNNs, and SSMs), training algorithms (autoregressive training, diffusion modelling, RL, and normalizing flow) and dataset construction. 

- Scaling World Models prediction and generation across language, vision, and control: Investigating how integrating visual, auditory, and textual data improves realism World Models.

- World Models in general domains: Exploring World Models in robotics, AI, healthcare, natural and social sciences, and beyond to improve prediction and decision-making. 

- Benchmark, Dataset, and Demonstration about World Models such as environment simulation.

S4ab1d26dc168.title: Balancing Accuracy and Speed: A Multi-Fidelity Ensemble Kalman Filter with a Machine Learning Surrogate Model
attribution_passages: Currently, more and more machine learning (ML) surrogates are being developed for computationally expensive physical models. In this work we investigate the use of a Multi-Fidelity Ensemble Kalman Filter (MF-EnKF) in which the low-fidelity model is such a machine learning surrogate model, instead of a traditional low-resolution or reduced-order model. The idea behind this is to use an ensemble of a few expensive full model runs, together with an ensemble of many cheap but less accurate ML model runs. In this way we hope to reach increased accuracy within the same computational budget. We investigate the performance by testing the approach on two common test problems, namely the Lorenz-2005 model and the Quasi-Geostrophic model. By keeping the original physical model in place, we obtain a higher accuracy than when we completely replace it by the ML model. Furthermore, the MF-EnKF reaches improved accuracy within the same computational budget. The ML surrogate has similar or improved accuracy compared to the low-resolution one, but it can provide a larger speed-up. Our method contributes to increasing the effective ensemble size in the EnKF, which improves the estimation of the initial condition and hence accuracy of the predictions in fields such as meteorology and oceanography.

S145a94dda3b0.title: COMPUTE-EFFICIENT SCALING OF LARGE SEQUENTIAL RECOMMENDATION MODELS UNDER DYNAMIC USER BEHAVIOR
attribution_passages: Transformer-based sequential recommenders are increasingly scaled up and retrained as interaction logs grow, yet user behavior drifts between retraining cycles, and repeated from-scratch training of large models consumes compute that rarely yields proportional accuracy. This paper studies how model scale, update strategy, and training compute interact under a streaming protocol in which a model trained on earlier blocks of a chronologically ordered log serves the next block. On MovieLens-1M and Amazon Grocery, widening a SASRec-style model from 6.6K to 397K non-embedding parameters raises training compute by 4.4-13.3x relative to width 32 without a consistent accuracy gain, and models that are not refreshed lose 36% and 82% of their NDCG@10, respectively. Building on these observations, we propose SPROUT, a compute-aware update framework that warm-starts each update from a recency-aware replay stream, expands capacity with an exactly function-preserving width-doubling operator for pre-LayerNorm Transformers, and accepts growth only when a paired validation test shows a gain larger than one standard error. Over four update cycles, SPROUT stays within 1.3% of the best periodic-retraining accuracy on MovieLens-1M with 44% less cumulative compute than the retrained small model and 93% less than the retrained large model, and it achieves the highest accuracy on Amazon Grocery, 5.0% above the best retraining baseline, with 47% less compute than retraining the large model. Its growth-free configuration offers the most economical operating point, reaching 99.1% and 102.1% of the retraining accuracy with 33% and 51% of its compute.

Sb061834ec4d7.title: Counterfactual Analysis for Web Service Optimization: Leveraging Causal Models to Predict Performance Under Hypothetical Interventions
attribution_passages: The increasing complexity of modern web service architectures necessitates sophisticated approaches to performance optimization that go beyond traditional correlation-based methods. This paper presents a comprehensive framework for counterfactual analysis in web service optimization, leveraging causal models to predict service performance under hypothetical interventions. We propose a novel methodology that integrates Structural Causal Models with Directed Acyclic Graphs to enable what-if analysis of web service systems. Our approach addresses the fundamental challenge of distinguishing causal relationships from spurious correlations in observational service monitoring data, thereby enabling more reliable predictions of intervention outcomes. The framework employs a five-stage pipeline encompassing data collection, monitoring, causality graph building, cause inference, and ranking to systematically identify performance bottlenecks and evaluate optimization strategies. We demonstrate how this methodology overcomes the limitations of traditional predictive models that fail to account for confounding variables and selection bias inherent in web service environments. Through systematic evaluation on Kubernetes-based microservice architectures, our approach reveals that causal-based counterfactual reasoning provides more accurate performance predictions compared to conventional machine learning techniques when evaluating system modifications. The results indicate that organizations can leverage this framework to make data-driven decisions about resource allocation, service configuration, and architectural changes with greater confidence in predicted outcomes.

Sae24b8c646fe.title: Lymph Node Evaluation in Robot‐Assisted Versus Video‐Assisted Thoracoscopic Esophagectomy for Esophageal Squamous Cell Carcinoma: A Propensity‐Matched Analysis
attribution_passages: Abstract Objective Radical lymph node dissection (LND) along the bilateral recurrent laryngeal nerve (RLN) is a surgically challenging procedure with a high rate of morbidity. Here, we assessed in a retrospective manner the adequacy of LND along the RLN performed with robot‐assisted thoracoscopic esophagectomy (RATE) versus video‐assisted thoracoscopic esophagectomy (VATE) in patients with esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (ESCC). Methods This was a single‐center, retrospective, propensity‐matched study. ESCC patients who underwent McKeown esophagectomy and bilateral RLN LND with a minimally invasive approach were divided into two groups according to the use of robot‐assisted surgery or not (RATE vs VATE, respectively). Using propensity score matching, 34 balanced matched pairs were identified. The number of dissected nodes as well as the rates of RLN palsy and perioperative complications served as the main outcome measures. Results No conversion to open thoracotomy occurred in either group. Intraoperative blood loss and the need of blood transfusions did not show significant intergroup differences. The mean number of dissected nodes was similar in the two study groups, the only exception being the left RLN area. Specifically, the mean number of nodes removed from this region was 5.32 in the RATE group and 3.38 in patients who received VATE ( p = 0.007). Notably, the RATE and VATE groups did not differ significantly with regard to rates of both RLN palsy (20.6 vs 29.4%, respectively, p = 0.401) and pulmonary complications (5.9 vs 17.6%, respectively, p = 0.259). Conclusions Compared with VATE, RATE resulted in a higher lymph node yield along the left RLN without increasing morbidity.

S1432f4dbac2d.title: FOCUS: object-centric world models for robotic manipulation
attribution_passages: Understanding the world in terms of objects and the possible interactions with them is an important cognitive ability. However, current world models adopted in reinforcement learning typically lack this structure and represent the world state in a global latent vector. To address this, we propose FOCUS, a model-based agent that learns an object-centric world model. This novel representation also enables the design of an object-centric exploration mechanism, which encourages the agent to interact with objects and discover useful interactions. We benchmark FOCUS in several robotic manipulation settings, where we found that our method can be used to improve manipulation skills. The object-centric world model leads to more accurate predictions of the objects in the scene and it enables more efficient learning. The object-centric exploration strategy fosters interactions with the objects in the environment, such as reaching, moving, and rotating them, and it allows fast adaptation of the agent to sparse reward reinforcement learning tasks. Using a Franka Emika robot arm, we also showcase how FOCUS proves useful in real-world applications. Website: focus-manipulation.github.io .

S36f6b536fe08.title: Learning visual appearance from language is mediated by causal intuitive theories
attribution_passages: What and how do people learn about visual appearance from language? We test the hypothesis that in the absence of sensory evidence, people born blind use abstract causal knowledge to infer object appearance. Congenitally blind (n=19) and sighted adults (n=59) reported how many colors two types of artifacts were likely to have: artifacts for which having many colors is intended to facilitate function (n=30, e.g., fairytale book, fruit candies), and artifacts for which colorfulness is irrelevant or distracting (n=30, e.g., instructional manual, painkillers). The number of colors estimated per object was highly correlated across groups. Blind and sighted people assigned more colors to artifacts for which colorfulness facilitates function and appealed to makers’ intentions in open-ended explanations. A text-only version of GPT-4 generated similar but non-identical colorfulness estimates compared to humans. Our findings suggest that people infer the appearance of unseen objects using causal ‘intuitive theories’ informed by linguistic evidence.

draft.title: Causal-Interventional Rollout Evaluation for Small-Scale Video World Models
draft.literature_gap: Video world models are increasingly judged by pixel-level generation quality (e.g., FVD, PSNR) and visual realism, while their ability to support counterfactual/interventional prediction of environment dynamics is less systematically measured. Prior work spans model-based RL world models (e.g., Dreamer-family latent dynamics), video generative models (e.g., Sora/Genie-style environments), object-centric representation learning (e.g., Slot Attention), and sequence backbones (Transformers, RNNs, SSMs), but there is little controlled evidence under fixed small-scale compute on whether architecture/objective choices improve interventional rollout accuracy beyond pixel fidelity. This leaves unclear whether scaling visual generation actually improves causal/physical rule capture or merely appearance.
draft.hypothesis: Under a fixed small-scale compute budget, video world models' accuracy on held-out counterfactual physical interventions is driven more by action-conditioned latent/object-centric bottlenecks and training objective than by pixel-generation fidelity; models matched on FVD can differ significantly in interventional state-rollout error.
draft.method: Build a procedurally generated 2D physical-dynamics video dataset with simulator ground-truth states: colored objects with mass, velocity, gravity, elastic collisions, and occlusion. Create compositional splits with held-out interventions (unseen mass ratios, initial velocities, collision pairings, and occlusion patterns). Train small models at matched parameter/compute budgets: (1) pixel-space autoregressive transformer on frame stacks; (2) action-conditioned latent state-space model (Dreamer-lite RSSM); (3) an ablation with object-centric slot bottleneck if time permits. All models see identical data and action/context lengths. Evaluate 20-step rollouts on held-out interventional test episodes. Extract object states from generated frames with a frozen color/shape detector validated against simulator states, and compute object-state MSE and physical-violation rate. Compare against pixel metrics (FVD/PSNR) and run 3 seeds per model with bootstrap 95% CIs. Ablations: action conditioning on/off, context length, and latent vs pixel bottleneck.
draft.minimal_test: Train the pixel transformer and latent RSSM at matched parameter count and GPU-hours on the synthetic dataset (3 seeds each, ~15 GPU-hours/run), then evaluate 20-step counterfactual rollouts on held-out interventions. Compute interventional object-state MSE, physical-violation rate, FVD, and PSNR. Use 3 seeds and bootstrap CIs; run a small human plausibility rating on 200 clips (40 annotator hours) as a secondary check.
draft.decisive_metric: Held-out interventional object-state rollout MSE (and physical-violation rate) with 95% bootstrap CIs across seeds; secondary metric is the correlation between FVD and interventional MSE across models and ablations.
draft.supporting_result: The action-conditioned latent/object-centric model achieves significantly lower interventional rollout MSE than the pixel transformer (non-overlapping 95% CIs or >20% relative reduction) despite similar FVD, and/or the across-model FVD-interventional-MSE correlation is weak (r<0.3), indicating pixel fidelity is not a sufficient proxy for causal/physical prediction.
draft.falsifying_result: FVD strongly predicts interventional rollout MSE across models and ablations (r>0.7), and after controlling for FVD there is no significant architecture/objective effect on interventional error, meaning pixel-generation quality is sufficient and the proposed gap is not empirically supported.
draft.related_work: Model-based RL world models (e.g., Dreamer/PlaNet latent dynamics), video-generation world simulators (e.g., Sora/Genie-style), object-centric representation learning (e.g., Slot Attention), sequence backbones for dynamics (Transformers, RNNs, SSMs), and physical-reasoning video benchmarks (e.g., Physion, CLEVRER, Something-Something). The proposal does not claim new citations beyond these known research lines.
draft.limitations: Synthetic 2D dynamics are lower-dimensional than real-world video and may not transfer to complex 3D scenes; models are deliberately small due to the 200 GPU-hour budget; object-state extraction from generated frames introduces measurement error; rollout horizons are short (20 steps); human evaluation is limited to 40 annotator hours; and only a few seeds are feasible, so CIs may be wide.
draft.resource_plan.gpu_hours_breakdown: Dataset/simulator and detector validation: 10 GPU-hours; main pixel transformer runs (3 seeds x 15h): 45; main latent RSSM runs (3 seeds x 15h): 45; object-centric/ablation runs: 40; action-conditioning and context-length ablations: 30; final evaluation and reruns: 20; buffer: 10.
draft.resource_plan.timeline: Weeks 1-2: simulator, dataset splits, state extractor validation. Weeks 3-5: main model training and ablations. Week 6: rollout evaluations and metric computation. Week 7: human plausibility ratings and statistical analysis. Week 8: write-up and release plan.
draft.resource_plan.api_usage: Reserved for optional LLM-assisted scenario-description generation and evaluation-prompt paraphrasing; capped at $200; no dependency on API for core results.
draft.resource_plan.annotator_usage: 20 hours rating physical plausibility of 200 generated clips; 20 hours validating a subset of automatic state extractions and violation labels against simulator ground truth.
draft.resource_plan.statistics: 3 seeds per main condition; bootstrap 95% CIs for MSE and violation rates; paired tests across held-out intervention episodes; report effect sizes and CIs rather than only p-values.
